topics.title: [Post-training][RLVR] Resolving Complex Closure Failures with Multi-Domain RLVR -- Snowball 67B A2B
topics.body:
# Jointly training mechanical closure skills with verified token-level feedback

## TL;DR

We built an evaluation to capture several mechanical closure failures, then built an online training loop to optimize these skills jointly: closing JSON objects, arrays and strings; closing nested structures in the right order; and completing tool-call delimiters, reasoning blocks and code fences. In this limited sense, this is multi-domain reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR): several format-specific verifiers supply signals to one shared training procedure. The actual objective combines token-level preference optimization with supervised loss on verified repairs.

The signal was strongly positive on several custom closure evaluations and moderately positive on BFCL-Parity, a fixed 123-task agentic cohort derived from the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, evaluated through the Pi agent. The released checkpoint improved BFCL-Parity from **30.76% to 36.04%**, a 5.28-percentage-point gain across six runs per model. Four of six non-tool closure families met the target of reducing syntax failures by at least 75%. Nested JSON and strings improved but missed that target. Some unfinished-content controls regressed.

The four-benchmark development comparison is complete. HumanEval+ improved, IFBench loose changed little, and MATH500 declined. Results from the full evaluation-policy sweep remain outstanding for this report; the development subset does not establish broader capability gains. The campaign has ended, and further training ideas below are proposals for a separate experiment.

Released artifacts:

- [Complete experiment archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Complex-Closure-RLVR-Snowball-67B-A2B-Artifacts): exact configurations, synthetic data, retained custom traces and audit records.
- Code: [Marin #10078](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10078) and [MarinSkyRL #991](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/991). These publication branches include later fixes and unrun follow-ups; the immutable runtime pins below identify the released run.

- [Continuation + Tool Retention model, immutable revision](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Continuation-Tool-Retention/tree/9a9213cbb6c9ae80368bf9002176ae96546932f6): run `2026.10.13.18`, checkpoint `global_step_2`.
- [Structure-Closure-BFCL native-v6 evaluation and scorer](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Structure-Closure-BFCL-v6/tree/44353e76f5a9a911a6e1473e0fe0d802ad852bca).
- [Initializer](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Protocol-FTPO/tree/d761ea0a94500c2aa24aa4cd71b5a149d962e5c8).
- Earlier work: [single-failure intervention #10043](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043) and [follow-up scope #10061](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061).

## Benchmark design

The benchmark uses BFCL-derived synthetic completion tasks with known reference content. Training and validation use disjoint source tasks. The validation cohort contains 14,784 cases derived from 704 source tasks; these are related constructed cases, not 14,784 independent source problems.

An exact task-ID audit found zero overlap among the 2,814 training source tasks, 704 custom-validation tasks and 123 BFCL-Parity tasks. The [split audit](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Complex-Closure-RLVR-Snowball-67B-A2B-Artifacts/blob/d62ce3939fa900b2dad9344428bb7ac16917127a/artifacts/release-review/task-split-audit.json) publishes the identities and original split hash. This excludes direct task-ID overlap in this campaign; it does not establish absence of semantic similarity or prior pretraining exposure.

Each task supplies a partial structure. Format-specific parsers check whether the generated continuation closes it legally. The evaluation also checks content preservation and trailing output. These measures matter separately: a model can produce valid JSON after dropping a required value, or close a code fence and then continue generating unwanted text.

The cohort covers JSON objects, arrays, nested JSON, escaped strings, tool delimiters, reasoning delimiters and code fences. It also contains controls where the correct action is to continue unfinished content and examples that test retention of the earlier repeated-tool-opener repair. A closing token is not automatically a correct answer.

We revised prompt construction during development. An early compact tool-call representation gave misleadingly low closure scores. With the model's native tool serialization, the initializer and all reported candidates close 704/704 tool cases correctly. That corrected subset has a ceiling and supplies no evidence of improved native tool closure. Compact-format protocol retention remains a separate diagnostic.

The public native-v6 benchmark contains the evaluation cases, construction notes, scorer and usage instructions. The non-tool closure results below come from the campaign's compact-format development evaluations; the native tool column comes from the corrected native-v6 audit. This is a development benchmark used to guide iteration, not an untouched final test set. Synthetic training rows and retained custom rollout traces are published separately in the experiment artifact archive.

## Training protocol

We start from the previously released Grug-67B-A2B protocol-FTPO model. The mixed training cohort supplies multiple closure families to one learner, with a small parser for each format. Online generations determine which local mistakes receive supervision.

The shared mechanism uses three kinds of feedback:

1. **Wrong token at a verified boundary:** final-token preference optimization (FTPO) raises valid alternative-token logits relative to the rejected token under the same sampled history. Verification constrains which alternatives are admitted.
2. **Missing closing sequence:** masked supervised loss trains on the verified repair sequence, which can span multiple tokens.
3. **Premature closure:** when a known reference proves that content remains unfinished, a verified continuation preference favors continuing that content. The procedure does not invent missing argument values.

The final recipe also lets retention examples without a detected repeated opener receive the shared closure or continuation supervision. This is a joint local-repair objective; it does not apply whole-trajectory DPO or treat every token in a failed response as equally bad.

The released run used two optimizer updates with batch size 64, AdamW learning rate `4e-6`, zero weight decay and gradient clipping at `0.5`. It used 40 H100s: 32 policy GPUs and eight inference GPUs. Training sampling used temperature 1, top-p 1 and up to 32 candidate next-token log-probabilities per position. FTPO used margin 2, `min_p=0.01`, at most 20 chosen alternative tokens at the selected position and repair-SFT weight 1. The exact configuration below contains the remaining loss coefficients and parallelism settings. Custom validation ran before training and after each update; the reported Pi capability results came from separate checkpoint-linked evaluations.

Reproducibility references:

- [Exact .18 run configuration](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Complex-Closure-RLVR-Snowball-67B-A2B-Artifacts/blob/d62ce3939fa900b2dad9344428bb7ac16917127a/artifacts/configs/closure-smoke-2026.10.13.18.json).
- [Marin launch revision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7f5c03692c73c95d8d6fdd4ed4cbbd8381ef8671).
- [MarinSkyRL runtime](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/822d200ed79ec2b6fc0cbdb2b56122eb7110cef1).
- [Shared Marin runtime libraries](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c0b0d23f774c7b3bea1d6bb84e010921ff434ea9).
- [Complete local experiment tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10079#issuecomment-6147640457), including failed and superseded runs; [human-readable candidate summary](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10079#issuecomment-6147639678).

The configuration filename retains the word `smoke`: this two-update full-pipeline run produced the released checkpoint. It did not consume the entire available training cohort. Later prepared data and selector changes were not trained and are excluded from the released runtime.

The Marin launch revision supplies the experiment recipe and dataset-construction modules. The separately pinned Marin runtime supplies RolloutEngine's parsers, verifiers and local-target selection inside the isolated learner environment. MarinSkyRL supplies the training integration and loss. The archive README provides tested rescoring commands at a pinned publication revision; those commands replay saved generations without rerunning training.

## Closure results

All scores below are percentages. Each closure-family score has 704 cases. The base row is the tracker's initializer evaluation; the 75% failure-reduction decision uses the selected run's own pre-training evaluation, whose sampled counts differ slightly.

| Measure | Base | Released checkpoint |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| JSON objects: syntax closed | 50.14 | 100.00 |
| JSON arrays: syntax closed | 00.00 | 94.03 |
| Nested JSON: syntax closed | 42.33 | 76.99 |
| JSON strings: syntax closed | 38.92 | 49.15 |
| Native-format tool calls: syntax closed | 100.00 | 100.00 |
| Reasoning blocks: syntax closed | 29.83 | 100.00 |
| Code fences: syntax closed | 18.32 | 83.24 |
| Compact tool-protocol retention | 35.09 | 99.86 |

Compact retention requires a first call with valid JSON, a nonempty string `name`, object-valued `arguments`, a properly placed closing delimiter and no immediate repeated opener. It does not measure successful execution or task-answer correctness.

Objects, arrays, reasoning blocks and code fences passed the 75% syntax-failure-reduction target. Nested JSON achieved 59.80% failure reduction and strings 16.74%, relative to the run's own pre-training evaluation. The campaign therefore did not meet its original all-family objective.

For that decision, the .18 pre-training → final correct counts are: objects 357→704, arrays 0→662, nested JSON 301→542, strings 274→346, reasoning 189→704 and fences 129→586, each out of 704. Failure reduction is `1 - (704 - final_correct)/(704 - initial_correct)`.

Syntax gains also conceal remaining errors. Only 114/704 string cases both close and preserve the reference content, versus 346/704 that close syntactically. Premature closures increased from 364 to 446 on unfinished-string controls, 49 to 121 on array controls, and 2 to 39 on code-fence controls, each out of 704. Joint training improved multiple closure skills, but did not yet balance closing and continuing reliably.

## Capability transfer

These are six-repeat means on fixed cohorts. Each repeat contains 123 BFCL-Parity tasks, 500 MATH500 problems, 164 HumanEval+ problems or 300 IFBench prompts. All repeats have complete scored coverage. Repeats measure run variation; they do not create additional independent tasks.

The three recipes are separate runs from the same initializer, not sequential training stages. We selected .18 because it restored compact tool-protocol retention while retaining broad closure gains. Subsequent evaluation found the highest BFCL-Parity mean among the three candidates. It does not dominate the alternatives: .13 is stronger on nested JSON, and .16 on strings and HumanEval+.

| Candidate | BFCL-Parity @ Pi | MATH500 | HumanEval+ | IFBench loose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Base model | 30.76 | 92.33 | 66.87 | 27.00 |
| Closure repair (.13, step 2) | 31.57 | 91.40 | 73.88 | 25.50 |
| Closure + continuation (.16, step 2) | 34.42 | 91.63 | 76.42 | 27.44 |
| Continuation + tool retention (.18, step 2; released) | 36.04 | 91.17 | 72.56 | 27.17 |

BFCL uses Harbor with Pi 0.87.0 and Daytona evaluation containers: chat-template transport, model-default thinking, 32,768-token context and an 8,192-token per-turn output limit. Setup, agent and verifier deadlines are 360, 1,800 and 300 seconds. Earlier native shell-agent BFCL diagnostics do not satisfy this policy and are excluded from these comparisons.

The other three benchmarks use Evalchemy revision `97fffeb7df60875c5a5c14ec215dd4e7683102c5`, zero-shot prompts, seed 42 and a 73,664-token evaluator limit. Thinking is enabled for MATH500 and disabled for HumanEval+ and IFBench. IFBench uses loose **prompt-level** accuracy under the campaign policy; this should not be confused with loose instruction-level accuracy or the full release policy's strict metric.

The released checkpoint's MATH500 decline is 1.17 percentage points from the unrounded means, or 2.19 baseline sample standard deviations. A one-sided run-level permutation test gives p=0.0184 before correction and p=0.0736 after Holm correction across four benchmarks. It does not trigger the predeclared harm flag, which requires both a decline above two baseline standard deviations and adjusted p≤0.05. That result does not prove equivalence or absence of harm. The runs retain seed 42 in their configurations; they are repeated serving executions, not an independently seeded statistical design.

The BFCL and HumanEval+ gains support further study of transfer. This experiment does not isolate which loss component caused them. The complete policy sweep is needed before making a broader claim; no missing sweep scores are treated as zero or as evidence of no effect.

The permutation p-values are an exploratory execution-level diagnostic under the [predeclared comparison rule](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Complex-Closure-RLVR-Snowball-67B-A2B-Artifacts/blob/d62ce3939fa900b2dad9344428bb7ac16917127a/artifacts/configs/capability-comparison-v2.json). Same-seed serving repeats do not establish the test's exchangeability assumptions, so these p-values should not be read as independent-task evidence of general capability preservation.

## Follow-up experiments

- **Improve continuation-target coverage.** A replay of 69 retained continuation-control traces found one eligible premature-close position. These traces were retained preferentially for failures, so this is not a full-batch rate. A prepared training-only variant moves prefixes closer to the known reference completion while preserving validation bytes. Test that change alone and measure eligible targets and actual learner use before scaling it.
- **Separate selector and batch-size interventions.** A local selector extension identifies the first token that departs from the known reference during a verified premature closing sequence. It passed focused tests but found no additional eligible positions on those .18 traces. Larger batches and the selector extension remain untested training proposals, not explanations for the current gains.
- **Target escape state and nested closing order.** Keep content-preservation and continuation controls alongside syntax scores. Rewarding an early close would improve one metric while damaging the intended behavior.
- **Build a harder native-tool diagnostic.** Find genuine initializer errors under the required model serialization. The current 100% baseline cannot measure improvement.
- **Complete the broader evaluation comparison.** Report all policy-required results and uncertainty, including negative results. Revisit the MATH500 decline with fresh matched runs before claiming that the intervention preserves general capabilities.

## Evidence and reproducibility limits

The model export is public under OpenMDW 1.1. All 48 publication file identities, including 39 weight shards, passed readback verification. The model card records the recipe, capability scores, limitations and custom Grug runtime requirement.

Supporting public records: [final capability audit](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Complex-Closure-RLVR-Snowball-67B-A2B-Artifacts/blob/d62ce3939fa900b2dad9344428bb7ac16917127a/artifacts/trials/candidate18-final-capability-audit.json), [four-benchmark comparison](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Complex-Closure-RLVR-Snowball-67B-A2B-Artifacts/blob/d62ce3939fa900b2dad9344428bb7ac16917127a/artifacts/trials/candidate18-four-capability-pi-comparison.json), [closure counts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Complex-Closure-RLVR-Snowball-67B-A2B-Artifacts/blob/d62ce3939fa900b2dad9344428bb7ac16917127a/artifacts/trials/candidate18-selection-and-step2-summary.json), [continuation regressions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Complex-Closure-RLVR-Snowball-67B-A2B-Artifacts/blob/d62ce3939fa900b2dad9344428bb7ac16917127a/artifacts/trials/trial18-control-regressions.json), and [native-format audit](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Complex-Closure-RLVR-Snowball-67B-A2B-Artifacts/blob/d62ce3939fa900b2dad9344428bb7ac16917127a/artifacts/trials/native-tools-candidate18-2026.10.13.3-case-id-audit.json). The closure-selection record is a historical snapshot from before capability and native evaluations finished; the final audits supersede its pending-status fields.

The public artifact archive includes exact configurations, synthetic training and validation data, custom evaluation generations, retained training trajectories and the audits cited here. Raw general-capability benchmark prompts and traces are withheld pending per-source redistribution review. Intermediate model weights and optimizer states are not in that archive. Exact public replay of every capability result, or bitwise reproduction of the training run, is therefore not possible from this release alone. Historical private S3 locations are provenance identifiers, not public access routes.

The broader release policy includes additional math, knowledge, code, long-context and agentic evaluations such as GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench. Their results for this checkpoint are not reported here. This report does not assert that the outstanding full sweep has been launched or completed.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the build step DAG and its memo store
topics.body:
Add the author and build stages of Taskforge as `stage30_author` and `stage40_build`. An author writes async steps decorated with `@rl_env_build_step`, which takes a step's inputs from its parameters after the context, and a final step decorated with `@rl_env_build_sink`, which reads its inputs the same way and refuses any return annotation other than `TaskSpec`. `rl_env_build_program(*steps, sink=...)` orders the steps by Kahn's algorithm, breaking ties by declaration order and running the sink last. It refuses duplicate names, unknown inputs, cycles, a step taking the sink as an input, and a step whose output reaches neither another step nor the sink, since that output would never enter the task. A step receives an `RLEnvBuildContext` (item id, model, sampling policy) and then its inputs by name, where a parameter called `proposal` receives the caller's proposal, an opaque JSON value at this point in the stack. `static_author` hands back a hand-written program as an author. `run_program` returns the sink's `TaskSpec`, and `run_build` writes it to `draft/task.json` with an `ItemBuildProvenance` in `draft/provenance.json`, which lists every step's stored memo beside that build's hit or miss status for it. The status belongs to the build and stays out of the stored memo, which the store writes only on a miss.

Each step's output is memoized under a key of `SDK_VERSION`, the sha256 of the step's own source, the content digest of each declared input, and a model digest over the model id and the sampling policy. Because inputs enter the key by content, a step that reruns with an identical output leaves its consumers cached. A helper read from outside a step body is not in the key, so changing one needs a declared input or an `SDK_VERSION` bump. Item ids belong to the caller and are only checked for file safety.

The store is a hand-rolled memo of about 60 lines over rigging's `StoragePath` and `atomic_rename`, holding content-addressed JSON blobs and per-item memos under a local path or an object-store URL. joblib keys on function identity and clears a function's whole cache when its code changes, so it reuses nothing across program revisions, and Marin's `StepSpec` hashes no code and costs a status file and a distributed lock per step. Its `load` and `store` take a caller-built key, and `memoized` is the one call the runner and a driver use, so a driver can memoize a helper against the same store with a key it builds. `memoized(store, name, key, output_type, compute)` loads under such a key and on a miss awaits `compute` and stores the result, and `run_program` calls it for every step.

Stage packages are numbered by tens in pipeline order (proposal 10, triage 20, author 30, build 40), and `tests/test_imports.py` fails when a stage imports a higher-numbered one.

The design comes from draft #9993. Later PRs bring back the proposal package, the ledger, the author's programs written by the language model, the validate and review stages, and the stage coordinator.

topics.title: [iris] GC can turn successful Kubernetes tasks into worker failures
topics.body:
Iris GC measures its one-hour retention period from pod creation. A long-running pod is therefore eligible for deletion as soon as it finishes, before the controller records its outcome. After three reconciliation polls find no pod, Iris reports `WORKER_FAILED` and retries the successful task.

Reproduced locally: the same eleven-hour-old pod reports `WORKER_FAILED` when GC runs first and `SUCCEEDED` when reconciliation runs first.

Could the one-hour retention period start at pod completion instead? Using the latest container `finishedAt` would include the output uploader, which can finish after the task itself. This would give the controller an hour to observe the final outcome before GC deletes the pod, regardless of how long the task ran.

[Investigation](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/702).

<details>
<summary>Local reproducer</summary>

Reproduce:

1. Save the script below as `/tmp/iris_completion_gc_race.py`.
2. From the Marin repository root, run `uv run python /tmp/iris_completion_gc_race.py`.

Tested at `f2a9447295c4172a515915d81512f0394fc23f0a`. It uses the real Kubernetes backend with an in-memory Kubernetes service; no cluster is needed.

```python
from copy import deepcopy
from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta

from iris.cluster.backends.k8s.tasks import K8sTaskProvider, _pod_name, _task_hash
from iris.cluster.config import TaskOutputPolicy
from iris.cluster.controller.task_state import RunningTaskEntry
from iris.cluster.platforms.k8s.fake import InMemoryK8sService
from iris.cluster.platforms.k8s.types import K8sResource
from iris.cluster.types import JobName
from iris.rpc import job_pb2
from iris.testing.k8s import k8s_backend_descriptor, make_batch, pod_config


def run_case(age_hours, gc_first):
    k8s = InMemoryK8sService(namespace="iris")
    provider = K8sTaskProvider(
        descriptor=k8s_backend_descriptor(), kubectl=k8s,
        pods=pod_config(task_outputs=TaskOutputPolicy()), cluster_scan_interval=0.0,
    )
    entry = RunningTaskEntry(
        task_id=JobName.from_wire("/diagnostic/completion/0"), attempt_id=0,
        attempt_uid="0123456789abcdef", state=job_pb2.TASK_STATE_RUNNING,
    )
    name = _pod_name(entry.task_id, entry.attempt_id, entry.attempt_uid)
    now = datetime.now(UTC)
    pod = {
        "kind": "Pod", "metadata": {
            "name": name,
            "creationTimestamp": (now - timedelta(hours=age_hours)).isoformat(),
            "labels": {
                "iris.managed": "true", "iris.runtime": "iris-kubernetes",
                "iris.task_hash": _task_hash(entry.task_id.to_wire()), "iris.attempt_id": "0",
            },
        },
        "status": {"phase": "Running", "containerStatuses": [
            {"name": "task", "state": {"terminated": {
                "exitCode": 0, "reason": "Completed", "finishedAt": now.isoformat(),
            }}},
            {"name": "output-uploader", "state": {"running": {}}},
        ]},
    }
    batch = make_batch(running_tasks=[entry])
    try:
        k8s.seed_resource(K8sResource.PODS, name, deepcopy(pod))
        first = provider.sync(batch)[0]
        assert first.new_state == job_pb2.TASK_STATE_RUNNING
        assert first.status_message == "finalizing task outputs"
        # The uploader finishes between reconciliation cycles.
        pod["status"]["phase"] = "Succeeded"
        pod["status"]["containerStatuses"][1]["state"] = {
            "terminated": {"exitCode": 0, "reason": "Completed", "finishedAt": now.isoformat()}
        }
        k8s.seed_resource(K8sResource.PODS, name, deepcopy(pod))
        if gc_first:
            provider.collect_garbage()
        updates = []
        for _ in range(3):
            update = provider.sync(batch)[0]
            updates.append(update)
            if update.new_state != job_pb2.TASK_STATE_RUNNING:
                break
        states = [job_pb2.TaskState.Name(update.new_state) for update in updates]
        if not gc_first:
            provider.collect_garbage()
        deleted = k8s.get_json(K8sResource.PODS, name) is None
        expected = job_pb2.TASK_STATE_WORKER_FAILED if gc_first and age_hours > 1 else job_pb2.TASK_STATE_SUCCEEDED
        assert updates[-1].new_state == expected
        print({"age_hours": age_hours, "gc_first": gc_first, "states": states,
               "deleted": deleted, "error": updates[-1].error})
    finally:
        provider.close()


run_case(11, True)
run_case(11, False)
run_case(0.02, True)
```

Expected: all three cases report `SUCCEEDED`. Currently, the old-pod/GC-first case reports `RUNNING`, `RUNNING`, then `WORKER_FAILED` with `PodDeleted: pod was deleted while the attempt was active`.

</details>

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`_gc_terminal_resources()` ages terminal pods from `creationTimestamp`, so an old task pod becomes eligible as soon as its output uploader finishes. If GC deletes it before `_poll_pods()` sees the terminal phase, three missing-pod observations turn the successful attempt into `WORKER_FAILED`.

**Relevant code**
- [`tasks.py#L2940-L2965`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L2940-L2965) — terminal pod age and deletion selection
- [`tasks.py#L3050-L3115`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L3050-L3115) — terminal lookup and missing-pod failure
- [`test_provider.py#L1118-L1185`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/tests/cluster/backends/k8s/test_provider.py#L1118-L1185) — current GC retention coverage

# Proposed Fix

GC selects a terminal pod by creation age, deletes it, then reconciliation cannot read its final state and reports `WORKER_FAILED`. Start terminal-pod retention at the latest container `finishedAt` (including the output uploader), for both ordinary and gang pods; use creation time only when Kubernetes supplies no container finish time. Add a regression that runs GC before reconciliation of an old, newly completed pod.

🤖 Merged in #10083. Terminal-pod retention starts at the latest regular or init-container finish time, including the output uploader. The successful-task and stage-workdir failure regressions pass; 2,887 safe Iris tests, all-files lint, and branch review pass on current main.

topics.title: [iris] Retain terminal pods from their finish time
topics.body:
Retain terminal Kubernetes pods from the latest init or regular container `finishedAt`, including the output uploader. Ordinary pods keep their one-hour window and gang pods keep their one-minute window. GC previously measured both from pod creation, so an old task could lose its pod immediately after completion or an init-container failure, before reconciliation recorded its outcome.

Pods without a container finish timestamp continue to use creation time for cleanup. GC-before-reconciliation regressions preserve success and staging failure outcomes; 2,887 Iris tests pass on current `main`.

Fixes #10082

topics.title: [grug] Add a separate QK multiplier for hero global layers
topics.body:
Add `GrugModelConfig.qk_mult_long_scale`, an extra Q multiplier on the hero's global layers (every `global_every`-th layer and the last: full causal, RoPE disabled). Global layers multiply Q by `qk_mult` and then by `qk_mult_long_scale`. Local sliding-window layers use `qk_mult` alone. The field, its 1.0 default, and the order of the two multiplies match `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/model.py` and the pinned vLLM GrugMoE backend, which reads the same config key. A scale of 1.0 adds no op, so the live hero and existing checkpoints trace unchanged. Otherwise the layer scan's traced `is_global` flag selects the scale with `jnp.where`, which keeps one scan body for all layers and covers both RoPE paths.

Q and K are RMS-normalized, so the Q multiplier sets the softmax temperature. Moving the hero from 4K to 16K context leaves the local layers' 2048-token window unchanged, so the YaRN-style mscale, 1.3 × (0.1·ln(s) + 1), applies only to the global layers. Trial arms can raise the global scale and hold the local layers at 1.3: a long scale of 1.1386 gives 1.48, and 1.2964 gives 1.68.

The HF config export writes `qk_mult_long_scale`. A config without the key loads with 1.0. `launch_diagnostics.py` takes `--qk-mult-long-scale`. `launch_scaling_ladder.py` and `trigger_hero.sh` are unchanged because #9689 also changes them; the production flag will follow after it lands.

Part of #9615

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the stage coordinator over the build DAG
topics.body:
Add `stage_coordinator`, which runs an item through triage, author, build, validate and review with the stage functions a caller passes in `StageFunctions`. Each stage returns an event with an exit, and a transition table gives the next stage. The item's state is a fold over its events (`derive_state`). `ItemBudget` bounds build revisions and validation retries, and the coordinator spends them when it records `AUTHOR_FAILED`, `BUILD_FAILED` or `DECIDED`. A build error from the program's own code, `BuildFailure` or any other exception, costs a revision. `BuildInfrastructureFailure` (the build host failed: a sandbox did not start, an image did not pull, a pod died), `ModelUnavailable` and `OSError` (a storage fault, a missing blob or memo) are failures the author cannot fix. Those fail the item in place at the build stage, and the next `run_item` builds the same program again with its revisions unspent. When the author raises `StructuredOutputError` because its structured reply stayed invalid after the repair turn, as when the output limit cut it, the coordinator records `AUTHOR_FAILED`, spends a revision from the same budget, and asks the author again with `Revision(AUTHOR_FAILURE, ...)`.

The `OPENED` event records the digests of the proposal and the budget, and the coordinator's model digest, the model part of every step key. A relaunch with any of them changed raises `ValueError`, so every build of an item runs under one model. The author returns an `AuthoredProgram`, the program with the Python source it came from. The coordinator writes the source to `rounds/<n>/authored/<k>/program.py`, beside the manifest `program.json`, with `k` the item's build failures so far. The build stage loads the program from that file with `StageFunctions.load_program`, so a sampling model author is called once per revision. Each author call gets its own directory, so a process killed after re-authoring leaves the program of the saved `AUTHORED` event in place for the relaunch. `stage30_author/loader.py` is the plain loader; the author PR replaces it with a restricted one (allowed imports, safe builtins). A program defined in Python, as `static_author` returns, has no source, and for it the build stage asks the author again. In both cases a build whose program digest differs from the `AUTHORED` event raises.

Events stay in an `ItemEventLog` (in memory here) while the item runs. When the item reaches a terminal, `run_item` saves the log through an `ItemEventStore`. `JsonEventStore` writes `items/<item_id>/events.json` after every other file of the item, and the next `run_item` with an empty log restores the log from it. An accepted or rejected item then returns without running a stage or writing a byte. When the store lacks the final log, as after a failed save retried with the same in-memory log, `run_item` saves it before returning. An abandoned item re-enters validation with its retries reset, and a failed item resumes at the stage that raised, with the step store under `<root>/store` serving the build steps already run. A process killed mid-item restarts from the last saved terminal, or from triage. The ledger PR adds a file-backed log saving each event on append.

The triage verdict and the review `Decision` types come along as the vocabulary the machine records; `Retry.cause` and `Modify.findings` are strings until validate returns. Validate and review are caller functions: the coordinator writes the validate summary to `validation.json` and passes review the JSON read back from it. `stage_coordinator` sits above the numbered stages and may import every one of them, and nothing imports it. The capability experiment runs a catalog entry through the coordinator with its example program as a sink-only build, to an accepted task.

The design is cut from draft #9993, and the base is #10081.

topics.title: [task-curation] Add Dockerfile toolchain fragments and a Lean grader image
topics.body:
An `Environment` can name a checked-in, self-contained Dockerfile fragment that installs a toolchain the package lock cannot provide. A fragment forces placement in a built image, its bytes enter the environment identity, the build refuses an untracked fragment, and the generated Dockerfile runs its lines after the apt step and before the lock sync so toolchain layers stay cached across lock changes. A fragment may use only `ARG`, `ENV` and `RUN`; the declaration refuses `FROM`, `USER`, `WORKDIR`, `SHELL`, `COPY`, `ADD`, `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD`, which would replace the base, break the generated package steps or change the grader container. The existing build CLI pushes the image to the public iris-task package and records its digest, so pinning follows from the identity.

The environment artifact record now carries the identity, the built image digest, and the lock digest and `data` the worker runtime reads back from the record beside the lock. The copies of `apt`, the Python version, the base image, the fragment digest and the pushed tag are gone; the identity already hashes them and nothing read them.

`LEAN_GRADER_PACKAGES` uses the fragment to add elan, Lean leanprover/lean4 v4.12.0 and Mathlib v4.12.0 (commit 809c3fb3) with prebuilt oleans at `/lean4/my_project`, the layout the NeMo Skills sandbox uses, so the vendored Lean feedback parser finds diagnostics at the path it expects. `LocalLeanSandbox` compiles a proof with `lake env lean` in that project and answers with the NeMo Skills server's `lean4` response fields. The Nemotron Ultra Lean grader can then run inside the network-denied grader sandbox instead of calling an in-cluster sandbox service. This PR adds the image and the sandbox class only; the Lean converter and controls land in #10077.

The image built locally in 109 s for the Lean and Mathlib layer (2.39 GB; 3.8 GB total). With networking disabled and as uid 65534, a Mathlib `simp` proof completes in 4 s warm and 38 s cold, a bad tactic fails with the diagnostic at the project path, and a `sorry` proof completes with the warning the status parser maps to `has_sorry`. The cold time exceeds the vendored scorer's default 30 s timeout, so the converter needs a larger timeout. The Lean and Mathlib pins match every NeMo Skills sandbox build since October 2024; the private sandbox image MarinSkyRL pins by digest does not record its revision, so the pin is not confirmed against that exact image. No artifact for the environment has been built or pushed yet.

topics.title: [iris] gVisor sandbox pods fail to start on cw-us-east-02a H100 nodes
topics.body:
On cw-us-east-02a, sandbox jobs are scheduled onto `gd-8xh100ib-i128` GPU nodes, which carry `node.coreweave.cloud/gvisor=true`, and never start. These are `CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX` jobs, not the legacy `GVISOR` profile #9855 keeps temporarily; the Kubernetes backend gives both profiles `runtimeClassName: gvisor`. The kubelet retries pod sandbox creation every 10-15 s with:

```
Failed to create pod sandbox: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to start sandbox "<id>": failed to create containerd task: failed to create shim task: OCI runtime create failed: creating container: cannot create sandbox: cannot read client sync file: waiting for sandbox to start: EOF
```

The pod stays in `ContainerCreating` until the caller gives up. On 2026-10-13, a Taskforge queue job on 02a lost all 4 of its build machines: each sat in `ContainerCreating` until shellbox's 600 s scheduling timeout. I read node and events for one of them, which is where the error above comes from; the earlier pods' events had already expired. The machine image was the public `docker.io/library/python@sha256:a6e34c598f2467ed0e9a8d349809fcd8b5c603269512df273a0bb1784edc11b1` (python:3.12-slim). The same sandbox spec and image start on cw-rno2a, where gVisor sandboxes were measured at 512 concurrent with no failures, so the run moved there.

Of the 36 nodes labelled gVisor-capable on 02a, 32 are H100 nodes. Only 4 are CPU nodes: 3 in Iris pool `cpu-genoa`, plus 1 with no pool label. Sandbox jobs request CPU and memory only, so nothing keeps them off the GPU nodes. #9696 covers an earlier 02a failure in which leaked `runsc` sandboxes exhausted node cgroups; that may be related, but I have not checked cgroup counts on the affected node.

Expected: a sandbox job on 02a starts on a node where `runsc` works.

Done when either the H100 nodes no longer advertise gVisor or `runsc` starts sandboxes on them, and 02a has enough CPU gVisor capacity for sandbox workloads (a Taskforge queue runs up to a few hundred concurrent sandboxes).

The same error has recurred on 02a since 2026-10-06 ([incident 631](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/631)). Every failing node recorded there (g83d142, g73b892, g856b8a, g82d828) and this one (g8247ba) is a `gd-8xh100ib-i128` node.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Iris maps both `CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX` and legacy `GVISOR` to RuntimeClass `gvisor`, with no profile-specific node selector; the CoreWeave-managed RuntimeClass selects any node labeled `node.coreweave.cloud/gvisor=true`. That permits the reported H100 placement but does not explain the `runsc` startup EOF. [Incident 631](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/631) reproduced the EOF with public and base images on 02a while the same probes started on cw-rno2a, so an image pull or longer scheduling wait is unlikely to fix it. The live NodePools report 4 CPU and 32 H100 nodes; this session cannot read individual nodes or the ClusterQueue because its Kubernetes role forbids those requests.

**Relevant code**
- [`tasks.py#L1068-L1078`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a030a9df36cf7d095650ed7561d68812ea0ef4a/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L1068-L1078) — RuntimeClass and node selector.
- [`kueue_manifests.py#L96-L100`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a030a9df36cf7d095650ed7561d68812ea0ef4a/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/kueue_manifests.py#L96-L100) — one flavor spans CPU and GPU pools.
- [`cw-us-east-02a.yaml#L176-L217`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a030a9df36cf7d095650ed7561d68812ea0ef4a/lib/iris/config/cw-us-east-02a.yaml#L176-L217) — four CPU and 32 H100 nodes.

# Proposed Fix

1. With node-read access, compare a failing H100 node with a CPU node, including a bounded `gvisor` startup probe on the CPU node. Record their gVisor labels, taints, `runsc` and containerd versions/configuration, kubelet and runtime errors, and cgroup counts. Check whether the cgroup exhaustion from [#9696](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9696) recurred; the current EOF alone does not establish that cause.
2. Repair the H100 `runsc` setup and prove a sandbox starts there, or remove the gVisor label at its CoreWeave-owned source so RuntimeClass cannot select those nodes. Check the fourth CPU node's label and runtime before making it eligible. Keep any Iris placement change in a separate PR only if node labels cannot express the verified runtime capability.
3. Compare the allocatable CPU and memory on healthy gVisor nodes, Kueue quota, and existing load with the actual Taskforge per-pod requests at its peak concurrency of a few hundred. Increase healthy CPU capacity or fix H100 runtime if the four CPU nodes cannot admit that load.
4. Run one public-image sandbox canary, then a bounded Taskforge-scale batch on 02a. Require all admitted pods to reach Running within the 600 s scheduling budget, no `FailedCreatePodSandBox` EOF events, and stable shim/cgroup counts after teardown. Record the node and quota measurements in this issue before declaring the incident fixed.

topics.title: [taskforge] Fail a length-cut structured reply without a repair
topics.body:
complete_structured now raises StructuredOutputError as soon as a reply ends with finish_reason length, carrying the completions so far, and keeps the repair loop for every other validation failure.
A repair request replays the whole cut reply as the assistant turn, so on a live run a reply cut at the 131k output limit made a repair prompt of about 175k tokens, which overflowed the 262k context window with a context_overflow 400.
The retry with max_tokens lowered to about 100k could not finish either, since the repaired reply runs under the same output limit and the repair only spends a full prompt.
The capability-driven task generator already catches StructuredOutputError and records the failure on the item, so its behavior is unchanged apart from the skipped repair request.

complete_structured now appends schema_instruction(output_type) as the final user turn of every request and repair, a plain-text line per field with its type and description, because the chat template renders nothing from response_format and the model never saw the field names or descriptions.
On a live run of 27 author calls, 16 needed a repair, and in every sampled first reply the source field held a short label while the program sat only in the reasoning, so each repair cost a second 40k to 100k-token reasoning pass and was the main path to the 131k output cut.

topics.title: [taskforge] State field bounds in the structured-output instruction
topics.body:
`schema_instruction` now states each field's JSON-schema constraints in words after its type, covering length and item-count bounds, numeric bounds, enum and const values, and patterns, as in `notes (string, at most 1000 characters, required)`, with item bounds on lists prefixed by `each`.
The server's grammar already enforced these bounds without the instruction stating them, so on a live run with a `max_length=1000` field the model drafted 1,100 to 1,400 characters and 16 of 19 replies stopped at exactly 1,000 where the grammar closed the string mid-word.
After the cut, the model wrote a stub into the next field or emitted whitespace between JSON members until max_tokens, and one reply held 131,072 tokens of whitespace.
The instruction also renders models nested at any depth, indenting each level under its field with the nested model's docstring as the first line, and writes a model that recurs inside itself as one line such as `Section (same fields as above)`, so a constraint stated on a field of a model inside a list now reaches the prompt without the caller repeating it.

topics.title: [haliax] Run the tile-map ragged_dot kernels on NVIDIA GPUs
topics.body:
Hopper (sm_90) and data-center Blackwell (sm_100 and sm_103) GPUs now run the Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM behind `ragged_dot` with the tile-map kernels from #10009, which AMD Instinct GPUs already use. Until now they ran the group-grid kernels, which launch a full row grid for every expert. Other NVIDIA GPUs, such as A100 and consumer Blackwell (sm_120), keep the group-grid kernels: the tuned configs need about 192 KiB of shared memory per block in bf16, more than those GPUs allow. Block configs were swept on H100 and GB200 at the June (G=32, K and N of 1280-2560) and Mixtral-like (G=8, 4096x14336) expert shapes. On H100, drhs (the weight gradient) uses 128x128x32 blocks below 2048 rows per expert; with the 128x256x64 blocks it uses above that, it was 4-8% slower than group-grid at 512 rows per expert.

Per call in bf16, against group-grid, at M from 16384 to 196608 rows with balanced and Zipf-skewed routing:

| GPU | Tile-map faster | Speedup |
|---|---|---|
| GB200 | 54 of 54 cases | 1.03-2.47x |
| H100 | 49 of 54 cases | 1.04-2.50x |

The other 5 H100 cases are drhs at 512 and 1024 rows per expert, at 0.98-1.00x.

On one 8xH100 node, an 8-layer June model (batch 64, 8-way expert parallelism, full recompute) took 0.817 s per step with tile-map and 0.848-0.849 s in three group-grid runs, a 3.9% throughput gain, with the same loss after 20 steps.

`lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py --kernel-families group_grid tile_map` reproduces the balanced per-call timings.

topics.title: [grug] Hero vibe-check samples pre-switch checkpoints with the current model config
topics.body:
The hero completions sampler stamps every discovered checkpoint with the current `HERO_MODEL_CONFIG`, so after the 16K context switch (#9615) a rebuilt or re-released sample store would sample checkpoints from before step 257553 with `qk_mult` 1.48 instead of the 1.3 they trained with. Nothing flags the mismatch, because `model` is excluded from `sample_id`.

Requests already in the store are safe: `SampleStore.save_request` writes a request only once, and the stored requests for steps 246000, 252000, and 257553 record `qk_mult` 1.3 and `max_seq_len` 4096. The risk appears only when `spec.release` is bumped (the documented backfill knob) or the store root changes.

`sampling_model()` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ops/vibe_check/config.py` should choose the model per checkpoint. `hero_checkpoint_paths` already reads each ancestor run's W&B config and could carry its `model` along; alternatively the context history could record `qk_mult` per phase.

Found in the independent review of the 16K deploy PR.

topics.title: [taskcompendium] Start the grading machine in the grader's workspace again
topics.body:
The grading machine now starts in the grader's workspace unless its environment specifies a `working_directory`. This restores the behavior before #10021 when the environment names no directory and preserves an explicit directory when it does.

Since #10021, every script-graded task has failed while creating its grading machine on Iris. `_grade_staged` previously passed `workdir=grading.workspace`; the move to `prepare_machine_spec` dropped that argument. When the grader environment names no directory, `prepare_machine_spec` retains the spec's workdir, which is empty for an image machine because `rolloutengine._machine_spec` leaves it empty. Docker interprets an empty workdir as the image's `WORKDIR`, so laptop grading continued to work. Iris instead runs `mkdir -p ""` and fails:

```
RuntimeError: Failed to create Iris workdir : mkdir: cannot create directory ''
```

The Taskforge ladder dry run on cw-rno2a hit this failure in every grader sandbox. Solver and control machines were unaffected because `draft.requirements` names `/workspace`.

A test checks the spec passed to the factory with and without an explicit `working_directory`; the grader-workspace case fails on main. The ShellSim-backed taskcompendium suite passed locally. The bubblewrap-backed tests require Linux, and CI runs the full suite.

topics.title: [task-curation] Declare grader requirements, files and env
topics.body:
An `Environment` declares what a grader environment wants, and the build resolves it:

- `requirements`: exact `name==version` pins or `name @ https://...` URLs naming a commit. The build compiles them with `uv pip compile --generate-hashes --exclude-newer <date>` and stores the lock in the artifact; the cutoff date is a constant in the build module and part of the identity, so every build of an identity resolves the same transitive packages. `grader.in` and `grader.lock` are deleted; the pins live in `datasets/environments.py` as per-scorer tuples, and the four previously unpinned entries take the versions the lock had resolved.
- `files`: absolute guest paths, each receiving a member of an https archive pinned by URL and SHA-256. The build downloads, verifies and extracts the member into the build context. A built image gets `COPY files/ /`; the artifact stores `files.tar` and `environment.json` (paths, archive digest, env) for the worker. A path under a host system directory, which bubblewrap binds read-only, or inside another placed path is rejected at declaration.
- `env`: variables for the grader in both placements, rendered as `ENV` lines in the image and set on the worker sandbox.
- `apt`, `image` and `dockerfile` are unchanged.

The NLTK-only `data` slot is gone. `GRADER_PACKAGES` places the English `punkt_tab` tokenizer from a pinned `nltk_data` archive at `/srv/nltk_data/tokenizers/punkt_tab/english` with `NLTK_DATA=/srv/nltk_data`. `wordnet` had no consumer and is dropped. The Punkt models carry no license in `nltk_data`, so the tables are fetched at build time rather than checked in.

The worker runtime downloads the lock and hashes it itself instead of reading a digest from the artifact record, and reads `environment.json` and `files.tar` beside the lock when present; the lock and archive digests both enter the cached environment's identity. `taskcompendium.runtime.local` loses `LockEnvironment`, the `.artifact.json` reader and the NLTK downloader. The artifact record keeps only the identity and the built image digest.

shellbox's `HostImage` gains `mounts`, host files or directories shown read-only at another guest path with a plain `--ro-bind`. The local backend treats its read-only directories as mounts at their own paths and refuses a guest path inside a system directory, inside another mount, or as the workdir; uploads to a mounted path are rejected. QUICK mode records the lock URL the environment's artifact would have under the active artifact prefix.

Placement does not change: the base grader and compiler environments run in bubblewrap on the Zephyr worker, and Lean runs in its built image. The first `python -m experiments.post_training.task_curation.images --all` build verifies the `punkt_tab` archive digest against the live download.

topics.title: [datakit] Shuffle MinHash LSH buckets as uint64 keys
topics.body:
Shuffle MinHash LSH buckets through the connected-components group_by as
Python ints instead of decimal strings. `_emit_bucket_records` casts each
batch's `buckets` column to `list<uint64>` with pyarrow and yields the ints;
`CCInput.bucket` and the CC reducer and combiner annotations become `int`. The
bucket is only a routing key for that group_by. CC never writes it to its link
or node files, so nothing persisted changes.

`fuzzy_minhash.py` is untouched: on-disk MinHash attrs stay `list<string>`,
`MINHASH_ATTR_DATA_VERSION` stays 3 and `FUZZY_DUPS_ATTR_DATA_VERSION` is
unchanged. No step hash, output path or hero-manifest entry moves, and the
final fuzzy-dup output is identical to main. String-encoded and `list<uint64>`
attrs canonicalize to the same int key, so mixed sources still link. Main
already had that property through `str(b)`; the cast keeps it with int keys. Bucket values that do not parse as uint64
now raise `ArrowInvalid` instead of becoming a key that never matches.

This is phase 1. Writing `list<uint64>` attrs on disk, with the matching
`MINHASH_ATTR_DATA_VERSION` bump, is deferred until the planned MinHash rerun,
since it invalidates cached attrs.

Measured on 1,046,080 arXiv chunks (about 3 KB each, 4.02 GB raw, 50,000
injected near-duplicates; 27,198,080 bucket records at 26 bands) under the
local client with eight subprocess workers on a 16-core, 62 GB machine.
Medians of 3 interleaved runs per arm; ranges shown where wall times are close:

| | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bucket scatter on disk | 1,640.9 MB | 1,577.0 MB (-3.9%) |
| shuffle payload + key | 3,584.6 MB | 2,950.9 MB (-17.7%) |
| bucket map peak RSS | 3,403 MiB | 3,166 MiB (-7.0%) |
| bucket reduce peak RSS | 2,241 MiB | 2,087 MiB (-6.9%) |
| bucket map CPU, all shards | 377.4 s | 339.2 s (-10.1%) |
| bucket map wall | 52.1 s (49.8-53.1) | 47.2 s (47.1-50.6) |
| bucket reduce wall | 42.3 s | 41.8 s |
| fuzzy stage wall | 210.5 s (204.5-211.5) | 204.1 s (199.0-210.6) |

Scatter bytes are deterministic and RSS spread is a few MiB. zstd hides most
of the 55.9% smaller msgpack key on disk. Bucket reduce, CC and whole-stage
wall times are within spread, so the gain is less shuffle data and lower
bucket-stage memory, not end-to-end speed. A third arm with `list<uint64>`
attrs on disk produced byte-identical shuffle output to this PR and saved
24.2% of attr parquet bytes, which is the case for phase 2.

Tests: `test_connected_components_extreme_uint64_buckets_link` runs CC under
the local client with buckets 0, 2\*\*63-1, 2\*\*63 and 2\*\*64-1, and
`test_fuzzy_dups_links_sources_across_bucket_types` links a string source
with a `large_string` or `uint64` source at 2\*\*63+5 and 2\*\*64-1. String-label
fixtures in `test_fuzzy.py` become decimal strings; the on-disk
`list<string>` and `v3` assertions are kept. Both new test files also pass
against main. The dedup, hero-data and reference-pipeline-hashing suites pass.

topics.title: [grug] Fix intermittent ring EP MoE test deadlock on MI300X
topics.body:
On GPU, the forward and gradient jits in `test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available` now pass the compiler option `xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES`, so each device runs one collective at a time. Only the test changes.

On 8x MI300X, the ring-backend cases `[all_valid-ring]` and `[padded-ring]` hung until the pytest timeout in 10 of 52 runs. The hang happened on both cluster nodes and on main before #9860 added `ring_gather_combine`. The ring forward launches its psum-scatter over the expert axis (a 2-device RCCL communicator) asynchronously on a second stream. The drop-count psum over all 8 devices does not depend on it, so it runs on the compute stream while the psum-scatter is in flight. In the backward, the weight-gradient psum over the data axis (4 devices) overlaps the same psum-scatter. Which of the two collectives a rank starts first can differ between ranks and runs. In hung runs, rocgdb showed one RCCL kernel running on every GPU and work pending on a second hardware queue, consistent with each rank waiting for peers that are in the other collective. NCCL documents that operations on different communicators can deadlock when ranks issue them in different orders ([Using multiple NCCL communicators concurrently](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/usage/communicators.html#using-multiple-nccl-communicators-concurrently)).

With the fix, both cases passed 24 of 24 runs, and RCCL logs showed each device launching all of its collectives on one stream. The same flag set through `XLA_FLAGS` on unmodified main also passed 24 of 24.

Production MoE paths still use async collectives, so MI300X training could hit the same overlap. We have not seen this hang in training or measured what synchronous collectives would cost there. `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py` already forces synchronous collectives for the ragged all-to-all EP transport, where overlapping collectives hung or gave run-to-run different gradients on GB200.

topics.title: [shellbox] Keep a ShellSim machine open after a command outruns its timeout
topics.body:
The ShellSim backend closed the machine whenever one command exceeded its `command.timeout`, because the simulator's interpreter thread cannot be interrupted, and every later call then raised `Machine is closed`. In the Taskforge adversary trials that meant one slow computation by the agent lost the rest of its session: 58 trials since this morning ended as unclassified and were retried to abandonment. Inside the simulation `sleep` costs no wall time, but CPU work does, and the wall clock does not advance, so both a heavy computation and a clock-based loop reach the timeout.

The machine now stays open. The timed-out command keeps simulating on its thread, and the next operation on the machine, a command, an upload or a download, waits for it under the lock before using the simulation, so two operations never run on the one-threaded simulator at once. The caller still gets `TIMED_OUT` at the timeout, and the machine is usable again as soon as the slow command ends. A command that never ends leaves the machine as unusable as before, now by each later call timing out instead of a closed error.

One test runs a simulated shell loop past a short timeout and then an `echo` on the same machine. It fails on main with `Machine is closed` and passes here; no other outcome in the shellbox suite changes.

topics.title: [iris] Sandbox exec through the cw-rno2a controller saturates at ~2,000 live sandboxes
topics.body:
Shellbox's Iris backend runs every command in a sandbox, including the base64 file transfers that upload grader files, as an `ExecInContainer` RPC through the controller (`lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/iris/machine.py:92-115`; it already retries when the controller sheds an exec because its pool is full). On cw-rno2a on 2026-10-14, a Taskforge queue with about 2,150 live gVisor sandboxes (8 coordinator jobs, `/muchanem/gen1000-s*r`) saturated that path. Between 08:52 and 09:42 UTC its validation trials recorded these ungraded causes:

| Cause | Count |
|---|---|
| solver `grader_timeout` | 699 |
| solver `tool_execution` | 562 |
| control `grader_timeout` | 397 |
| build/grader-step `RolloutInterrupted` (machine start) | ~245 |
| `machine_start_timeout` | 44 |

The sandbox pods themselves were Running. An earlier read-only diagnosis of the same controller (04:30 UTC, ~1,700 sandboxes) found the controller creates pending sandbox pods only once per control tick, that the tick had grown from ~30 s to 80–160 s, and that the tick shares the controller process with all shellbox exec traffic (128 exec threads) and 64 RPC handler threads. Slow-RPC logs showed `ListTasks` at ~10.8 s and `LaunchJob` at ~12.9 s. Kubernetes, Kueue and node capacity were not the limit: a gVisor pod runs ~6 s after creation, and the cluster holds ~4,800 sandboxes at these requests.

That diagnosis also found that sandbox child jobs of a killed coordinator kept running. 52 tasks under cancelled `/muchanem/gen1000-s*n` coordinators still showed Running hours later, and their pods had to be cancelled one job at a time.

Expected: a sandbox command's latency does not grow with the number of live sandboxes on the cluster, and cancelling a coordinator ends its sandbox children.

Done when exec traffic no longer shares the controller's critical path with the control tick (an exec path that bypasses the controller, or an exec pool sized separately from the tick), and cancelling a job tears down its sandbox children.

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

Shellbox sends every command, including each 64 KiB upload chunk, through the controller's `ExecInContainer` RPC. [#9828](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9828) gave exec a separate 128-thread pool, but each call still looks up the attempt in the controller database and opens a Kubernetes exec websocket from that process; [today's read-contention record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/726) does not establish how much exec contributes to the shared read-pool delay. Iris already cancels descendants present in its transaction, while child admission checks the parent's state before the insert transaction; a racing launch could pass that check and insert a child after cancellation, but the 52 reported survivors need submission and parent-finish timestamps to confirm this mechanism. Open [#9844](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9844) addresses retries after machine close, not controller isolation.

**Relevant code**
- [`machine.py#L96-L148`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/73b28f52809c07d93ba62df625ad298f2796dd35/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/iris/machine.py#L96-L148) — exec and chunked upload.
- [`dashboard.py#L225-L260`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/73b28f52809c07d93ba62df625ad298f2796dd35/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/dashboard.py#L225-L260) — dedicated in-process exec pool.
- [`attempts.py#L236-L263`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/73b28f52809c07d93ba62df625ad298f2796dd35/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/attempts.py#L236-L263) — task lookup and exec dispatch.
- [`jobs.py#L661-L695`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/73b28f52809c07d93ba62df625ad298f2796dd35/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/jobs.py#L661-L695) — parent check before insertion.
- [`batches.py#L326-L363`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/73b28f52809c07d93ba62df625ad298f2796dd35/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/batches.py#L326-L363) — cancellation of present descendants.

# Proposed Fix

## Challenges

Moving exec work out of the controller must preserve owner authorization, attempt identity, command timeouts and the sandbox network boundary from [#9816](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9816). The existing pool protects handler threads but still shares the controller process and database read connections.

## Design

1. First inspect a small sample of the reported orphaned children: compare each child's `submitted_at_ms` with its parent's `finished_at_ms`, and check job state and cancellation events. Capture controller tick duration, read-pool wait, exec admission/queue, and RPC latency at a fixed sandbox count and command rate. If children existed before cancellation, trace the reconcile-to-pod teardown path before changing admission.
2. For Kubernetes sandboxes, move command execution to a separately deployed Iris exec gateway with Kubernetes `pods/exec` permission and bounded concurrency. A new controller `ResolveExecTarget(task_id)` call checks ownership once per running attempt and returns a short-lived, attempt-bound capability containing the pod UID and gateway address. The gateway verifies the capability, live pod UID and absence of a deletion timestamp before each command, then returns the existing exit code/stdout/stderr/error contract. Shellbox refreshes the target on attempt change or capability expiry; ordinary commands and file chunks no longer open controller RPCs or DB reads. Keep the worker-daemon exec route for non-Kubernetes backends.
3. In the child insert transaction, reject a child when its parent is terminal. This makes the parent-state check serialize with cancellation and closes the read-then-insert gap. Keep the existing recursive cancellation for children already admitted. If step 1 shows pre-existing children survived, fix that teardown path as a separate part of this issue.

## Testing

Add tests for cancellation before child launch, both transaction orderings of concurrent launch/cancel, and recursive cancellation of existing children. Exercise gateway authorization, expired and wrong-attempt capabilities, pod UID changes, timeouts, and full-pool shedding. On a dev Kubernetes cluster, verify Shellbox upload, command and grader paths while an owner can exec only into its own task. Compare controller tick and RPC latency and exec success at the same command mix near 2,150 live sandboxes before canarying cw-rno2a; include child teardown after coordinator cancellation.

## Costs / Risks

The gateway adds a deployment and Kubernetes exec credentials. Its concurrency limit must shed load before it overloads the Kubernetes API, and its capability must never be available inside the untrusted sandbox. A gateway outage would fail sandbox commands, so deploy and validate it before switching Shellbox traffic.

## Open Questions

- Were the 52 children submitted after parent termination, or did already-admitted children survive cancellation?
- What exec command rate and tail-latency target should the cw-rno2a canary sustain at about 2,150 sandboxes?

topics.title: [levanter] Repair DPO exports and explicit-mesh sharding
topics.body:
Full-model DPO on current main has three handling gaps. First, the HF export cadence is wrong: the separate-reference export hook fires on the legacy step counter, so exports land on the wrong updates and the final update can be missed or saved twice. This registers the hook on completed optimizer updates and makes the forced final save idempotent, with the interval-final naming semantics documented.

Second, the export path cannot produce serving-ready DPO artifacts: no dtype control, no tokenizer revision pinning, an always-Auto CPU mesh that breaks explicit-mesh Snowball and MoE models, and reference-code copying that breaks on URL-like checkpoints while risking trained-weight overwrite. This adds export_dtype (bfloat16 halves artifact size), name@revision tokenizers, explicit CPU meshes for explicit-mesh models, and URL-aware code copying with unconditional weight protection; the DPO save path exports only the policy subtree since the reference copy is frozen scaffolding.

Third, explicit-mesh sharding is dropped by framework and model reshapes, breaking context-parallel training, and the jagged store returns stale slices for repeated row-0 batches. This threads sharding through each reshape (including the one-line Haliax companion the grad-accum fix depends on) and fixes the row-0 offsets.

Validation is numerical parity on explicit meshes, byte-exact export round-trips, a no-double-write cadence tripwire, and row-0 regression tests: 101 passed with 1 device-gated skip, plus both 8-device Snowball tests.

Part of #10040.

topics.title: [rl] Support separate reference roles and remote artifact steps
topics.body:
SkyRL role planning on current main cannot express a separate reference footprint: colocation is hardcoded, capacity accounting ignores reference GPUs, backend YAML checks duplicate topology concerns, and a Megatron forward/train microbatch mismatch allocates GPUs before failing. This promotes policy/reference colocation to validated topology fields with footprint and capacity checks, removes the superseded YAML checks, rejects microbatch mismatch before submission, and updates every role-plan call site plus the SkyRL lock so the isolated launcher resolves on all platforms.

Remote artifact steps are broken in the lazy framework: a RemoteCallable is not directly callable for local runs, the lowered spec drops remote metadata, and Iris submissions double-write the step record. This unwraps the callable for local execution, preserves remote-ness in the spec, and skips the redundant record write on the submit path.

The RL coordinator also lacks the dedicated Daytona keys, so rollout and eval workloads cannot use separate credentials. This forwards DAYTONA_RL_API_KEY and DAYTONA_EVAL_API_KEY alongside the existing key.

One known gap: the Iris double-write guard has no direct test yet.

Part of #10040.

topics.title: [taskcompendium] Tell a failed grading preparation from a failed grader
topics.body:
Grading preparation failures now have a distinct `STAGING` kind. Previously, failures while preparing the verifier machine, unpacking or removing the staged archive, creating the workspace, or creating reward-file directories were recorded as `EXECUTION` or `TIMEOUT`, like failures in the grader command. Only the message distinguished them. A verifier deadline that expired before the grader command ran was also reported as a grader timeout, leaving callers without a typed way to separate task failures from host failures. In a Taskforge generation run with a saturated cluster controller, host-caused grading failures of this kind consumed 235 of 279 program revisions, including 269 deadline expiries during staging commands.

The runtime now uses `GradingFailure.STAGING` for its preparation commands. Commands chosen by the task author, the grader command, environment setup commands, and collect commands retain `EXECUTION` and `TIMEOUT`. Reward-file preparation moves from the script grader's run into staging. `grade_in_sandbox` sets `GradingProgress` to `STAGING` when it starts and to `GRADER` when the grader command starts. The rollout engine's verifier deadline covers both phases: an expiry before the grader command is `STAGING` with "Verifier deadline expired while preparing the verifier machine"; an expiry during the grader command remains `TIMEOUT` with its existing message. Sessions grading without the sandbox path retain the `GRADER` phase and their existing behavior.

The archive-removal failure test now expects `STAGING`. A runtime test observes `STAGING` for all five preparation commands and `GRADER` for the grader command and reward read. A rollout test stalls the verifier machine during unpacking and during the grader command, checking the failure kind and message for each deadline.

Taskforge's validation classifier and build-time grading will map `STAGING` to a host cause instead of a task cause in a separate change after this lands.

---

topics.title: Spec-Driven Large-Scale Pretraining Data Curation from Common Crawl
topics.body:
## Description

The current pipelines for transforming web scrape data to training data for LLMs are multi-stage and a somewhat specifically engineered [[1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794)] [[2](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.840/)].  We hypothesize that LLMs may do a better job at converting raw web data into useful tokens for pre-training or mid-training, especially on more challenging to parse contents like latex, tables, math, etc. [[3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06786)].

Preliminary testing has been positive for getting better quality extraction from LLMs rather than heuristic rules ([writeup here](https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4)) however this is way too expensive to run at the full web scale.  Our 8b LLM curator is predicted to take 42 years even on the generous compute we do have.

That is why we are currently experimenting with more efficient distilled pipelines from our 8b model.  The lifecycle would thus be: **Write spec for curation** -> **Run with LLM on subset of internet** -> **Distill into faster pipeline** -> **Run at webscale**.  We also noticed that a lot of decent data OUTSIDE of math/code/science is getting discarded by current pipelines.  Our new spec ([See below](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/2351#issuecomment-5074349445)) keeps way more data, and we are making the bet that data mixing/data selection will be a better fit than data filtering for deciding how to weight data for training.  This way we preserve web content that may be decent quality but not beneficial to math/code/science benchmark scores.


### Definition of Done

Two main deliverables with more additional artifacts.

1. **A scientific paper on our spec driven curation methodology and philosophy**: Preliminary drafts are [already completed](https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4), but a more polished version for ICLR is in progress.
2. **A 30T+ token dataset of more diverse common crawl data (extracted better)**: Using our distilled pipeline and new design philosophy (optimize data for coverage NOT "quality") we plan to re-run extraction on common crawl and build a production ready data pool for marin with removal of copywritten content.  With any additional time we will also incorporate [safety pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16980) practices into the dataset.

Why do TPU and GPU differ? RoPE bug in vllm-tpu version :( Our TPU inference stack (vLLM + Google's `tpu-inference`) has two ways to run a model: a JAX re-implementation of each architecture (the default for dense Qwen3, Qwen2, Llama) and a path that runs vLLM's PyTorch model definition through torchax. The JAX Qwen3 implementation reads the model's RoPE settings from the Hugging Face config like this: ```python self.rope_scaling = getattr(config, "rope_scaling", None) ... if rope_scaling: # truthy dict -> apply Llama-3 long-context scaling timescale = apply_rope_scaling(timescale, rope_scaling) ``` With transformers 4.x, a model that uses no RoPE scaling (Qwen3's `config.json` says `"rope_scaling": null`) returned `None` here, and nothing happened. transformers 5 changed the API: `config.rope_scaling` is now an alias of `rope_parameters` and returns `{"rope_type": "default", "rope_theta": 1000000}`. That dict is truthy, so the JAX port started applying `apply_rope_scaling`, which never checks `rope_type` and uses hard-coded Llama-3 defaults (scale 8, cutoffs at 2k and 8k tokens). Result: 37 of Qwen3's 64 RoPE frequency bands were rewritten, the lowest divided by 8. topics.title: Experiment: Add instruction-following format PPL coverage
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tracks instruction-following and formatting PPL coverage under #5819 without using IFBench/IFEval prompts as regular tracking data. The research pass found that Marin already has the needed scoring and bundle infrastructure, including supervised target-only loss, and the main missing piece is a generated registry of constraint-family slices. The current recommendation is a deterministic, in-repo template-generated bundle covering JSON emission, tabular output, exact-count bullets, constrained rewrites, field preservation, negative constraints, sort/filter tasks, and refusal formats. Implementation is waiting on maintainer choices about source strategy, family list, default bundle registration, and target size.

### Helpful links
- Parent: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5819
- Research and proposed approach: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5824#issuecomment-4483266849
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Part of #5819. Add instruction-following and formatting validation coverage without using exact IFBench prompts or other held-out benchmark items.

Current format probes cover delimiter/numeric/structured surfaces, but the core suite needs natural-language instructions with constraints: rewrite, count, filter, sort, transform, emit JSON/table, follow style constraints, preserve fields, and obey negative constraints.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Create generated or mined train/validation slices by constraint family, scored with supervised target-only loss where possible. The eval should move smoothly before e19/e20 flops and catch regressions in instruction adherence and output formatting without requiring full judge-based generation.

Potential slices: prompt -> JSON object, prompt -> TSV/CSV row, prompt -> bullet list with exact count, prompt -> transformed string/table, prompt -> constrained rewrite, and prompt -> refusal/abstain format where appropriate.

### Links

* Parent: #5819
* Chat/agent PPL context: #4963

## Results

Open. Pick constraint families, generation templates, and a small regular tracking subset.

topics.title: Experiment: Add professional-document PPL coverage
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment covers professional-document PPL slices under #5819 as a GDPval-like surrogate without using GDPval-AA tasks or reference answers. The research pass found that existing Marin PPL slice registries can support the work and that Common Pile mirrors already cover several candidate families, including caselaw, regulations, government publications, patents, and PubMed. The recommended initial cut is legal cases, regulations/policy, patents, medical/clinical text, and financial filings, with net-new ingestion mainly for SEC EDGAR and DailyMed/FDA labels. The issue is currently a design handoff: implementation should wait for maintainer decisions on source families, license posture, held-out strategy, and whether to share scaffolding with sibling #5819 issues.

### Helpful links
- Parent: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5819
- Research and proposed approach: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5827#issuecomment-4483266974
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Part of #5819. Add professional-document competence validation coverage as a GDPval-like distributional surrogate, without using GDPval-AA tasks or reference answers.

Current structured/table coverage helps, but we need more workplace/legal/financial/medical document surfaces: disclosures, contracts, filings, policy text, memos, and tabular report sections.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Add non-benchmark PPL or target-only slices from public professional documents that move before e19/e20 flops. Candidate sources: SEC EDGAR filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, exhibits, financial tables), contracts from Pile of Law / public SEC exhibits, CourtListener or other public legal corpora, patents, FDA labels / DailyMed, clinical guidelines, PubMed Central medical review text, earnings-call transcripts, government audit reports, and procurement documents.

Some slices should be raw document text; others can be supervised transformations such as section heading -> section text, table context -> row/cell text, clause context -> next clause, or report prompt -> structured summary. Avoid using benchmark QA/tasks derived from these corpora as core tracking.
