topics.title: datakit: decontam is precision-favoring — low recall on embedded/short-line contamination
topics.body:
## Description
Decontamination flags very few documents (~0.01% overall; 0% on arXiv/news). This is **not** a coverage gap and **not** a verbatim-recall failure — it is the recall cost of a deliberately precision-favoring matching design. The question for the team is whether that tradeoff is calibrated where they want it.

### What's confirmed
- Benchmark coverage is comprehensive: 600 families incl. MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, HellaSwag, GPQA, MATH, DROP, SQuAD, TriviaQA, BBH, AGIEval, …
- Verbatim contamination in a ≥13-word paragraph **is** caught (reproduced a real flagged doc at 0.867 overlap).
- By design, decon (`marin.datakit.decon`) matches 13-word n-grams per paragraph and flags at ≥50% paragraph overlap, and **intentionally ignores paragraphs with <13 words** — the whole-paragraph fallback was removed in #5656 because it produced ~18% phantom contamination from trivial stubs (`"..."`, `"A."`, `"##"`).

### Recall cost of that design (injection test — see comment below)
- **Short-line contamination escapes entirely**: the same contaminated text re-wrapped to 8-word lines → overlap 0.87 → **0.00**. Affects MMLU/ARC options, tables, poetry, any line-broken benchmark text.
- **Embedded contamination is diluted below threshold**: the same paragraph + 1× filler → 0.87 → **0.02**, because overlap is a fraction of the paragraph.

### The decision
Is ~0% flagging the intended operating point — accept missing short-line/embedded leakage in exchange for near-zero false positives — or should recall be raised at the cost of more false positives? If the latter, options that keep the `"..."` artifact suppressed: length-normalize or lower the threshold, add a short-paragraph sliding-window path with a minimum length, or flag on an absolute count of matched n-gram hits rather than the paragraph fraction.

Add StructEval conversion tasks (CSV/JSON/XML/YAML/TOML) to lm-eval-harness — item 4 of #7090
topics.body:
🤖 Picks up part of **item 4 (structured generation)** of #7090.

## Proposal

Add the **conversion subset of StructEval** as tasks in lm-eval-harness, so structured-generation compliance can run alongside our other harness evals.

- Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/TIGER-Lab/StructEval (single parquet, 2,035 rows)
- Paper: [StructEval: Benchmarking LLMs' Capabilities to Generate Structural Outputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20139) (TIGER-Lab)
- Project page: https://tiger-ai-lab.github.io/StructEval/

## Scope: the non-renderable conversion tasks

StructEval has two halves. The renderable half (HTML/React/Vue/SVG/Mermaid/TikZ…) is scored by rendering + VQA, which doesn't fit lm-eval-harness. The **conversion half between data formats is mechanically scorable** and maps cleanly onto the harness:

| Task family | Tasks |
|---|---|
| CSV → JSON / XML / YAML | 150 |
| JSON → CSV / XML / YAML | 150 |
| XML → CSV / JSON / YAML | 150 |
| YAML → CSV / JSON / XML | 150 |
| TOML → JSON / YAML | 100 |

700 examples total (50 per direction), filtered from the parquet by `task_name` (e.g. `"CSV to JSON"`). Each row carries `query` (the full prompt including the source document), `feature_requirements`, and `raw_output_metric` (keyword list for scoring).

## Implementation sketch

1. One lm-eval-harness task group (e.g. `structeval_conversion`) with a sub-task per conversion direction, all reading `TIGER-Lab/StructEval` with a `task_name` filter.
2. Metrics, two layers:
   - **Syntactic validity**: extract the output block and parse it with the target format's parser (`json.loads`, `yaml.safe_load`, `csv.reader`, `xml.etree`, `tomllib`) → binary parse-success.
   - **Content fidelity**: StructEval's own `raw_output_metric` keyword match; optionally stricter round-trip equality (parse source and output to Python objects and compare) for the directions where that's well-defined.
3. Generation config: greedy, stop on closing code fence; prompts are already self-contained in `query`.

## Notes / open questions

- StructEval prompts are instruction-shaped ("Please output JSON: …"), so this slots in as a chat/instruct eval; a base-model variant would need light prompt surgery (few-shot completion form).
- This covers the *format compliance* part of item 4. The "**large amounts** of compliant data" axis (does compliance survive 500-row CSVs, deeply nested JSON?) is not in StructEval and is left for a separate, fully programmatic eval (generate N ground-truth records → render in format X → score by parser round-trip, sweeping N). XLSX likewise isn't covered here.
- Upstreaming: worth checking whether EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness would take this as a PR; otherwise it can live in our task fork.

topics.title: [Proposal] Recurring per-crawl data ablation: a standing Marin × Common Crawl feedback loop
topics.body:
🤖 *Drafted with agent assistance on behalf of @hammer.*

## Proposal

Turn the one-shot focus-crawl ablation (#6570) into a **standing, per-crawl loop**: each new Common Crawl release → WET ingest → decon annotation → quality/BPB scorecard → published report. The Common Crawl Foundation has asked directly whether model training can be integrated into their crawl feedback loop ("every X new tokens crawled → train and evaluate"); everything needed exists in the repo as proven, separately-running components.

## What already exists (assembly, not construction)

1. **WET → datakit ingestion** (`marin/datakit/download/common_crawl_wet.py`, from #6570): manifest from `wet.paths.gz` or index parquet, seeded sampling, streams from `data.commoncrawl.org`.
2. **Decon as a cheap annotation pass** (#5519): 13-gram Bloom containment (~270MB filter covering AA-Index + lm-eval-harness evals) on 2-CPU workers — 45M docs in ~2.5h.
3. **Cheap ladder economics** (#6570): the full 8-run, 4-rung comparison cost ~80 v5p-8-hours, absorbing preemption; a 2-rung (d512+d768) per-crawl check is a few v5p-8-hours.
4. **Recurrence machinery**: the canary ferry and datakit CI tiers already run daily ingest/train/eval on schedules — this proposal is one more scheduled lane.
5. **The new primitive — mixing-via-embeddings (#6969)**: a never-swept dataset can be *priced* against the mixture surrogate from **one embedding pass + a CPU refit** (validated preregistered at ~8σ on dolma_starcoder). Per-crawl pricing without any proxy-model training.

## Proposed loop (per new CC crawl)

1. Sample N WET files (seeded) → normalize → tokenize.
2. Decon annotation vs. the standard eval Bloom; report contamination rate.
3. **Cheap tier**: embedding-pass pricing (#6969) → predicted mix value vs. prior crawls.
4. **Confirm tier** (optional, or every Kth crawl): 2-rung ladder (d512 ≈ 0.6h, d768 ≈ a few hours on v5p-8) → uncheatable-eval BPB + Paloma deltas vs. the previous crawl's cells.
5. Publish a per-crawl scorecard (the #6757-style table shape); longitudinally, this becomes a crawl-quality time series both projects can steer by.

## What each side gets

- **Common Crawl**: model-grounded feedback on crawl changes (seed-list updates, focus crawls, extraction changes) within days of a release — the loop they asked for, without operating training infrastructure.
- **Marin**: standing freshness monitoring of the largest raw source, early detection of web-distribution drift, and a steady stream of priced candidate data for mix updates. Also a natural venue for the #6750 web-graph/harmonic-centrality features (per-crawl graphs are synchronized with releases — @wumpus has offered the data, and @malteos has expressed interest in contributing data to Marin).

## Open questions

1. Compute line: preemptible/idle v5p seems sufficient (the swarm precedent) — does this need a formal allocation or just a low-prio queue lane?
2. Cadence: every crawl, or monthly batches? Ladder every crawl or every Kth?
3. Ownership: natural fit for the datakit/canary infrastructure owners, with CC folks (@wumpus, @malteos) as data-side collaborators?
4. Which eval set for the decon Bloom, and should the scorecard include the contamination trend as a first-class metric?

Related: #6570 (the one-shot precedent), #6113 (science-crawl assessment), #5519 (decon), #6969/#7067 (embedding pricing), #6750 (web-graph centrality), and Percy's "squeezerun" data-efficiency-run idea. Feedback welcome — especially from the datakit and data-mixing folks on whether the cheap tier alone is trustworthy enough to run per-crawl.

topics.title: Experiment: State-Prediction Separation (SPS) transformer variant
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment proposes testing the State-Prediction Separation (SPS) transformer on the Grug ladder. SPS doubles the sequence by pairing each input token with a learned prediction token and computes loss only on prediction positions, aiming to separate state maintenance from next-token prediction. The feasibility review found that the idea maps mostly onto existing Grug infrastructure, but it needs a new variant, explicit RoPE position IDs for paired tokens, custom loss alignment, and a new SPS attention mask with Splash lowering. The central decision is whether SPS can beat the compute-optimal baseline at matched FLOPs despite roughly doubling per-token compute; implementation should wait for human sign-off on the RoPE core change and the Splash block-skipping/layout risk.

### Helpful links
- Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01218
- Reference implementation: https://github.com/lil-lab/sps
- Feasibility review: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7165#issuecomment-4968709649
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

SPS (code: https://github.com/lil-lab/sps) doubles the sequence to (x1,p1,...,xt,pt) with each pair sharing a RoPE position id. Loss is computed only at predict positions. Attention: input queries attend causally to input entries plus a sliding window w of recent predict entries; predict queries additionally see their paired input. The persistent KV cache holds only input entries; predict entries are read by at most w later queries.

Implementation maps onto existing infra:

- New Grug variant file, per the variant-as-new-file convention (#1687, `change-grug` skill). Interleaving happens inside the forward pass (no data-pipeline changes); position ids are floor(i/2).
- SPS attention mask as an `AttentionMask` variant with Splash lowering, following the prefix-LM pattern from #6330 on the shared lowering from #6314. Validate against a dense-mask reference at d512. If the interleaved layout defeats Splash block skipping, try a de-interleaved layout (inputs stacked before predicts) before writing a custom kernel.
- Loss restricted to predict positions via standard LmExample loss masks.
- Evals: Levanter-native loss/bpb only (paloma macro_loss). Generation-based evals require paired decode steps in the inference engine - out of scope unless gates pass.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Separating state maintenance from next-token prediction improves loss per unit compute. Success criterion: effective speedup > 1 vs the compute-optimal baseline at matched FLOPs. The ~2x per-token compute overhead is the central risk: a win at matched tokens but not matched FLOPs is a negative result.

Gate 1: d512 @ 2.19e17 and d768 @ 1.70e18 vs compute-optimal sweep baselines (process as in #4807). Gate 2, if gate 1 passes: d1024 @ 9.0e18 and d1280 @ 2.83e19. Sweep the predict-window w only after gate 1 passes.

## Status

Not started.

## Links

* Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01218
* Reference implementation: https://github.com/lil-lab/sps
* Splash mask infrastructure: #6314, #6330
* Gate process example: #4807
* Logbook:
* W&B Report:

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

topics.title: Harnessed MMLU / HumanEval / GSM8K: measure the harness delta (harness ≠ chat template)
topics.body:
🤖 Related to the evals wish-list in #7090. This idea predates this issue: it was raised in eval planning (2026-07-08) as a dream eval — **dynamic conversion of common lm-eval-harness / evalchemy evals into harbor agentic evals** ("can model X solve simple benchmark Y in harness Z?"), with the observation that Qwen 3 conserves most of its accuracy when a benchmark is moved into a harness while Qwen 2.5 / Llama 3 do not. It appears to have been missed when the wish-list was transcribed into #7090, so it should likely be appended there as a new numbered item.

This issue scopes the **static, easy first step**: three fixed benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval) in one minimal harness contract, measuring the harness delta. The full ambition — treating the harness itself as a variable (Z), converting arbitrary lm-eval-harness/evalchemy tasks dynamically, and running the same items across multiple harness contracts — is the follow-up ladder above it.

## Proposal

Build **"harnessed" versions of MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K**: the same underlying items, but posed inside an agentic harness instead of as raw completion or chat Q&A.

## Harness ≠ chat template

These are two independent axes, and conflating them muddies eval comparisons:

- **Chat template** — tokenizer-level formatting: role markers, special tokens, turn structure. A property of *how text is rendered*.
- **Harness** — the environment contract: tool specifications in context, a required tool-call syntax (e.g. JSON calls), a loop that parses calls, executes them, returns results, and a termination condition (e.g. a `submit_answer` call or EOS). A property of *what the model must do to act*.

They compose into a 2×2, and all four cells are meaningful:

| | no harness | harness |
|---|---|---|
| **no chat template** | classic lm-eval-harness MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval (raw completion) | e.g. [mcp-atlas-easy](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/mcp-atlas-easy)-style: tool spec + JSON call in plain text |
| **chat template** | chat-formatted benchmark Q&A | full agent stack (Claude-Code-like) |

The interesting new cells are the right column. The headline metric is the **harness delta**: score(harnessed) − score(raw) for the same model on the same items — isolating "can the model deliver what it knows *through a tool contract*" from "does it know it." A model that drops 20 points when the answer must arrive as a JSON `submit_answer` call has a harness problem, not a knowledge problem.

## The three evals

- **Harnessed MMLU** — the question is presented with a `submit_answer` tool spec (enum A/B/C/D). The model must answer via a syntactically valid tool call. Optional variant: also provide a scratchpad or `python` tool and measure unnecessary-tool-use rate on pure-knowledge items.
- **Harnessed GSM8K** — word problem with a `calculator` (or `python`) tool plus `submit_answer`. Scores: final-answer accuracy, tool-call validity, and appropriate tool reliance (multi-digit arithmetic through the tool rather than guessed). Overlaps the tool-fallback gap noted for item 6 of #7090.
- **Harnessed HumanEval** — the task arrives as a harness task with either a single `submit_code` tool or a minimal `write_file` + `bash` pair; unit tests run in the loop and results feed back (0–k repair turns). pass@1 both with and without the repair loop. The 0-repair-turn variant stays cheap and single-step; the repair variant is the difficulty ladder.

## Design constraints

- **Same items as the originals** — no new questions, so the harness delta is attributable to the harness alone.
- **Both template cells**: each harnessed eval should run in plain-completion form (base models, mcp-atlas-easy conventions: spec + request + `Tool call: ` prefix, target ends with EOS) and chat-template form (instruct models), so template and harness effects separate cleanly.
- **Mechanical scoring**: parse the tool call JSON; MMLU/GSM8K by exact answer match, HumanEval by test execution. No LLM judges.
- **Termination discipline is part of the score**: emitting the call then stopping (EOS / no trailing junk) is a first-class metric, as in mcp-atlas-easy.

## Sketch of the work

1. Transform script per benchmark: wrap each item with the tool spec block + harness instructions (both template variants); publish as datasets under `marin-community/`.
2. Scorer: shared tool-call parser + per-benchmark answer checkers; HumanEval needs the sandboxed test runner (existing HumanEval execution code can be reused).
3. Report harness deltas across the model suite.

topics.title: Generic lm-eval-harness adapter for Harbor (harness-robustness eval)
topics.body:
🤖 The general form of the harness-robustness dream eval: run any lm-eval-harness benchmark inside real agent harnesses and measure how much accuracy each model conserves in-harness ("can model X solve simple benchmark Y in harness Z?"). #7169 is the static, hand-built first step (MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval in one minimal contract); this issue is the machinery that makes it automatic. Related to the evals wish-list in #7090.

## Motivation

Benchmark accuracy measured by raw completion or chat Q&A does not predict accuracy through an agentic harness — models differ sharply in how much they conserve (Qwen 3 conserves most of its accuracy in-harness; Qwen 2.5 / Llama 3 do not). Making every existing lm-eval-harness benchmark runnable in-harness turns the whole benchmark corpus into a harness-robustness probe for free.

## Approach: a generic Harbor adapter

Harbor already has the right extension point: the [`adapters/`](https://github.com/laude-institute/harbor/tree/main/adapters) directory contains ~85 per-benchmark adapters (aime, mmmlu, humanevalfix, bfcl, arc_agi_2, …), each a package that downloads a source benchmark and generates Harbor tasks following shared conventions — dockerized per-task environments, oracle solutions, agents writing their answer to `/app/answer.txt`, and tests verifying the answer.

Rather than hand-writing one adapter per benchmark, this issue proposes **one generic `lm_eval` adapter, parameterized by lm-eval-harness task name**:

- **Input**: an lm-eval task identifier (e.g. `gsm8k`, `mmlu_abstract_algebra`, `humaneval`). The adapter resolves the task's dataset, prompt rendering (`doc_to_text`), gold target (`doc_to_target`), and metric config from lm-eval's own task registry.
- **Task generation**: each doc becomes a Harbor task — instruction = rendered prompt + the standard answer-channel sentence; environment = minimal Ubuntu/Python container (sandboxed test runner for code tasks); oracle = writes the gold answer.
- **Verifier**: the lm-eval metric applied to `/app/answer.txt` contents (exact match / regex extraction / unit-test execution), reusing lm-eval's metric code where possible so scoring stays parity-comparable with native runs.
- **Conventions**: follow the existing adapter template (README with provenance/scope/modifications, auto data download, per-task isolation) so it can be upstreamed to harbor.

Existing per-benchmark adapters (aime, mmmlu, humanevalfix) validate the pattern; the generic adapter subsumes future hand-porting for anything already in lm-eval's registry.

## Metric

Per (model, benchmark, harness): in-harness accuracy vs. native lm-eval accuracy → a **harness conservation ratio**. Sweep harnesses (Terminus-2-style bare JSON+bash, a Claude-Code-like stack, others Harbor supports) to get a robustness profile rather than a single number.

## Scoping / phasing

1. **Phase 1 — `generate_until` tasks with mechanical metrics** (GSM8K, triviaqa-style exact match): cleanest translation.
2. **Phase 2 — multiple-choice tasks** (MMLU, ARC): native lm-eval scores these by loglikelihood over options, which has no in-harness equivalent — the converted task submits a choice letter instead. The conversion changes what's measured (generative vs. discriminative), so report as a separate track, not a like-for-like delta.
3. **Phase 3 — execution-verified tasks** (HumanEval, MBPP): unit tests run in the container; optionally allow k repair turns as a difficulty ladder.

## Open questions

- Few-shot handling: keep lm-eval's few-shot examples in the instruction (simpler, keeps parity) vs. re-rendering as episodes.
- Answer-extraction parity: lm-eval extraction regexes are tuned for completion output; the answer channel makes extraction trivial — decide whether native baselines should be recomputed under a strict answer-channel protocol for fairness.
- Cost: full MMLU in-harness is expensive; support seeded subsampling (tinyBenchmarks-style) for the sweep matrix.
- ~~Upstreaming: target `harbor/adapters/lm_eval` upstream vs. incubating in marin first.~~ Resolved: develop in the existing fork at [marin-community/harbor](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor) (`adapters/lm_eval/`), then PR upstream to harbor-framework/harbor once the phase-1 tasks validate. evalchemy tasks (a superset wrapping lm-eval) could be a follow-up source format.

## Deliverables

1. The generic `lm_eval` Harbor adapter (task name in → Harbor task dir out), following upstream adapter conventions.
2. Generated task sets for a starter suite (GSM8K, MMLU, HumanEval — superseding the hand-built #7169 once parity is shown).
3. A harness-conservation report across the model suite and ≥2 harnesses.

topics.title: [Levanter] Investigate June 67B logprob differences across GPU and TPU execution paths
topics.body:
The June 67B step-42150 checkpoint has three observed top-25 results: the existing H100 E2E golden, a compact Levanter TPU golden, and a more instrumented Levanter TPU reference. The two TPU results have exact two-run evidence; the H100 result has repeated regression passes at its `1e-5` assertion tolerance but no retained fresh-process bitwise comparison.

**Collection PR:** `<https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7182>`  
**Evidence:** [gist README](<https://gist.github.com/yonromai/c79b0f680486cca07ff1d6d03ebd193c/955acc3ef2ed3de4016c1d705e86c78efe6a0706#file-readme-md>) · [manifest](<https://gist.github.com/yonromai/c79b0f680486cca07ff1d6d03ebd193c/955acc3ef2ed3de4016c1d705e86c78efe6a0706#file-manifest-tsv>)

All three agree on the top prediction and the complete top-25 token set; no token moves more than two ranks. They differ slightly in logprobs and nearby-candidate ordering. Because the two TPU paths also differ, this evidence does **not** isolate the difference to GPU versus TPU hardware.

| Comparison | Rank changes | Strict reversals | Max abs logprob delta | Max relative probability change |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| H100 GPU -> compact TPU | 9 | 2 | 0.0638661 | 6.1869% |
| instrumented TPU -> compact TPU | 7 | 0 | 0.0315976 | 3.2102% |
| H100 GPU -> instrumented TPU | 8 | 0 | 0.0642138 | 6.2195% |

Only H100-to-compact contains strict preference reversals: `Ar` moves below `India` and `Football`. Most other rank changes involve exact BF16-logit ties. The evidence neither identifies a cause nor justifies a cross-runtime tolerance from one prompt.

The evidence does **not** retain the full probability-vector bytes. Each instrumented run records only the computed vector's SHA-256 digest, element count, sum, and top-25 payload; matching digests are the basis for the exact-repeatability statement.

<details>
<summary>Execution paths</summary>

### H100 GPU E2E

- Existing source/golden landed in `d678955ce` (#7142).
- Eight H100s in `cw-us-east-02a`, one process, mesh `(data=8, expert=1)`.
- Same-region S3 copy of checkpoint step 42150.
- Input is eight copies of the four-token prompt; the final position is scored.
- Checkpoint parameters are FP32 and use `params=float32,compute=bfloat16,output=bfloat16`.
- The golden forces resolved MoE configuration `sonic`. With `expert=1`, dispatch uses the local Sonic backend: grouped ragged GEMMs plus Sonic's Triton gather/combine. Non-TPU attention uses the reference implementation.
- `model.logits` computes the full `B x S` projection before selecting the final position; `log_softmax` is FP32.

### Compact TPU E2E

- One `v6e-8` in `us-east5-b`, one process, mesh `(replica_dcn=1,data=8,expert=1,model=1)`.
- Same-region GCS checkpoint step 42150.
- Input is eight copies of the prompt padded to 128 tokens for Splash attention; causal position 3 is scored.
- Parameters restore directly as BF16; pending QB betas remain FP32.
- Native Splash attention and resolved MoE configuration `ring`. Because the expert axis has size one, dispatch bypasses the expert-parallel ring branch and executes local `scatter`: argsort-grouped dispatch, `ragged_dot(auto)`, and indexed scatter-add. The TPU source default prefers Megablox and falls back to XLA after a warning-causing Python exception. The recorded commands do not set `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL`, and both retained instrumented-run logs completed without the fallback warning, but the ambient environment was not captured. This supports “Megablox-preferred with no fallback warning observed”; it does not prove Megablox executed because no lowered/optimized HLO or kernel trace was retained.
- The golden's `moe_implementation` field records resolved configuration (`ring`), not the selected local backend. Its `mp` field is a provenance/schema label, not a runtime-policy check. The compact test verifies the actual direct-restore property separately by requiring every inexact parameter leaf to be BF16.
- Returns only top-25 logprobs, token IDs, and per-layer capacity overflow. The checked-in golden uses exact equality as a same-graph regression contract.

### Instrumented TPU reference

- Same TPU type, checkpoint, mesh, input, BF16 parameters, pending-QB handling, Splash attention, local-scatter MoE path, singleton projection, and FP32 `log_softmax` as the compact TPU path.
- Computes the full 128,256-way probability vector and returns it to the host for validation, along with top-k values/IDs, capacity overflow, and finiteness flags over hidden state, logits, logprobs, probabilities, and router metrics. The persisted JSON records only the vector digest, count, sum, and top-25 payload.
- Two fresh processes recorded the same full-vector SHA-256 and exact top-25 payload; all eight lanes were identical, every checked value was finite, and all 26 overflow values were zero. The vector bytes themselves were not retained.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Focused compact-versus-instrumented diff</summary>

The instrumented caller applies `eqx.filter_jit`; the compact decorator versus external instrumented caller does not mean that one path is unjitted.

```diff
--- compact/top_k_tpu_logprobs.py
+++ instrumented/_full_reference_forward.py
@@ -1,21 +1,33 @@
-@eqx.filter_jit
-def top_k_tpu_logprobs(
-    model: VendoredTransformer,
+def _full_reference_forward(
+    model: Transformer,
     pending_qb_betas: jax.Array,
     token_ids: jax.Array,
-) -> tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array, jax.Array]:
-    model = apply_pending_qb_betas(model, pending_qb_betas)
-    model = jax.tree.map(
-        lambda leaf: leaf.astype(jnp.bfloat16) if eqx.is_inexact_array(leaf) else leaf,
-        model,
-    )
+) -> dict[str, jax.Array]:
+    model = _cast_inexact_bf16(_apply_pending_qb_betas(model, pending_qb_betas))
     hidden, router_metrics = model(token_ids)
+    scored_hidden = hidden[:, SCORED_POSITION : SCORED_POSITION + 1]
     logits = jnp.einsum(
         "bsh,hv->bsv",
-        hidden[:, SCORED_POSITION : SCORED_POSITION + 1],
+        scored_hidden,
         model.output_proj,
         out_sharding=P(("replica_dcn", "data", "expert")),
     )[:, 0]
-    logprobs = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits.astype(jnp.float32))
+    logprobs = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits.astype(jnp.float32), axis=-1)
+    probabilities = jnp.exp(logprobs)
     top_logprobs, top_token_ids = jax.lax.top_k(logprobs, TOP_K)
-    return top_logprobs, top_token_ids, router_metrics["capacity_overflow_per_layer"]
+    finite_flags = jnp.asarray(
+        [
+            jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(hidden)),
+            jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(logits)),
+            jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(logprobs)),
+            jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(probabilities)),
+            *[jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(value)) for value in router_metrics.values()],
+        ]
+    )
+    return {
+        "probabilities": probabilities,
+        "top_logprobs": top_logprobs,
+        "top_token_ids": top_token_ids,
+        "capacity_overflow_per_layer": router_metrics["capacity_overflow_per_layer"],
+        "finite_flags": finite_flags,
+    }
```

This changes the output/materialization contract, so a different compiled graph is one plausible explanation. The optimized HLO was not preserved and compared, and the retained memory report does not establish any XLA canonicalization, fusion, or materialization behavior.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Complete numerical comparison</summary>

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hypotheses tested</summary>

- Rank-2 `bh,hv->bv` versus singleton-sequence `bsh,hv->bsv` projection produced the same compact values at logged precision. This is output evidence only; no retained HLO shows how the compiler treated the two forms.
- `jmp.Policy.cast_to_compute` versus explicit BF16 tree casting produced the same compact values at logged precision. This did not reproduce the instrumented result in the observed runs, but the evidence is not bitwise.
- Casting the model template inside shape evaluation versus casting resulting `ShapeDtypeStruct` leaves produced the same compact values at logged precision. The latter aligns the template with the proven loader; it did not reproduce the instrumented result in the observed runs.
- Direct BF16 loading has separate focused evidence: a local serializer regression and an H100 validation covering requested metadata for all 27 full-model leaves plus exact representative two-layer parameter/post-QB comparisons. It did not compare the complete 67B FP32 and BF16 trees on TPU.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Remaining uncertainty and suggested follow-ups</summary>

- Preserve and compare optimized HLO for the compact and instrumented TPU paths before making any compiler-cause claim, especially around the output projection, `log_softmax`, probability materialization, top-k, and returned diagnostics.
- Add one change at a time to the compact return contract to find the smallest graph change that reproduces the instrumented vector.
- Repeat on more prompts/checkpoints before discussing any cross-runtime tolerance.
- Keep exact equality for same-graph regression tests; define any cross-runtime contract separately from the compact TPU golden.
- Review and, if approved, publish the prepared evidence gist before the `ttl=30d` artifacts expire.

</details>

topics.title: Experiment: Sanity-check MXFP8 training on Blackwell
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

The full hybrid MXFP8 quality gate is complete. BF16 and MXFP8 each trained a d2560/L26/E128/top-4 Grug MoE for 31,474 optimizer steps / 66.006B tokens with the same data order, seed, schedule, optimizer, and 32xGB200 topology. Both arms finished with 8/8 task exits, zero failures or preemptions, final W&B evaluation rows, and audited non-temporary `step-31474` checkpoints.

MXFP8 increased mean non-compile throughput from 788,954 to 845,920 tok/s (+7.220%) and reduced measured runtime to the terminal evaluation by 5,460.6 seconds (91.0 minutes, 6.092%). It also produced slightly higher final losses than BF16: +0.001301 aggregate eval (+0.0562%), +0.002885 Paloma (+0.1105%), and +0.004287 uncheatable (+0.2088%). Aggregate eval favored BF16 at all 32 paired evaluations, and MXFP8 did not reach BF16's final held-out targets within the fixed schedule.

The tested hybrid recipe is therefore a speed-quality tradeoff, not quality-neutral. #7282 subsequently attempted uniform MXFP8 for grouped and dense GEMMs, but the available distributed path aborts before execution at EP2 and EP4. Its training-quality result remains unmeasured.

### Helpful links

- [Final W&B comparison, tables, trajectory chart, and CSV artifact](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-comparison)
- [Detailed experiment logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c189a6a31/.agents/logbooks/mxfp8-quality-7271.md)
- [BF16 full-run W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-bf16-s31474)
- [MXFP8 full-run W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-mxfp8-s31474)
- [Uniform MXFP8 feasibility result in #7282](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5028942402)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Work stream from #6998 ("Sanity Check FP8 training on Blackwell"). Get MXFP8 working for both GMM (MoE expert/ragged matmuls) and dense GEMM on B200, then train a small ~A2B MoE model to compute-optimal and compare against a BF16 baseline on a wall-time-matched basis.

Builds on the prior FP8 work on Hopper (per-token-scaled fp8 ragged dot, #6880) and the B200 MFU work in #7012; Blackwell adds native MXFP8 (block-scaled) tensor-core support, which has not yet been validated in our training stack.

## Hypothesis or Goal

MXFP8 GMM+GEMM training on Blackwell is quality-neutral: a small ~A2B model trained to compute-optimal shows no regression against BF16 when matched on wall time.

## Status

The hybrid quality gate is complete. Both 31,474-step arms succeeded and their terminal W&B histories and S3 checkpoint metadata were verified. MXFP8 delivered a 7.220% throughput gain with a small persistent fixed-token quality cost. It did not reach BF16's final aggregate eval, Paloma, or uncheatable target within the schedule. Uniform grouped+dense MXFP8 quality remains unmeasured because the current distributed implementation aborts before execution; see #7282.

## Links

* Logbook: [mxfp8-quality-7271.md at `c189a6a31`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c189a6a31/.agents/logbooks/mxfp8-quality-7271.md)
* W&B comparison: [MXFP8Q-007 final BF16 vs MXFP8](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-comparison)
* W&B group: [MXFP8 quality group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/mxfp8-quality-7271)
* Source runs: [BF16](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-bf16-s31474), [MXFP8](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/MXFP8Q-007-full-mxfp8-s31474)
* Implementation: [quality launcher snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/485e23f7f4d89d1d2f218c777766497d6a8d7ae4), [stabilized smoke implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/f8be94f87), [final logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/c189a6a31)

## Decision Log

* Keep stochastic rounding and Hadamard rotation as reserve numerics levers if loss degradation can be attributed to quantization.
* Treat the first smoke's data-loader failure as a shortened-run configuration bug, not a quality result.
* Fix evaluation casting so tagged eval reuses the training cast for ordinary weights while preserving FP8 state.
* Treat the initial hybrid MXFP8 NaN as a w2 weight-gradient issue; stabilize by consuming the fused w2 gradient and recomputing only invalid w2 gradients from BF16 saved operands.
* Launch the full matched 31,474-step pair only after finite 20-step smoke training, forced final evaluation, and checkpointing succeeded.
* Do not classify the tested hybrid recipe as quality-neutral. Its 7.220% throughput gain comes with a small persistent fixed-token quality cost.
* Resume uniform MXFP8 grouped+dense quality work when the distributed backend can execute it; the current EP2 and EP4 paths abort before training (#7282).

## Conclusion

The quality-neutral hypothesis is not supported for the tested hybrid recipe. MXFP8 increased throughput by 7.220% and saved 91.0 minutes, but final aggregate eval / Paloma / uncheatable losses were 0.0562% / 0.1105% / 0.2088% higher than BF16. Aggregate eval favored BF16 at all 32 paired evaluations. MXFP8 finished before BF16 reached step 30,000 and was better than BF16 at that earlier equal-wall-time boundary, but it never matched BF16's terminal held-out targets. Strict time-to-BF16-final-loss is censored rather than improved.

topics.title: Experiment: MXFP8 block-scaled GEMMs for grug MoE on Blackwell
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

MXFP8 on Blackwell is viable for Grug MoE expert GEMMs, but only when the block-scaled quantization producer is fused into the expert-MLP path. Dense matmuls should stay on the delayed per-tensor FP8 path: native dense MXFP8 lowered and produced reasonable numerics, but standalone block quantization erased the GEMM win. The best supported direction is the hybrid recipe now encoded behind `GrugFp8Config(recipe="mxfp8")`: delayed per-tensor FP8 for dense attention/shared MLP matmuls, fused MXFP8 grouped kernels for ragged experts, and `recompute_all` as the production remat mode. The latest EP1 apples-to-apples D6144 run is an important caveat: with FP8 wire communication disabled, MXFP8 was 0.749x BF16 end-to-end on that topology, so the production recommendation still depends on profiling, communication settings, and the #7271 quality/perf gate rather than the early grouped-GEMM microbench alone.

### Helpful links
- Latest EP1 apples-to-apples result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5037422197
- Uniform MXFP8 feasibility decision: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5028942402
- Research branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Implement and tune a Blackwell-native FP8 path for grug MoE training on B200/GB200, using the hardware's MXFP8 (block-scaled, 32-element blocks with E8M0 scales) tensor-core support instead of the Hopper delayed per-tensor-scaling recipe:

- **Dense GEMMs** (attention q/k/v/o, shared-expert MLP): `jax.nn.scaled_dot_general` / cuDNN-cuBLASLt block-scaled matmuls, replacing `Fp8DotGeneralOp`'s per-tensor path where profitable.
- **Grouped expert GEMMs** (`w13`/`w2` ragged dots): an SM100 block-scaled grouped kernel -- CUTLASS via `cutlass_call` or a Mosaic-GPU tcgen05 port of the Hopper kernels.
- MXFP8 scaling is computed per-block on the fly (stateless -- no amax history), which should simplify the train-step state handling that per-tensor delayed scaling required.

Base: PR #7079 (FP8 end-to-end wiring: #6880 `Fp8RaggedDotOp` expert GMMs, #6660 `Fp8DotGeneralOp` dense GEMMs, FP8 wire collectives, `GrugModelConfig.fp8` + train-step state). The FP8 wire (per-token scaling) is hardware-agnostic and expected to carry over unchanged.

Part of the #6998 "Sanity Check FP8 training on Blackwell" work stream. This issue tracks the implementation and kernel/perf tuning; the compute-optimal training quality check (MXFP8 vs BF16, wall-time matched) is #7271 and consumes this work.

## Hypothesis or Goal

MXFP8 on B200 matches or beats the Hopper per-tensor FP8 speedups at the canonical grug shape (d2560/F1280/E256/K4): grouped GEMMs >=1.3x vs bf16 at the layer level, dense GEMMs >=1.2x isolated, with a simpler stateless recipe and numerics adequate for #7271's regression gate.

## Status

E2E goal met for the early d2560/L26/B64 GB200x4 configuration (MXFP8-005, 2026-07-17): mxfp8 beat bf16 and per-tensor fp8 under `recompute_all`, with loss parity near 4e-4/step. Later production-shape checks added caveats: uniform dense MXFP8 is not ready in the current distributed stack, and the latest EP1 D6144 same-config pair showed MXFP8 slower than BF16 when FP8 wire communication was disabled. Treat the hybrid path as promising but still gated on topology-specific profiling and #7271.

## Links

* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/mxfp8-blackwell.md` (on the research branch)
* Branch: [`research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/mcwitt/7282-mxfp8-blackwell)
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:
  * Latest EP1 apples-to-apples result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5037422197
  * Uniform MXFP8 feasibility decision: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7282#issuecomment-5028942402

## Decision Log

- 2026-07-16 (mcwitt): stay on MXFP8 for its numerics upside; push perf to per-tensor class rather than falling back to a per-tensor grouped kernel. (Logbook: "Direction decision", MXFP8-002c.)
- 2026-07-16: dense GEMMs stay on per-tensor `Fp8DotGeneralOp`; dense mxfp8 shelved unless #7271 shows per-tensor numerics insufficient. (MXFP8-001b.)
- 2026-07-17 (mcwitt): benchmark only production-viable configs (>120B total / >15B active). The #7012 slim-vjp/`all_but_moe` port is dropped -- those modes OOM 3-12x at the d5120/L48/b1024 64-GPU reference config (#7012 branch logbook, B200MFU-032), leaving `recompute_all` (already our benchmark mode) as the production mode. New top item: MXFP8-006 production-shape ladder. (Logbook: "production-viability filter" entry.)
- 2026-07-21 (mcwitt): same-source, same-config EP1 D6144 pair found MXFP8 at 0.749x BF16 with FP8 wire disabled; do not use the earlier EP-confounded comparisons as isolated MXFP8 effects.

## Conclusion

topics.title: FP8 loss-curve validation: bf16 (main) vs FP8 (PR #7079) at row-13 scale on 64x H100
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment validated the FP8 changes from PR #7079 against a bf16 control at the row-13 Grug MoE scale, using identical seed and data order and a full 24,000-step schedule on H100s. After smoke debugging reduced the run to one 8-H100 node per arm and fixed allocator fragmentation with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`, both arms completed cleanly. The loss-curve gate passed: FP8 ended with a matched-step gap of about +0.0040, flat through the cooldown tail and inside the <=0.01 acceptance bar, while running about 5.5% faster by throughput. The campaign also found two follow-ups that do not block the gate: BFC allocator fragmentation can silently deadlock training collectives without `cuda_async`, and FP8 currently uses about 1.66x the bf16 transient step arena because XLA keeps cast/transpose FP8 operands resident for backward GEMMs.

### Helpful links
- [Final result comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7298#issuecomment-5010209991)
- [W&B overlay group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/fp8-loss-val-7079)
- [Final comparison artifact](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/99ec4cac-2537-494c-b9e2-1b285311fa32)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Part of #6699. Validates PR #7079 (FP8 expert GEMMs + FP8 EP wire + FP8 dense GEMMs for attention/shared-expert) against a bf16 control on real data — the loss-curve gate flagged in the PR before FP8 defaults can flip.

**Motivation:** before FP8 can become a default, we need evidence that enabling it does not perturb the training loss at production scale. This experiment runs a bf16 control (main) and an FP8 test arm (PR #7079) in parallel on the CoreWeave H100s from identical init and data order, saving the full per-step loss trajectory for both, and compares them. The run is sized (~8 h, cached in-cluster dataset, full LR schedule) to show substantial loss movement while resolving 0.01-level precision deltas — using the cluster-resident SlimPajama cache to avoid cross-region data costs and staying within a 64-H100 budget.

## Design

Two arms in parallel on cw-us-east-02a, 4 nodes / 32 H100 each (64 total):

| arm | code | precision |
|---|---|---|
| `fp8val-bf16-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val-ctl` = main + launcher | bf16 |
| `fp8val-fp8-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val` = PR #7079 merged with main + launcher | `GrugFp8Config(wire=True, dense=True)` |

- **Model:** row-13 flagship shape — d2560, 26 layers, 64 experts top-4 (+shared), MHA 20×128, seq 4096, sliding window 2048, qk_mult 1.3, ~18B params; `ring` MoE backend, EP8 intra-node, FSDP over 4 nodes, `gpu_fa4_cute` attention, `recompute_all` remat. Identical in both arms; seed 0 in both (same init + data order).
- **Optimizer:** production MuonH (`lr=1e-3`, `adam_lr=1e-4`, warmup 10%, cooldown to 0) run through the **full schedule** — #6486 showed precision gaps surface in the cooldown tail, so a truncated schedule can show false parity.
- **Data:** SlimPajama-6B llama3-tokenized cache already materialized under this cluster's `MARIN_PREFIX` (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin`, in-cluster LOTA endpoint) — zero cross-region traffic. Feistel block shuffle.
- **Budget:** ~11k steps × 128 seqs × 4096 tok ≈ 5.8B tokens/arm, sized from measured H100 throughput to finish inside ~8 h (final step count calibrated by a short smoke run). Precedent: #6486 resolved 0.01-level loss deltas at 1.4B tokens.
- **Trajectory:** W&B project `marin_moe`, group `fp8-loss-val-7079`, `log_every=1` (per-step `train/loss`).

**Acceptance:** matched-step train-loss overlay; gap ≤0.01 at end of schedule (the #6486 threshold for a meaningful difference), with specific attention to the last 10% (cooldown tail). Divergence, NaNs, or a growing gap fails the gate.

Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md` on `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val`.

Note: not filed under the #4281 recipe-ablation family — this is infra/precision validation for #6699, not a recipe-change experiment.

topics.title: Build Harbor sandbox images off-slot via Cloud Build; add stress canary
topics.body:
PR #7450 builds Dockerfile-task sandbox images in-trial on the worker's own daemon (DOCKER_ACCESS sibling containers). The build occupies one of the harbor job's n_concurrent_trials slots for its full duration — up to ~8 minutes measured on apt-heavy OpenThoughts-TBLite environments — and the content-keyed tag caches per worker, so a fresh worker rebuilds. Over long eval and RL runs, slow builds form head-of-line blocking on trial slots (see the discussion on #7450).

Shape agreed in the PR discussion (rjpower, penfever):

- Resolve the dataset's full environment-hash set before opening the trial queue; the registry provides every task's environment up front.
- Dispatch missing builds to Cloud Build in parallel, pushing content-keyed tags to Artifact Registry; trials run against prebuilt images only.
- Dockerfile tasks then become ordinary prebuilt-image jobs: no DOCKER_ACCESS, no sibling machinery, the un-gated gvisor profile applies, and the k8s backend works.
- Reuse harbor's per-task environment hash if it covers file permission bits (COPY preserves them); otherwise keep the hash in marin/harbor/iris_environment.py.
- Add an intermittent stress canary measuring sandbox scheduling latency, environment-ready time, and exec round-trip (mean and tail), so any saturation-aware admission policy is grounded in measured data.

Blocked on an operator decision: Cloud Build service account (builds.editor plus AR write for the eval parent's identity) and billing.

Done when:

- A full OpenThoughts-TBLite run performs no in-trial docker builds; images build once globally and are pulled by trials on docker-worker and k8s backends.
- The stress canary runs on a schedule and reports scheduling-latency, environment-ready, and exec round-trip percentiles.

topics.title: [iris] Expose admitted topology labels for placement audits
topics.body:
## Status

This is a non-blocking observability enhancement, not a reproduced placement-correctness blocker. PR #7225 requests required and sliced topology from Kueue at admission. Recent B200 research has not shown an admitted gang violating those constraints or drifting after startup.

The reproduced gap is narrower: Iris status includes pod-to-node assignments but omits the configured topology-domain values needed to independently verify the realized placement. The probe on branch `agent/b200-repro-placement-audit` therefore returned `UNOBSERVABLE`, not `VIOLATION`.

Kueue remains the enforcement authority. This work should provide provider-independent readback and diagnostics, not act as a second scheduler or make jobs query provider APIs.

## Reproduction

Run against any admitted topology-constrained Iris gang:

    iris rpc controller get-kubernetes-cluster-status | python -m iris.cluster.topology_audit --task-prefix TASK_PREFIX --topology-key TOPOLOGY_KEY --expectation single-domain -

Current result: `UNOBSERVABLE` when the requested topology key is absent from the admitted node records.

Expected result: Iris exposes the configured topology values for admitted nodes, allowing the audit to return `MATCH`, `VIOLATION`, or `UNOBSERVABLE` for genuinely incomplete data.

## Recommended progression

### 1. Expose allowlisted realized topology

- Add a topology-label map to `NodeStatus`.
- Populate only label keys referenced by configured Kueue topology levels; do not expose every Kubernetes node label.
- Add provider-independent tests for present, missing, and partially populated labels.

This is the smallest useful increment and should be kept separate from remediation policy.

### 2. Make requested-versus-realized placement first-class

- Surface the requested topology mode, topology key, and slice size alongside the realized pod-to-node placement.
- Audit required single-domain and exact sliced placement without caller-supplied provider details.
- Return explicit `MATCH`, `VIOLATION`, or `UNOBSERVABLE` results, including enough context to diagnose a mismatch.
- Handle partial admission, retries, and missing or deleted node records without reporting false violations.

### 3. Add operational presentation if useful

- Surface the audit in the CLI or dashboard and optionally emit alerts.
- Validate it during scheduler upgrades or configuration changes.
- Consider automatic abort or retry only if violations are actually observed and an explicit policy is agreed. Automatic remediation is not part of this issue.

## Non-goals

- Replacing Kueue's admission-time enforcement.
- Hardcoding provider-specific topology labels or querying provider APIs from training jobs.
- Exposing arbitrary node labels.
- Automatically aborting jobs based on the initial audit implementation.

## Done when

Required single-domain and balanced sliced placement can be audited after admission without provider-specific API access, with requested intent and realized placement clearly distinguished.

Source: #7225
Repro branch: `agent/b200-repro-placement-audit`
Non-blocking follow-up to #6710

topics.title: [grug][EP] Preserve expert sharding through MuonH 4D Newton–Schulz
topics.body:
## Problem

At EP64, MuonH's 4D Newton–Schulz path merges `(L, E) -> LE` with `PartitionSpec(None, "data", "model")`. When `data=model=1`, this gathers and fully replicates the BF16 `[L·E,D,I]` expert stack before it can be redistributed.

## Reproduction scope

- GB200, 64-GPU expert axis
- Grug MoE: d5120, L48, E256, top-8
- MuonH with scanned 4D expert stacks
- `data=model=1`, `expert=64`
- Reproduction branch: [`rav-grug-moe-ep64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/rav-grug-moe-ep64)
- Originating result: [#7201 EP64 report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5048941489)

## Observed behavior

The merge creates a roughly 300 GiB replicated stack; the run OOMs around 310 GiB before step 1.

## Expected behavior / fix boundary

Transpose the `expert` axis to the front before merging so each shard remains contiguous and the merged value keeps an expert-sharded spec without a gather. The change should be a no-op for EP1/FSDP and allow the EP64 configuration to reach training.

## Done when

- The EP64 reproduction reaches training without this pre-step OOM.
- EP1/FSDP parity is covered.
- A focused sharding test proves no full expert-stack gather is introduced.

topics.title: [grug][EP] Shard non-expert weights and optimizer state across the expert axis
topics.body:
## Problem

Grug defines `data = devices / (replica · expert)`. At EP64 this collapses `data` to 1, so non-expert weights—attention, shared MLP, LM head—and their optimizer state are replicated on every device.

## Reproduction scope

- GB200, 64-GPU expert axis
- Grug MoE: d5120, L48, E256, top-8
- `data=model=1`, `expert=64`
- Reproduction branch: [`rav-grug-moe-ep64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/rav-grug-moe-ep64)
- Originating result: [#7201 EP64 report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5048941489)

## Observed behavior

Non-expert parameters and optimizer state consume roughly 148 GiB/GPU and OOM before step 1.

## Expected behavior / fix boundary

Use the combined FSDP axis `("data", "expert")` for non-expert weights, e.g. `P(Pfsdp, "model")` / `P("model", Pfsdp)`. The expert axis is intra-rack, so the required all-gathers remain on NVLink. At EP1 this must be equivalent to the existing `P("data", ...)` layout.

## Done when

- The EP64 reproduction reaches training without replicated non-expert-state OOM.
- EP1 retains equivalent sharding and numerics.
- Tests cover parameter and optimizer-state partition specs.

topics.title: [grug][EP] Expose ragged-all-to-all capacity factor and overflow telemetry
topics.body:
## Problem

The EP ragged-all-to-all launcher needs an explicit receive-capacity control. Without environment-driven capacity-factor plumbing, production EP64 shapes cannot size receive buffers safely or monitor token overflow consistently.

## Reproduction scope

- GB200, 64-GPU expert axis
- Grug MoE: d5120, L48, E256, top-8
- `ragged_all_to_all`, capacity factor 1.0
- Reproduction branch: [`rav-grug-moe-ep64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/rav-grug-moe-ep64)
- Originating result: [#7201 EP64 report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5048941489)

## Expected behavior

Expose `SCALE_CAPACITY_FACTOR` with default 1.0 and compute receive capacity as:

`capacity_factor × tokens_local × top_k`

Report `train/router/capacity_overflow_rate_mean` so configurations that drop tokens are visible.

## Done when

- The launcher accepts and propagates `SCALE_CAPACITY_FACTOR`.
- Default behavior remains 1.0.
- Receive-capacity sizing and overflow telemetry have focused tests.
- The EP64 reproduction runs with explicit capacity 1.0.

topics.title: [datakit] Register the hero quality data as Datakit steps
topics.body:
Register the hero quality data as two Datakit steps and make the store-ready
dataset a StepSpec output. `bucket.quality_step` reads three co-partitioned leaves
of a source (the normalized shard for row order, the fusion score leaf, and the
content-type leaf), applies the per-type calibration, and writes one shard per
basename with `source`, `id`, `content_type`, `raw_score`, `score` and
`quality_bucket` in the normalized row order. Its artifact is the `QualityScores`
the store already consumes, so `build_clustered_store` reads it unchanged.
`hero_data.quality` resolves that step's identity, and `run.py --stage bucket`
produces it for every registered source.

`score_fusion.fusion_score_step` is the producer of record for the raw scores,
and follows the data flow #9694 gave the reference quality step: one Zephyr task
per shard on GPU workers reads each document's first 512 stored `input_ids` from
the source's Nemotron tokenize leaf (`iter_tokenized_documents` regroups chunk
rows) in lockstep with the normalized shard's ids, and the Harrier embedding by
position. No tokenizer runs on the worker. The step depends on the tokenize step
(`hero_data.tokenize_step_for(source, NEMOTRON_TOKENIZER)`), refuses a tokenize
artifact built from another normalize output or tokenizer repository before it
lists anything, and carries the tokenizer commit in its identity twice: through
the tokenize dependency's hash and through the pin. The Nemotron tokenize leaves
the August 14 run read were deleted from S3 after it, so the run's scores are
registered by path map as `hero_data.fusion_scores` rather than rescored; a
rerun of the score stage tokenizes the source again (the runner builds the
dependency) and lands at the step's own identity. The content-type leaves
written beside those scores are registered the same way as
`hero_data.content_type`, and `hero_data.harrier` now returns a frozen step so the
score step can depend on it.

Every input leaf of a source holds the normalized shard's documents in its row
order. A census over all 162,535 shards of the 292 sources found every
fusion-score, content-type and Harrier shard in exactly the normalized order, with
the same ids and row counts. Both steps therefore read their side inputs by
position and check each batch's ids against the normalized shard
(`AlignedColumn` for whole-column sides, `AlignedDocuments` for the streamed
tokenize side), so a leaf from a different normalize run fails its shard.
`QualityScores.samples_output_dir` is removed; the stage report reads its
spot-check text from the normalized shard of the same basename, and the reference
quality step from #9694 keeps its lockstep tokenize/normalize read without the
samples side output.

The model directory moves to `datakit/models/quality/nemotron_88k`, relative to
`MARIN_PREFIX`, with the config fields of the removed bigram, MoE, frozen-donor
and dtype arms dropped from `model.py` and the saved meta. `load_pooled_scorer`
resolves the artifact stem from the directory, so the token-window `PooledScorer`
from #9694 loads both `pooled_junkgate2_marin` and `nemotron_88k`. `QualityPin`
carries separate digests for the scorer artifacts and the calibration file,
checked by the worker before it writes, so a refit calibration moves the bucketed
dataset without moving or rescoring the raw scores. The calibration file parses
into a `Calibration` dataclass (global or per-type curves); `calibrate_model`
from #9694 writes it. Manifest entries for `harrier`, `fusion_scores`,
`content_type` and `quality` cover all 292 sources. The fusion checkpoint's
document-embedding weights form one optional `DocFusion` submodule whose field
order matches the serialized leaves, so the deployed checkpoint loads to identical
weights and scores.

The bucket stage has run over all 292 sources: 18,710,478,349 documents in
162,535 shards, equal to the fusion-score totals, in 2h50m with 12 sources in
flight on CPU workers. On `nsf_awards` (3 shards, 381,789 documents) the output
reproduced the normalized row order, the pinned raw scores and content types, and
the calibrated buckets on every row. The score stage was rerun on `nsf_awards`
from the tokenize leaf (Iris job `/muchanem/hero-quality-score-smoke-nsf`:
tokenize under Nemotron, then score against the pinned Harrier embeddings) and
matched the pinned scores row for row, same ids and order, to a maximum
difference of 1.56e-3 (mean 2.28e-4), the bf16 reduction-order noise of a
4,096-document batch against the earlier 32,768. A local end-to-end test runs
`score_fusion` over hand-written tokenize and embedding leaves with a tiny fusion
model and checks order, window truncation, chunk regrouping and the refusals.

topics.title: [levanter] load_config treats a cwd .config directory as legacy YAML
topics.body:
Levanter's `load_config()` currently falls back from `.levanter.yaml` to a deprecated cwd-local `.config` path using `.exists()`, then opens that path as YAML.

A normal process launched from a home-like working directory commonly has `.config/` as an XDG directory. In that case training setup fails before launch with:

```
IsADirectoryError: [Errno 21] Is a directory: '.config'
```

Current code:

```python
if LOCAL_CONFIG_PATH.exists():
    ...
elif DEPRECATED_LOCAL_CONFIG_PATH.exists():
    warnings.warn(...)
    config_dict = _merge_config_dicts(
        config_dict, _load_yaml_mapping(DEPRECATED_LOCAL_CONFIG_PATH)
    )
```

The legacy fallback represents a legacy *file*, so it should only activate for a file (for example `DEPRECATED_LOCAL_CONFIG_PATH.is_file()`). A regression test should cover a cwd containing a `.config/` directory and no `.levanter.yaml`.

This behavior is present on current `main` as well as earlier pinned lineages. A caller-side workaround is to use an isolated cwd with an explicit `.levanter.yaml`, but hardening the fallback upstream prevents ordinary XDG directories from being misinterpreted as Levanter config.

topics.title: [eval] Resume existing Harbor runs for selective recovery
topics.body:
Resume an existing Harbor evaluation with `--resume-run-id`, then optionally retry its unscored trials with `--retry-unscored-harbor-trials`. The launcher reads the saved record and reuses the original run ID and results directory instead of creating an empty output tree.

Recovery requires one Harbor evaluation with the original model, hosted judge, policy, runtime, and version. The current error taxonomy preserves scored outcomes, including zero-reward agent failures, and leaves unknown errors available for diagnosis. A launcher regression covers persisted results, selective recovery, and rejection of a changed checkpoint under the same model name.

Fixes #9100

topics.title: [grug] Add the H100 pipeline foundation
topics.body:
Add a stage-local JAXPP pipeline for the full MoE model blocks, including latent/shared experts, SConv, attention positions and QB routing. Standard 1F1B remains the default. The synthetic runner supports the main recipe with FP32 parameters, BF16 compute and compute-scaled MuonH; the historical BF16 capacity recipe remains available.

Each routed expert parameter bank now shares one Frobenius norm across its experts, matching the stacked EP model. `--expert-normalization per_expert` provides an explicit comparison mode. `--qb-bias-mode frozen` retains the current pending QB bias while expert and router weights continue updating; adaptive QB remains the default. Numerical CPU regressions cover stacked-versus-stage-local updates and both QB state transitions.

The historical 48-layer, 65K synthetic diagnostic ran on 192 H100s with BF16-stored parameters and per-expert normalization. Its PP24/EP8/CP1 layout placed two layers in each stage and kept expert traffic within eight-GPU workers. It was chosen to establish capacity; no matched PP8/EP32/CP4 Megatron comparison was performed. The README records the later CP2 result and the differences in batch size and attention helpers. Historical hardware results do not validate the new normalization or frozen-QB option, and no SFT/RL quality comparison has been run.

The affected safe suite passed 2,391 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Focused CPU checks passed 86 tests with one skip; required lint, full type checking, strict docs and source links passed.

#9662 is stacked above this foundation and adds checkpoint/data support, the GB200 launcher, tracked runtime setup and bounded main-recipe hardware validation. Before merge, this foundation still owns replacing the positional result from `initialize_stage_local_pipeline_state`, centralizing the repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers, and separating the synthetic runner lifecycle in `pipeline_smoke.main`. These deferred changes require compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation; #9662 then owns adapting its added checkpoint/data lifecycle.

topics.title: Support context parallelism in the Hero pipeline
topics.body:
Add context parallelism to the Hero pipeline mesh, shard attention metadata with query tokens, and form next-token labels before sharding so a context slice can target the first token in the next slice. The smoke runner accepts a context-axis size and calculates batch divisibility without counting context replicas. Update the pipeline environment to CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2, Flash Attention 4 beta 28 or later, and Quack 0.6.4 for SM90 backward.

This draft targets a dependency-only integration branch combining #9119, #9282, and #9279 (which includes #9278). Its five-file diff contains the CP adaptation and dependency update; the prerequisite implementations remain in their existing PRs.

The full 535B, 48-layer model completed ten updates with finite losses on 192 H100s with PP24 × EP4 × CP2, 65,536-token sequences, global batch 96, and 24 microbatches: 6,291,456 tokens per update. Median step time was 68.539 seconds and measured MFU was 9.877%; loss went from 11.792197 to 11.449181. All 24 workers exited successfully. Gate 06 launched c55ab40a29 with exact helper dependency overrides; 3ad8d3ce37 subsequently recorded those dependencies. Runtime and dependency files match 3ad8d3ce37; a later test-only fix compares discontinuous histogram router statistics at matching per-layer execution boundaries. Detailed results are in #9277.

The run still required scratch JAXPP overlays for host-memory mesh rebinding, forward activation-offload placement, and the Dime2 send-buffer lifetime backport. It also retained disposable warmup, host parking of model state, and CUDA synchronization after each step. The required overlays block a stock-install recipe, and the root cause behind the retained synchronization workaround remains unresolved. This is a bounded synthetic-data stepping result.

The integration passed the safe suite with 1,929 tests passed, 5 skipped, and 5 expected failures. After the histogram test fix, all eight affected pipeline tests passed, including the two-CPU CP2-versus-CP1 loss and all-gradient regression. Tolerances are unchanged. Scoped lint passed.

topics.title: [grug] Add the Hero-mix and quality-classifier fast tracks
topics.body:
* add two data fast tracks next to the model ladder. all three tracks train the same dense/MoE ladder (d512–d1280) on 8×H100 and compare on final Paloma macro loss
* model ladder: `fast-track` trains on the frozen `hero_tok/v16384_shuf/train` cache, as before
  * `launch.py` resolves the budget in `resolve_h100_ladder_budget` and takes a `TrainingSource`, so the data tracks use the same training wiring
  * add `--seed` and `--data-seed`. `--submit` forwards `WANDB_MODE` and accepts `WANDB_MODE=disabled` without `WANDB_API_KEY`
* hero mix plus a new dataset: sample the production Hero mixture and give a new Hugging Face dataset a fraction `p` of the training tokens
  * `hero_sample_cli` replays `harrier_mix_2026_08_18.json` over `store_4d2e363d` in the production loader order and retokenizes each source segment as BOS + text + EOS with `hero-bpe-v16384` into a `PreparedHeroSample`. build it once at the largest ladder budget (17,478,713,344 tokens) and use it again for all rungs
  * `add_dataset_cli` tokenizes a bounded HF prefix at an immutable revision, scales the Hero weights by `1 - p`, and caps the new data at `C = min(p·B, (N/T)·B)` to simulate the production epoch count [^1]
  * `hero_baseline_cli` trains the matched control on the same `PreparedHeroSample`
  * the Hero cell capacity check runs on the final mixture weights, so a small `p` cannot make the largest cell repeat its data
* quality classifier: sample raw text from all 292 registered sources in proportion to corpus size, score it with a frozen head, and train on the top documents
  * `corpus_sample_cli` builds a `RawCorpusPool` with `corpus-id-interval-v1`: one seeded cyclic interval in the 128-bit document-ID space for each source. it skips a row group only when its ID statistics show no overlap. `--label-exclusion-manifest` is required
  * `quality_labels_cli` freezes the GLM-5.2 labels and fits a ridge head on cached Harrier features (target `(quality - 1) / 4`, 80/10/10 split by duplicate group). the raw pool excludes all labelled duplicate groups
  * `quality_cli --stage features|score|select|train` scores the pool once at the largest rung. for budget `B`, it ranks the first `10·B` raw tokens and keeps whole documents until they fill `B`. `--selection-method candidate|incumbent|random` gives the matched controls
* the data-track CLIs default to MoE and derive `--data-seed` from `--seed`, the same as `fast-track`
* add `fast-track-long-string-v1` for HF and raw-corpus tokenization: split at the first whitespace at or after 10,000 characters, and reject a document above 64 MiB with its source and ID
  * bound native tokenizer batches by bytes. a local 32 MiB probe kept all 19,532,169 token IDs, and peak RSS went from 4.60 GiB to 2.85 GiB
* rename `max_train_batches` → `max_train_sequences` in `LmDataConfig`, so a component cap does not depend on the batch size
* fixes found during the runs
  * iris: repair missing CUDA toolchain files. put the child job and attempt in JAX coordinator names, because sibling training jobs connected to the coordinator of a different job
  * fray: pass actor concurrency to Iris RPC servers, because the 32-thread default let long waits block worker heartbeats. the inference broker sets its concurrency explicitly
  * datakit CPU drivers install the `cpu` group with `datakit`, so that they do not resolve the CUDA Torch wheel
  * artifact loading keeps absolute bucket paths, grug dispatch forwards `WANDB_MODE`, and levanter keeps eval metrics between detail intervals
* results at this time (seed 0, final macro loss from the training logs [^2])
  * hero mix, MoE, change against the Hero baseline at the same rung [^3]:

    | rung | 10% Paloma | 10% Uncheatable | 99% Paloma | 99% Uncheatable |
    |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
    | d512 | +4.22% | +1.95% | +58.70% | +68.40% |
    | d768 | +3.30% | +1.56% | +56.97% | +63.72% |
    | d1024 | +4.28% | +1.51% | +55.47% | +61.68% |
    | d1280 | not valid | not valid | +48.85% | +60.26% |

  * each valid mixed run is worse on all 23 evaluation datasets. for 10% at d512 dense, three matched seeds changed Paloma loss by +0.05%, +0.05%, and −0.14%
  * quality, four-source pilot (`cp/arxiv_abstracts`, `cp/wikiteam`, `docx-corpus/en`, `starcoder2/documentation`, 6,064,023 documents): ridge selection against random selection gave Paloma macro BPB 1.9051 against 1.6164, and 20 of 23 datasets were worse
  * these probes test the mechanics. they use assumed production counts and one seed, so they do not show the value of WikiText or of the ridge head
* open work
  * build the `resample-v2` Hero sample and run the four-scale Hero-mix comparison again on it
  * the all-292 raw pool stopped after about 14 h: `stack-v3` has documents of 79–213 MB, above the 64 MiB limit. a policy is necessary (drop and count, raise the limit, or exclude the source). no four-scale quality run exists yet
  * the 10% d1280 run resumed from a temporary checkpoint after a preemption near step 14.1k. its training loss went from 1.45 to 2.75 and did not recover, so the result is not valid. the cause is not known
  * training reads the new dataset in HF prefix order, because the Hero mixture uses `shuffle=False` and Levanter has no shuffle for one component
  * the pool excludes only the candidate's labels, not the training labels of an incumbent scorer
* remove the DataKit end-to-end track from this PR [^4]

[^1]: `N` is the number of available unique tokens in the new dataset, `T` is the production budget (default 18.75T), and `B` is the rung budget. the loader cap rounds down to whole sequences.
[^2]: these runs used W&B offline mode, so the values come from the `levanter.eval` log lines.
[^3]: these runs used the earlier resampler, which kept the source BOS as text and did not put an EOS after the last segment of a source example. the control and the treatment used the same sample, so each delta compares like with like, but the sample differs from `resample-v2`. old `PreparedHeroSample` and `PreparedAddDatasetCache` artifacts must be prepared again.
[^4]: this removes `--source-mode sample|registry`, the token-shuffle control, the shared Zephyr pool (`execution_scope`), and coordinator driver placement in the reference DataKit pipeline. the 25B-sample results and controls are in an earlier revision of this description.

Both TPU checks use v6e-8 in us-east5 and the same [64 frozen prompts](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/test-data/vllm/e2e/representative-eval-prompts/47863868cbfe336739c8097535f113f4d2dae4954f772eb91511c911433596e8.json), split across context buckets through 32K. H100 coverage remains native checkpoint, exported Levanter and vLLM at pipeline parallelism one and two; the last uses two nodes.

Keep the exported-model GPU references, native TPU reference and probability limits. TPU vLLM's maximum absolute probability error on native TPU reference tokens remains bounded by 0.04, 0.125, 0.10, 0.70 and 0.50 at 256, 1K, 4K, 16K and 32K tokens. The exact native GPU reference includes the intentional rounding correction merged in #10069.

Refresh onto maintained main, including #10069 and the mesh fix in #9401. Keep this draft until those fixes land, tpu-inference is pinned to one maintained-main commit containing all three fixes, and all six hardware checks pass at one final Marin revision. The [earlier hardware results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9400#issuecomment-6129427326) and [native GPU correction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9400#issuecomment-6133449648) retain their recorded scope.

Supersedes #7556. Part of #8323.

topics.title: Preserve eval filter identity and vLLM chat templates
topics.body:
Keep ungraded responses from different Evalchemy extraction filters as separate archive rows, including multiple filters in a single source record. Retain the existing streamed parsing and trial IDs for repeated evaluations.

Previously, vLLM could omit the tokenizer chat template advertised by the inference service. Load that template in both VllmBackend.serve() and direct start() calls and pass it to vLLM. Document that the launch-wide Evalchemy seed overrides task-file seeds and is stored in record.json under eval.evalchemy.seed.

The affected safe suite passes: 2,382 passed, 4 skipped, and 5 xfailed. This includes the 227 focused regression tests, which also pass in a separate run. Changed-file lint and full type checks pass; the advisory lint review reported no findings.
