topics.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
topics.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 each layer closes an AttnRes block, so the history at layer *i* is the embedding plus one sum per earlier layer. [¹](#arch-note) ```mermaid flowchart TB tok["token ids
B × 4096, packed documents"] --> emb["token embedding
16384 × 512"] emb --> en["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] en --> S0(["source 0
embedding"]) S0 --> L0 subgraph STACK["6 layers: local KDA ×4, global MLA ×2 (every 4th + last)"] direction TB L0["layer 0 · KDA + MoE"] --> L1["layer 1 · KDA + MoE"] --> L2["layer 2 · KDA + MoE"] L2 --> L3["layer 3 · MLA + Inkling + MoE"] --> L4["layer 4 · KDA + MoE"] --> L5["layer 5 · MLA + Inkling + MoE"] end L0 -. "block sum b0" .-> H L1 -. "b1" .-> H L2 -. "b2" .-> H L3 -. "b3" .-> H L4 -. "b4" .-> H S0 -.-> H H[("AttnRes history, read by every gate
[embedding, b0 … b(i−1)]
+ running partial")] L5 --> FG["final AttnRes gate
softmax over embedding, b0…b4, partial"] FG --> fn["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] fn --> head["lm_head (untied) 512 × 16384
fused CE, vocab tile 8192, z-loss 1e-4"] head --> loss(["next-token loss"]) ``` **2. One layer.** The two sublayers each have an AttnRes gate. The MoE gate also sees the attention output written just before it, as the running partial. ```mermaid flowchart TB Hin[("history
embedding + b0…b(i−1)")] --> GA subgraph GATE["AttnRes gate (one per sublayer, 13 at d512)"] direction TB GA["logit_n = q · rms_norm(source_n)
q ∈ ℝ⁵¹², zero-init (uniform mix)
frozen key norm"] --> SM["softmax over sources
weighted sum of raw sources"] end SM --> A1["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] --> MIX{{"mixer
KDA (local) or MLA + Inkling (global)"}} MIX --> SCA["ShortConv (MLA layers only)"] --> PA(["partial = attn out"]) PA --> GM["AttnRes gate
history + partial"] Hin --> GM GM --> M1["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] --> MOE{{"LatentMoE + 2 shared experts"}} MOE --> SCM["ShortConv"] --> PB(["block b_i = attn out + MoE out"]) PB --> Hout[("appended to history")] ``` **3a. Kimi Delta Attention, the local mixer (layers 0, 1, 2, 4 at d512; D = 512, 4 heads × 128).** ```mermaid flowchart TB kx["x"] --> kq["q = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_q))"] & kk["k = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_k))"] & kv["v = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_v))"] kx --> kg["decay g = −5 · σ(exp(A_log) · (x W_a↓ W_a↑ + dt_bias))
rank-128 gate, per channel; A_log per head"] kx --> kb["write strength β = σ(x W_β), per head"] kq & kk --> kn["L2-norm q, k; q × 1/√128"] kn & kv & kg & kb --> rec["delta rule, chunked Pallas kernels (chunk 16)
S_t = (I − β k kᵀ) Diag(e^g) S_{t−1} + β k vᵀ
o_t = S_tᵀ q_t · state resets at document starts"] rec --> kon["per-head RMSNorm (shared 128-wide scale)"] --> kog["× σ(x W_g), per channel"] --> ko["W_o → sublayer out
no RoPE, no window, no output ShortConv"] ``` **3b. MLA + Inkling, the global mixer (layers 3 and 5 at d512).** ```mermaid flowchart TB mx["x"] --> mq["q = x W_q (full rank, 4 × 128)"] mx --> ml["KV latent = RMSNorm(x W_dkv), 512 wide, learnable gain"] --> mk["k = latent W_uk"] & mv["v = latent W_uv"] mx --> rel["Inkling bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]
R = x W_r (16 per head) · P 16 × 1024, shared across heads"] mq & mk & mv & rel --> fa["FA4 causal attention (fwd + SM90 bwd)
logits × 1/√128 (qk_mult 1) · no RoPE · no QK-norm
Inkling bias added before softmax"] fa --> xsa["XSA: subtract each head's component along its own v"] --> mg["× 2σ(x W_gate), per head, zero-init"] --> mo["W_o → ShortConv → sublayer out"] ``` **3c. LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing (every layer).** ```mermaid flowchart TB ex["x (512)"] --> fused["one fused GEMM:
router · W_latent↓ · shared-expert gate/up"] fused --> rt["router logits (fp32)
top-(8+1) on logit − β_QB; 9th = threshold α"] rt --> qb["QB: β_e = global (1 − 8/384) quantile of logit − α
10k-bin histogram each step; router bias = −β, not trained"] rt --> cw["combine weights = σ(unbiased logits) of the top 8,
renormalized to sum to 2.5"] fused --> lat["latent = RMSNorm(x W_latent↓), 256 wide"] lat & cw --> ep["384 SwiGLU experts, hidden 256
pooled-wave EP all-to-all over 8 GPUs, capacity 1.15"] ep --> up["W_latent↑ 256 → 512"] fused --> sh["2 shared SwiGLU experts, 512 → 256 → 512
down projections fused into one GEMM"] up & sh --> sum["routed + shared → ShortConv → sublayer out"] ``` ¹ AttnRes rolls a new block at layer *i* while `i % max(1, L // 8) == 0` and fewer than 8 blocks exist. At d512 and d768 every layer closes a block. At d1024 (12 layers) and d1280 (14 layers) only layers 0–7 do, so layers 8 and up all accumulate into one running partial instead of their own blocks. **Optimizer routing:** - **MuonH:** every attention and MoE matrix, and every GatedNorm (KDA `W_β` at 2× the MuonH LR). - **AdamH:** lm_head. - **Adam:** embedding, router, attention output gate, norm gains, ShortConv kernels, KDA decay parameters, Inkling weights. - **Adam at 0.1× the Adam LR:** the AttnRes queries. ## Baseline: clean KMA Branch [`fasttrack-moe-kma`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/fasttrack-moe-kma) @ `4eba59cafa`. Build from this branch. The recipe below covers every model and optimizer component. Values are for d512 unless noted; the code is `experiments/grug/fast_track/{model,optimizer,heuristic,launch}.py`. **Shape** | Rung | Width D | Layers | Local (KDA) / global (MLA) layers | Heads × head dim | Batch | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | d512 | 512 | 6 | 4 / 2 | 4 × 128 | 128 | | d768 | 768 | 8 | 6 / 2 | 6 × 128 | 128 | | d1024 | 1024 | 12 | 9 / 3 | 8 × 128 | 256 | | d1280 | 1280 | 14 | 10 / 4 | 10 × 128 | 256 | - Every 4th layer and the last layer are global; all other layers are local. - The run uses a 16k vocab and sequence length 4096 with packed documents. Every ShortConv and the KDA state respect document boundaries (the KDA state resets at each document start). - Weights are initialized with std 0.5/√D. Compute is bf16. **Embedding and output** - Token embedding → RMSNorm → GatedNorm. The result is AttnRes source 0. - Output path: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → untied lm_head (`output_proj`). - The fused lm_head + cross-entropy loop uses a vocab tile of 8192. - GatedNorm (every GatedNorm in the model) is `x · sigmoid(W_up · SiLU(W_down · x))`, with a rank-128 bottleneck. **Block (every layer)** - **Attention sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → mixer (KDA or MLA). - **MoE sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → MoE → ShortConv on the MoE output. - Each ShortConv is a 4-tap causal depthwise conv. **Local layers: Kimi Delta Attention** (Kimi K3's layer) - **Projections:** q/k/v are D → N·128 with full heads (no GQA). Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up. Also every GatedNorm `W_down`/`W_up`. | | `kda_beta` | MuonH | 2 × MuonH LR | KDA `W_β` | | `adamh` | AdamH | MuonH LR | lm_head (`output_proj`) | | `adam` | Adam | Adam LR | token embedding; router; attention output gate; router bias slot (overwritten by QB); all 1-D norm gains; ShortConv kernels; KDA `W_a_down`/`W_a_up`, `A_log`, `dt_bias`; Inkling `W_r` and `P` | | `attn_res_query` | Adam | 0.1 × Adam LR | the AttnRes pseudo-queries | - **MuonH:** Nesterov momentum 0.95 → Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (5 quintic steps, bucketed across same-shape matrices) → a step along that direction, then projection back onto the matrix's Frobenius sphere. Each matrix's norm stays fixed at its init value. - **AdamH:** the Adam direction with the same Frobenius-sphere (hyperball) projection. - **Adam:** β1 0.9. Only the router and the attention output gate get decoupled weight decay (0.02). No other parameter gets weight decay, and there's no gradient clipping. - **Schedule:** 1% warmup, then linear decay to 0.05× peak. - **Peak values** from `MoeHeuristic` (they depend on tokens, width and batch): - Adam LR = `0.0876 · tokens^−0.346 · D^−0.345 · √(tokens per batch)`. - MuonH LR = 13/3 × Adam LR. - β2 = `0.999^(tokens per batch / 131072)`. - ε = `9.68e−18 · √(steps)`. - At d512 with 2384 steps: MuonH LR 0.0227, Adam LR 0.0052, β2 0.996, ε 4.7e−16. The agent picks up new comments at its next batch. The main goal of a single experiment should be to learn about the system. This means that if you tweak one knob and the loss goes off the rails, the experiment can still be considered a success! We better understand the system sensitivity! Building knowledge through failed experiments will bring us closer to the long term goal of better models. ## For the agent - Read `experiments/grug/fast_track/README.md` and `agent.md` first. topics.title: [datakit] Add the content-type step and chain the quality pipeline
topics.body:
Add `content_type.content_type_step`, which predicts each document's content type
from its Harrier embedding with the `domain_mlp_v1` classifier: one Zephyr task
per normalized shard on CPU workers, writing `id`, `content_type`,
`content_type_prob` and the full 7-way `content_type_probs` in the normalized row
order. It replaces `type_corpus.py`, the script that wrote the August content
types and never landed. The full distribution is kept because the classifier
under-recalls the residual `other` class, and correcting that is a per-class
logit shift that needs every class's probability. The classifier is pinned as
`hero_data.DOMAIN_MLP_V1` by the sha256 of its weight file and its label order,
and the step refuses other bytes or a head with other labels.

`run.py --stage pipeline` chains the three quality steps: fusion scores, content
types, then buckets, each fed by the one before and landing at its own identity.
`run.py --stage bucket` still rebuckets the inputs `hero_data` pins, at the path
`hero_data.quality` resolves. Nothing registered in `hero_data` moves: the pinned
content-type and fusion-score maps change only when a fresh run is deliberately
registered in their place, and the manifest test holds every hero path fixed.

The three quality steps share one per-shard driver,
`shards.map_normalized_shards`: it pairs the normalized shards with their side
leaves by basename, runs one Zephyr task per shard, and writes under the same
basename, with `ShardPool` carrying the worker, task and max-worker sizing. The
co-partition helpers move beside it from `score_fusion`. On a 2,000-document slice
run locally with the real fusion checkpoint, tokenizer and classifier, the fusion
score and bucket steps write bit-identical output before and after the move.

On `common-crawl-focus-2026-22` shard 0 (66,106 documents) the step reproduces
the August content types on every document and their probabilities to within
2.1e-6.

topics.title: Marin Belay Intake
topics.body:
🤖 **Marin Belay Intake: post research suggestions for [Marin Belay v1 (#9451)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451) here.**

Marin Belay is an agent-run experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, fixed 8-minute 8×H100 budget). The agent reads and acts only on the main thread (#9451), which is limited to users with write access. Suggestions from anyone else come in through this issue:

1. **Post your suggestion as a comment here.** One idea per comment, with a paper link or a short rationale if you have one.
2. **A maintainer reviews it.** When a member of the `marin-devs` team reacts with 👍, an automated workflow (every ~5 minutes) copies the comment verbatim into #9451, attributed to you and linked back here.
3. **The workflow then adds 🚀 to your comment**, meaning it has been transferred. It transfers each comment once; editing a comment after the 🚀 does not re-send it.

Suggestions that are off-topic, duplicate existing work, or ask the agent to do anything other than ML research on the ladder won't be approved. The main thread's Status section lists what has been tried and the current best recipe.

comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). Kept in, they swamp the overall variance, but the near-frontier numbers above barely move: for example, the gain is 1.38× instead of 1.48×.

topics.title: [eval] Check in the September evaluation campaign
topics.body:
Check in the model, evaluator, and launcher configurations for the September 2026 evaluation campaign, together with the runtime fixes needed for serving, retry, resume, and coverage. The launcher validates external pins, writes immutable effective-config snapshots, and accepts an optional submitter-controlled version label. That label does not attest policy conformance.

Harbor results are bound to the full model and hosted judge configurations, dataset, policy, runtime, and task limit. Resume checks this identity before submission and reuse. A changed checkpoint under the same served name is rejected, as are existing roots without model-bound provenance. Recovery retries known infrastructure failures and unscored trials while retaining scored outcomes and unknown errors.

The frozen Harbor runtime pins 94b118022fe3e677784a638daf33d57a836fa5fe and includes the Tau3 adapter. The Evalchemy lock and generated pin match Marin's external dependency configuration.

SWE-bench uses the native Mini-SWE adapter from merged [Harbor #232](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/232) and [#233](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/233). Its 32,768-token context includes the prompt and reply together. Mini-SWE counts the rendered prompt through the serving tokenizer, including tools and the generation prefix, and caps the reply within the remaining budget and server window. Harbor loads Mini-SWE's base configuration before applying overrides and selects its batch agent, which saves the trajectory on context exhaustion without prompting. Harbor can then verify the existing patch.

Sotopia uses the packaged agent from merged [Harbor #231](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/231). Judge failures become verifier infrastructure errors. The Marin agent wrappers and their harness dependencies are removed. Sotopia's native generation still does not enforce its declared context budget, so those results cannot establish conformance to the 32K context policy.

topics.title: Experiment: Hero throughput and expert drops at 8K and 16K context
topics.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

comments.body:
@mcwitt @ClassicLarry Short version: the qk arms will probably tie, so it may help to write down a tie rule before the 11-rack runs. The rule: keep the formula value (1.48 at 16K) unless another arm beats it, on both Uncheatable and the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText, by more than the noise the rehearsal measures. The details below build on Larry's 100-step test and the agent's one-rack rehearsal plan (2–3 seeds × 200 steps per arm).

**1. On the 67B, the qk arms were nearly tied, and the two metrics disagreed.**
- In the [67B qk test](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step39k_yarn_mscale01_test20) (five arms, 20 steps from step 39k at 65K packing), the arms spanned 0.009 on Paloma and 0.003 on Uncheatable at the last eval. The best two were 0.0002 apart on Paloma and 0.00002 on Uncheatable.
- All-layer 1.570, which the 67B cooldown then used, was first on Paloma and fourth of five on Uncheatable.
- The arms were still converging. Over the 19 steps after the first eval, their spread shrank from 0.013 to 0.009 on Paloma and from 0.015 to 0.003 on Uncheatable.

**2. PTB and WikiText make the full Paloma macro a noisy judge for this trial.**
- On the hero, the two carry 77% of the 16-subset macro's eval-to-eval variance. Over the last 30 evals, the SD of the change is 0.0049 for the full macro, 0.0026 for the other 14 subsets and 0.0012 for Uncheatable.
- Both look like exposures to copies in the training data (#9874). Over those evals, PTB or WikiText moved by up to 0.2 between consecutive evals, which is up to 0.012 on the macro.
- Arms that share batches see the same exposures, but they need not memorize them equally, and any difference lands in the comparison.
- In Belay, where paired arms also share batches, PTB's differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds (r = 0.10 near the frontier). Dropping PTB and WikiText there cuts the noise SD by about 20% ([analysis](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise)).
- On the 67B test, dropping them didn't change the ranking; the disagreement there was between Paloma and Uncheatable.

**3. The rehearsal can set the bar.**
- Its seeds give the seed-to-seed SD of each arm's difference from the 1.48 arm on these two metrics. With 2–3 seeds per arm, pool that SD across arms.
- The pooled SD will be rough, and probably conservative for 11 racks, since one rack runs 11× fewer tokens per step. Matching the trial's length helps.
- A rule written down in advance could be: keep 1.48 unless another arm beats it on both metrics by more than twice that SD. If the metrics disagree, it's a tie.
- Applied to the 67B test, this rule keeps the formula arm, which is what the 67B used.
- For selection, score the arms on the 16K-packed evals that the agent's plan adds, and use the 4K-packed evals as a retention check. qk_mult changes the model at every length, so a 4K score alone could favour a smaller qk for reasons unrelated to 16K quality.

Happy to compute the bar from the rehearsal runs once they're on W&B.

> 23\. Short version: the qk arms will probably tie, so it may help to write down a tie rule before the 11-rack runs. The rule: keep the formula value (1.48 at 16K) unless another arm beats it, on both Uncheatable and the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText, by more than the noise the rehearsal measures.

I like the idea of excluding PTB and WikiText! I agree that the default will be 1.48. (Also noting that the 67B started at 8k seqlen with 1.3 and not 4k seqlen, so it ended up with a lower qk_mult at each higher seqlen). Though I don't think we gain from fully automating the decision process up front. If the tests provide no differentiation we will go with 1.48 on all layers- but we may see signal in unexpected ways such as in gradient behavior on certain parameters, or stability of loss during its 200 steps.

Thanks! Agreed on 1.48 as the default. And yes, the 1.570 arm is the same formula from the 67B's 8K start, 1.3 × (0.1 ln 8 + 1); from the hero's 4K, the same X = 0.1 gives 1.48 at 16K.

On reading loss and gradient behavior, the existing step-180k restores show how noisy each one is:

- **Loss: compare arms step by step on the same seed.** Runs with the same seed and packing read the same batches: at 16K, the three seed-0 restores differ by an SD of 3–5e-4 per step, against 0.06 across seeds. On the 67B, whose arms also shared batches, the per-step gaps to 1.3 varied by an SD of 0.0005–0.002 after the first 5 steps, against 0.02 for the loss itself, and ranked the arms as Paloma did, up to a 0.0002 near-tie at the top, not as Uncheatable did.
- **Per-parameter grad norms mostly don't reproduce.** The same seed-0 runs match at the first step, but from step 10 on they differ by a median of 6–28% per logged step, close to the 10–20% across seeds. Only `output_proj` and the final norms reproduce well. These runs span three commits; same-commit reruns are untested.

Details and scripts: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/qk-trial-noise

🤖 Proposed QK sweep for the 4K→16K switch, following @ClassicLarry's and @bethehand's comments above. Edited: arms now run 100 steps, as Larry first proposed, with an extra eval at step 50 so each arm keeps training after an eval, and the 4K control arm is dropped because neither its evals nor its batches match the 16K arms. Corrected: arms do not pass `--num-steps` (see below), and the per-arm time includes a cold compile. The code is on main: #9888, #9890, #10086 (`qk_mult_long_scale`, an extra multiplier on the global layers only), and #9689 (the production launcher's context history and trial flags). Decisions needed before launch are listed at the end.

**How the arms launch.** Every arm runs from one trial branch whose only change is the deploy edit: `HERO_MODEL.max_seq_len = 16384` and `qk_mult = 1.48` in `heuristic.py`, the 4K entry `HarrierContextPhase(end_step=N, seq_len=4096)` in `HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES`, and `HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL` set to the parent's `throughput/total_gflops` × 1e9 at W&B `_step` N−1. Arms then differ only in launcher flags. Every arm uses the `trigger_hero.sh` launcher arguments plus:

```
--initialize-from-checkpoint <handoff checkpoint at step N> --eval-every 50 [--qk-mult X] [--qk-mult-long-scale Y]
```

The arms do not pass `--num-steps`: in this launcher it sets the schedule length as well as the stop step, so it would change the learning rate, data stages, and FLOPs budget. Each arm keeps the 390251-step schedule and is cancelled once its N+100 eval has been logged.

**Wave 1: A1–A3.** Every arm restores the same permanent checkpoint and uses the same seed. Same-seed arms read the same batches, so their losses can be compared step by step: the seed-0 16K restores differ by an SD of 3–5e-4 per step, against 0.06 across seeds.

| Arm | Context | `--qk-mult` | `--qk-mult-long-scale` | Global / local QK |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | 16K | — | — | 1.48 / 1.48 (default) |
| A2 | 16K | 1.58 | — | 1.58 / 1.58 |
| A3 | 16K | 1.68 | — | 1.68 / 1.68 |

A2 and A3 bracket the all-layer value above the default: 1.58 is close to DeepSeek-V2's mscale coefficient (about 1.57) and 1.68 is the squared YaRN form.

**Possible follow-up waves**, decided after wave 1:

| Arm | Context | `--qk-mult` | `--qk-mult-long-scale` | Global / local QK |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| G1 | 16K | 1.3 | 1.1386 | 1.48 / 1.3 |
| G3 | 16K | 1.3 | 1.2964 | 1.68 / 1.3 |

- G1 and G3 scale only the global (full-causal, no-RoPE) layers. The local layers keep a 2048-token window at both lengths, so their number of keys per query grows by at most about 25% (fewer queries sit near a sequence start), against 4× for the global layers. On the 67B, a global-only arm did worse; that run started from 1.3 at 8K, so its arms sat at different values from these. They are most useful if a higher all-layer value wins in wave 1, to check whether the gain comes from the global layers alone.
- A second seed for A1 and the best other arm, if wave 1's differences are close to the noise bar (decision 2).

**Shared settings.**

- 100 steps per arm at the production schedule (390251 steps), tokens per update (4,194,304 per rack, batch 2816 at 16K), and gate/router weight decay 0.02. The optimizer config is identical at 4K and 16K.
- Eval every 50 steps, so at N+50 and N+100. Eval packs at the training context, 16K. The mid-run eval exercises eval followed by more training, including memory after the dropless 16K eval, which has not run on GPUs yet.
- One checkpoint save and resume in at least one 16K arm.
- Capacity factor 1.15 in every arm, from `HERO_MODEL`. Expert drops at 16K were 16× the 4K value on one rack (3.1e-3 against 1.9e-4 on the current stack); the sweep records them, and a capacity change would be a separate decision.

**Reading the results.** The default is 1.48 on all layers. Another arm replaces it only if it is better on both Uncheatable and the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText at 16K packing, by a margin clearly above the noise, with no worse loss stability. bethehand's 2× pooled-SD bar is the guide, and the N+100 eval is the scoring point, since the arms are still converging at N+50; the final call is made by people, not by the rule. Also compare:

- step-by-step training loss against A1 on the shared batches;
- total grad norm, spikes, and loss stability over the 100 steps;
- per-parameter grad norms, only for parameters that reproduce across same-seed reruns (`output_proj` and the final norms), or for differences well above the 6–28% per-step rerun spread;
- expert drop fraction, tokens/s, and peak memory, which also set the rollback bands for the production run.

The hero's own steps before the handoff are the no-switch reference for loss stability, grad norm, drops, and throughput; a 4K arm would read different batches from the 16K arms, so its loss and evals would not line up with theirs either. A 4K-packed retention check of the 16K arms, since `qk_mult` changes the model at every length, needs a separate eval of each arm's final checkpoint; the launcher has no eval-only mode.

**Decisions needed**

1. **Racks.** On 11 racks (Larry's preference) each arm is about 22 minutes of training at 13–14 s/step, plus a 3–5 minute restore, a cold compile of about 30 minutes (the 16K executables and each `qk_mult` value are new to the compile cache), and two evals, so about 60–70 minutes per arm. Wave 1's three arms pause the hero for roughly 3–3.5 hours plus the hero's own restart, and each follow-up arm adds about an hour. On the one spare rack the hero keeps training, but each step has 11× fewer tokens, and the arms run one at a time.
2. **Noise bar.** With one seed per arm, the seed-to-seed SD of eval differences is not measured. Options: add a second seed for A1 and one other arm, or use the hero's eval-to-eval noise (SD of the change 0.0026 for the 14-subset Paloma macro, 0.0012 for Uncheatable).
3. **Handoff checkpoint.** It must be permanent and at a multiple of 50 steps, so the trial evals land at N+50 and N+100 (resumed runs skip the first-step eval). For the production switch, it should also sit a few hundred steps before a 3000-step eval boundary, so the first 16K eval comes soon after the deploy.
4. **Retention check.** Whether the 4K-packed eval of the 16K arms is worth adding eval-only tooling before the switch, or can be skipped given that the production run will train at 16K from here on.

🤖 Plot of the 67B YaRN 20-step probe from #6811 ([table](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6811#issuecomment-4931724369)): `train/cross_entropy_loss` per step for the six arms, resumed from step 39,000 at seq 65,536 and batch 1,024. All arms read the same batches. Color is the coefficient (grey 0.0, blue 0.1, orange 0.2); solid lines scale qk on all layers, dashed lines scale only the long (global) layers and keep the short layers at 1.3. The bottom panel subtracts the `all_00` control. The two controls are identical, so their lines overlap.

![67B YaRN 20-step probe: per-step training cross-entropy, six arms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/4886ea7987a1237df1ecd85db511e5db23f3c8b2/qk16k/yarn_20step_xent_6811.png)

- Long-only coef 0.2 (long qk 1.84, short 1.30) is lowest at almost every step, about 0.005–0.008 below the control from step 39,005 on.
- All-layer coef 0.2 (qk 1.84 everywhere) starts 0.010–0.015 above the control and only crosses below it around step 39,006.
- At step 39,019 the four scaled arms sit within 0.003 of each other, 0.002–0.005 below the control.

Note: that probe started from 1.3 at 8K, so its qk values (1.57, 1.84) are not the same points as the hero's 4K → 16K arms.

Artifact showing attention entropy as a function of position in document, qk_mult on local, qk_mult on global, layer, and head: https://claude.ai/artifact/53wrjEW1Ep4uPahyjf47pK. Entropy on local layers stays flat, regardless of global layer context length.

Comment above shows the earlier results from the 67B run. Long only is slightly better on train loss- evals may have some noise. Will see what results are for long only qk mult 1.68 on hero, estimating that will look best.

@ClassicLarry @mcwitt Paired per step on the shared batches, the arms separate more clearly than the eval totals in #10101 do, and this supports keeping 1.48: A2 roughly ties it, while A0 and G3 are behind at every step after step 20.

- A0 (1.3): +0.0164 at step 0, before any update, then +0.0022 over steps 1–49, +0.0012 over 50–99 and +0.0009 over 100–107, still closing slowly. At N+100 it is worse on Uncheatable (+0.0009) and on 15 of the 16 Paloma subsets (all but gab).
- G3 (1.68 on the global layers only): 0.0008 lower at step 0 and level through step 19, then behind: about +0.0005 over steps 30–89, +0.0008 over 90–99 and +0.0011 over 100–107. It is worse on all 16 Paloma subsets at both evals, and on Uncheatable (+0.0002, +0.0003).
- A2 (1.58): +0.0022 at step 0, closing to +0.0002 by step 10, then level (+0.00001 over steps 10–99; +0.0001 over 100–107).

For scale, the three same-seed 16K restores from step 180k that I compared above differ by under 0.0001 on average over steps 30–89, and are positive on 30–35 of those 60 steps; G3 is behind A1 on all 60.

On the hero, G3 and A1 were still level at step 19, where the 67B probe stopped, and the gap built up only from about step 25, so a 20-step run here would not have shown it. Later switches may need arms of 100 steps or more.

A2's +0.0012 at N+100 on the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText is mostly twitterAAE; the other 13 subsets average +0.0002. Over the hero's last 30 evals before step 252k, twitterAAE accounts for 58% of that macro's eval-to-eval variance, so it may be worth reporting the macro without it as well.
Going with 1.48 on all layers. Seems slightly better than 1.3, but this field is pretty insensitive at only a 4x context extension.

topics.title: [levanter] Add opt-in GPU paged decode with sliding windows
topics.body:
Add opt-in GPU paged decode over the existing interleaved KV cache, with causal positions and sliding windows. Mixed and prefill batches use the reference implementation. Existing model configs can select `gpu_pallas_bf16_3x`; backend defaults remain unchanged. Builds on #9652.

The initial FP32 IEEE attention-value dot regressed at Hero batch 8. Reconstructing its FP32 probabilities as three BF16 components permits tensor-core dots while retaining FP32 accumulation. For local Hero attention (batch 8, context 4096, window 2048, 12 KV heads, 4 query groups, head dimension 128, pages 128, 8 splits), H100 median host latency falls from 2,140 to 162 microseconds and summed CUPTI kernel time from 2,011 to 57.1. GB200 falls from 1,637 to 183 microseconds host and 1,474 to 43.7 on device. Twenty repeated calls exclude compilation, cache updates, and model work. Sixteen splits did not improve this workload.

All eight small GPU parity cases pass on both devices (integration aca7d8ec6c). The full-shape reference comparison passes local batch 1 and global batches 1/8; local batch 8 differs from the FP32 reference at 3 of 49,152 elements beyond atol=rtol=1e-4 on each GPU (maximum difference 0.00024414). A float64 oracle agrees with the candidate at all four investigated coordinates: the reference rounded three incorrectly, and the IEEE split-K path rounded the fourth incorrectly. The independent full-output float64 regression, using direct nearest-even BF16 rounding, passes all 49,152 outputs on both H100 and GB200, alongside all eight small cases (12.57 and 11.28 seconds). The candidate remains opt-in. FlashInfer XQA on the same arrays measures 35–67 microseconds host on H100 and 46–62 on GB200 across these shapes, with different output rounding. No full-model vLLM speed parity is established.

The benchmark reports compilation, synchronized host latency, optional CUPTI per-kernel or TPU XPlane module durations, full-output errors, and matched FlashInfer or pinned TPU-vLLM RPA comparisons. The default TPU RPA baseline ran successfully (181.5 microseconds versus 748.1 for reference on local batch 1, maximum output difference 0.00097656). Matching query/output packing enables its FP32 mode: 183.5 microseconds, maximum difference 0.00048828. These deviations are against the FP32 reference; a full float64 oracle check of those baselines is pending.

Removing query-padding launches and combining split outputs in one Pallas kernel preserves all eight small hardware parity cases. H100 measures 148 microseconds host / 53.2 on device; GB200 measures 216 / 39.7, so device time improves while host timing remains variable. The combined stack passes 33 focused cases with 37 accelerator skips. The inherited TPU precision port passes 56 strict cases with 9 GPU skips on each of v4, v5p and v6e, including the corrected full-output FP64 oracle and both DMA modes. Its v5p median host latency at batch sizes 1/8 is 359/1886 microseconds versus 748/3059 for reference; XPlane module time is 242/1747 versus 626/2935. Tiny BF16 Snowball and Hero EP2 generation also completes on v4/v6e. Retaining arithmetic residuals roughly doubles TPU latency relative to the earlier candidate that failed the full-output oracle. All numerical tolerances are unchanged.

The earlier float64-oracle passes used NumPy’s FP64-to-BF16 cast, which can double-round through FP32 near BF16 midpoints. The oracle now quantizes FP64 directly to nearest-even BF16; exhaustive midpoint and boundary tests cover the correction. GPU arithmetic is unchanged. The corrected nine-case gate passes on both GPUs in `grug-h100-direct-bf16-oracle-20261002` and `grug-gb200-direct-bf16-oracle-20261002`.

On the same TPU source/runtime, two DMA buffers reduce batch-8 device time from 1635 to 1161 microseconds (host 1769 to 1312), with identical numerical comparisons. Pinned vLLM RPA takes 277 microseconds on device for the same workload but has different output rounding. The one-buffer default remains unchanged. The benchmark emitted all thirteen expected rows; the initial compiler archive exceeded its size limit, and a subsequent bounded capture preserved 44.57 MiB of XPlane and schedule evidence.

The inherited TPU update replaces general division by a power-of-two scale with exact inverse-scale multiplication. The v5p strict gate passes 59 cases with 9 GPU skips. A same-process, identical-input comparison reduces batch-8 device time with two DMA buffers from 1245 to 1015 microseconds with bit-identical outputs; it measures the local attention entry point, excluding public-wrapper metadata.

The inherited component-packing candidate preserves all 65,280 finite BF16 bit patterns in CPU tests and passes the affected suite. Its accelerator parity and timing remain pending in #9652.

topics.title: [grug] Add GB200 launch and H100 validation support
topics.body:
Stack the GB200 launcher, checkpoint/data support and H100 validation runner on the pipeline foundation in #9279 for the model recipe from main `89ac0d770506f7e27ca217760ec5ca3246694e7e`. The launcher uses FP32 parameters, BF16 compute, compute-scaled MuonH, SM100 ragged transport and Flash Attention. It requests one hard NVLink domain in the opportunistic BATCH queue and separates queue wait from worker execution deadlines. Future run names use `pipeline-gb200-*` or `pipeline-h100-*`.

Executable `0da04acccf7b0842319a8668d71ccc697a7b10ec` completed the corrected eight-GB200 synthetic gate with two full-width layers, PP2/EP4 and sequence length 4096. The two losses were 11.806337356567383 and 0.4912489652633667. All eight native GPU processes, both Iris GPU tasks and the coordinator exited zero. All 48 startup task ABI records had zero input memory-kind mismatches. Both coordinator failure and preemption retry caps were zero; the SDK launch example sets both explicitly because the CLI retry option controls failure retries only. [GB200 setup and standalone commands](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/experiments/grug/moe_hero_pipeline/GB200.md) record prerequisites and acceptance criteria.

The combined H100 runner was validated at `a1e3ab278eeb05bb645db641dd3e7dabedf90dbb` on 16 H100s with two full-width layers, PP2/EP8 and sequence length 4096. Ten synthetic updates had finite losses from 11.804966926574707 to 0.4793720245361328. Twenty fresh Harrier updates consumed 2,621,440 tokens with finite losses from 11.8075590133667 to 7.612007141113281. All 200 raw components remained nonempty with their original mixture weights and order. Both GPU tasks and supervisors exited zero; fresh-data logs retain 15 individual rank exits, while the supervisor's child-reaping contract certifies all 16. No checkpoint was written in those full-width trials. Save/restore support is included, but hardware checkpoint validation is limited to the historical reduced-model comparison: a 90,018,826-byte scratch checkpoint and a resumed-versus-uninterrupted loss difference of 9.5367431640625e-7, within unchanged 1e-5 tolerances. The current full-width main-recipe checkpoint path has not been validated on GPUs. These runs used the explicit SM90 pooled-wave/FA4 adapter with SYRK disabled and establish no H100 ragged-transport parity. [H100 reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/docs/references/hero-pipeline-h100.md) separates these runs from the historical reduced-model checkpoint comparison.

The runtime pins upstream JAXPP `328f75a80cecf22c7cc030a82d8941d3c1e220b6` plus a tracked host-memory/startup overlay. JAX 0.11.1 overrides JAXPP's declared compatibility cap and remains experimental; CUDA dependencies with lower bounds are recorded per launch. Installer recovery avoids duplicate global reinstall flags, including on deployed older worker wrappers. The [Iris installer incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/600) distinguishes the initiating GitHub fetch failure from the broken recovery command. Main-recipe argument parsing rejects AdamW before distributed initialization. Shared pipeline configuration, process ownership, array predicates, data scheduling and loader cleanup consolidate the overlapping work from #9279 and #9460.

#9279 contains the shared expert-bank normalization correction, FP32 main-recipe precision and optional frozen QB bias, together with their CPU regressions and historical layout explanation. The hardware gates used FP32 parameters and BF16 compute, with per-expert normalization and adaptive QB. They do not validate the shared-bank normalization correction or frozen-QB mode.

The combined executable, runtime and test source is identical to the previously published `5c2d91a6e48a43573b7f0b09be7e5f16bfc3eddc` snapshot. The README now selects per-expert normalization explicitly in its historical reproduction command. Required lint, type checks, hooks, strict docs and source-link checks passed on that source. The affected safe suite passed 5,566 tests with 18 skips and six expected failures, using library imports from the current checkout. Focused CPU coverage passed 81 tests; the previous normalization fails the new layout regression. The committed-branch lint-catalog review completed; the new error-wording assertion finding was fixed. Before merge, #9279 owns the named compiled-initializer result, repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers and synthetic runner lifecycle cleanup. This extension then owns adapting its checkpoint/data lifecycle. Those deferred changes need compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation.

Full 48-layer main-recipe execution remains unvalidated. The 64-GB200 rack attempt acquired its allocation and started some native processes, then failed during runtime installation; it produced no finite training updates. The full 192-H100/48-layer/65K run remains held. This pull request remains draft.

topics.title: [inference] Add matched native and vLLM checkpoint fixtures
topics.body:
Export small Snowball and Hero BF16 checkpoints and benchmark the same weights and token workload in Levanter and the promoted Marin vLLM fork. Verify every exported tensor through native loading. Retain checkpoint identity, configuration, runtime topology, effective execution modes, and generated-token hashes. A separate non-unit normalization fixture changes only norm weights and records its seed and affected tensors.

Use packed expert banks, isolate Triton caches, and bound Ninja/nvcc concurrency. Expose expert parallelism, bounded KV memory, and eager or compiled execution. An optional hashed FlashInfer cache wheel loads and hashes precompiled MoE libraries with JIT disabled, preserving backend selection and autotuning. Setup and warmup remain outside measured samples.

The compare command verifies checkpoint, architecture, dtype, exact workload, and accelerator allocation, including native EP versus vLLM DP/EP or TPU SPMD data parallelism. Validate Grug aliases and derived defaults while retaining raw configuration differences. An untimed validation batch identifies the first divergent token; mismatched outputs suppress throughput ratios.

Bounded Snowball diagnostics compare shared-prefix logits, router precision, actual layer activations, and independent FP64 head reprojections. Native tracing records its effect on logits; named worker RPC captures every vLLM DP rank. Ordinary-engine generation independently varies embedding-gate SiLU and sigmoid precision without activation tracing. On H100, sigmoid-only FP32 matches all 32 vLLM tokens for both all-one and non-unit norm fixtures; promoting both functions still fails the non-unit fixture. Shared training and serving defaults are unchanged. An exhaustive standalone diagnostic evaluates all 65,280 finite BF16 sigmoid inputs against an independent FP64 reference, separating normal, subnormal, and saturated outputs. Both CPU runtimes execute successfully; fourteen focused tests and the delta affected-test run pass. Accelerator unary validation remains pending.

H100 EP2 tiny eager Hero produces identical 32 tokens using marin-community/vllm#83. On v5p, the combined short-convolution/cache stack passes twelve cases, then both runtimes produce identical 32 tokens for the same tiny Hero checkpoint with data parallelism four and tensor/expert parallelism one. Native measures 790.72 output tokens/second and eager vLLM 358.54 (2.205× for this workload only). The two-layer fixture exercises local and global attention because the final layer is always global. The measured pins, workload, and production Hero memory accounting are in the inference design docs.

GB200 Snowball starts with precompiled FlashInfer kernels and JIT disabled: 54.64 seconds of model/cache setup and a 12.01 GiB sampled cgroup peak under the unchanged 48 GiB limit. Unmodified Snowball outputs still disagree across runtimes, so its ratios remain withheld. Production checkpoints and Hero CUDA graphs remain unvalidated. Stacked on #9661. Part of #7219.

topics.body:
Score the student-selected candidate token IDs at each prompt position requested by SkyRL’s VLLMTeacherOracle. The paired SkyRL revision in marin-community/MarinSkyRL#911 runs VLLMTeacherOracle over native HTTP with unequal prompt lengths and masked response positions, matching analytic scores at unchanged 1e-6 tolerance. The affected suite passed 2,021 tests with 241 skips before the final normalization change. The final HTTP suite passed 39 tests with one skip; both paired selected-score tests also passed. Lint and advisory review passed.

Stacked on #9674. Zero-token requests avoid generation; the existing VLLMTeacherOracle still requests one unused completion token. This adds the scoring contract without changing Marin’s external fork pin or enabling remote FTPO recipes.

topics.title: Verify Snowball draft proposals against the paged target
topics.body:
Verify deterministic draft proposals with a single paged Snowball target forward. Greedy requests accept the matching prefix; stochastic requests use one-hot draft rejection sampling and report raw or temperature-only target logprobs. Returned committed lengths hide rejected KV suffixes, and token budgets, stop tokens, and cancellation truncate emitted tokens and auxiliary states. Capture selected residual boundaries for EAGLE without allocating auxiliary buffers in ordinary decode.

Five focused tests pass on a two-device CPU mesh, including sequential Snowball continuation after rejection and cancellation, full-forward residual parity, and a categorical-distribution check. The affected suite passed 2,399 tests with four skips and five expected failures. All five cases also pass in TPU CI and on H100 in 35.33 seconds at integrated revision 882bff. The TPU job had one inherited BF16 rollout-gate failure; the branch now includes its separately validated default-precision correction. The speculative-target hardware gates use the FP32 target, reference attention, and highest matmul precision; BF16 target verification and full learned EAGLE serving remain unvalidated.

This is a target prerequisite: draft checkpoint loading, draft-cache management, online refresh, and serving scheduler integration remain unimplemented. Defaults are unchanged; no speculative throughput improvement is claimed. The base branch combines the existing native Snowball serving dependencies.

topics.title: Load the pinned Snowball EAGLE3 draft and generate paged proposals
topics.body:
Load the pinned Snowball EAGLE3 draft from its nested Speculators checkpoint schema. Preserve auxiliary projection normalization, normalized residuals and recurrent outputs, reduced-vocabulary token mapping, and target-owned embeddings. Generate learned greedy proposals with a separate paged draft cache and feed them to the Snowball target verifier.

Two tiny Torch comparisons cover disk-loaded forward logits and six recurrent proposal steps; an actual Snowball test checks verified tokens, target logprobs, and subsequent target-cache continuation. All three pass on one and two CPU devices. The affected suite passed 2,399 tests with four skips and five expected failures.

The proposal cache remains tentative: accepted target residuals must replace predicted draft-state rows before another proposal round. Serving scheduler integration, cross-round reconciliation, and online refresh remain separate work; no throughput improvement is claimed. Stacked on #9679. The supported initial checkpoint is [laion/snowball-64k-eagle3-draft-r2egym at 4bdb47c](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-64k-eagle3-draft-r2egym/tree/4bdb47c08e5b5190bea3c7a93c3e14470230e469); validation uses synthetic tiny weights with the same tensor schema, not the full checkpoint.

A bounded H100 gate at integrated revision `cb6086e89d` passed nine native target/draft/reconciliation cases in 66.78 seconds and two independent Torch comparisons in 11.26 seconds. This used FP32 weights, reference attention, and highest matmul precision. It does not validate BF16, resident scheduler generation, or throughput.

topics.title: Reconcile EAGLE draft cache with accepted target residuals
topics.body:
Rebuild EAGLE draft KV entries from the target residual rows accepted by speculative verification. Predicted draft states can differ even when proposed token IDs match, so retaining their KV entries changes the next proposal round. Reconciliation preserves the committed prefix, keeps the final emitted token pending, and discards canceled rounds by retaining their original logical length.

Tests compare the next learned proposals and complete draft caches with fresh target-derived prefill after full acceptance, partial rejection, ordinary learned proposals, and cancellation. A second target round matches ordinary sequential Snowball tokens and behavior logprobs. Four native cases pass with two CPU devices; the affected suite passes 2,399 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Lint, type checks, and advisory review pass after correcting the checkpoint tensor annotation.

topics.title: Run resident EAGLE proposals through the Snowball scheduler
topics.body:
Run learned EAGLE3 proposals through the native Snowball generation loop when a resident draft and a positive proposal width are supplied. Target verification commits tokens through the existing stop-sequence and length checks, keeps only the final emitted token pending for target decode and cache insertion, and rebuilds draft KV from accepted target residuals. A short remaining budget uses ordinary decode; engine reset clears target and draft caches.

The initial path accepts one request and one choice with `top_p=1`, explicit page capacity, and no rollout top-K capture. Unsupported combinations fail before generation. Ordinary decoding remains the default. Twelve FP32/BF16 comparisons with ordinary target decoding pass on two CPU devices under default matmul precision, covering target tokens/logprobs, full acceptance and bonus emission, a stop inside an accepted block, cancellation with exact greedy continuation, and a one-token prompt. Existing engine tests pass, and the affected suite passes 2,399 tests with four skips and five expected failures. All twelve resident cases also pass on H100 under default matmul precision (69.55 seconds, integrated source `d818b8d1d6`). TPU CI passes 159 tests but fails the two abort-resume score comparisons; generated token IDs match. A same-prefix ordinary-retry diagnostic is pending to distinguish cache errors from prefill/decode numerical differences. Score tolerances are unchanged.

Stacked on #9681. Mixed batches, cloned choices, and online draft refresh remain unimplemented. No accelerator performance measurement is included.

topics.title: Batch EAGLE requests with independent budgets and random draws
topics.body:
Batch resident EAGLE requests with independent target and draft cache state per request. Compact draft rows as each request reaches its remaining token budget, and verify proposals with per-request random keys. Keep each surviving request's random stream unchanged when a peer is canceled. Each request retains only its final emitted token in the decode queue; released page slots can serve queued requests.

FP32/BF16 tests compare mixed-request tokens and behavior logprobs with ordinary Snowball decoding across cancellation, unequal prompts, and slot reuse. A stochastic test keeps a surviving request's exact tokens and scores after peer cancellation. The native draft/target/engine suite passes 38 tests on two CPU devices, and two independent Torch comparisons pass. The affected suite passes 2,399 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Matmul defaults and score tolerances are unchanged.

Stacked on #9682. One choice per request, `top_p=1`, and no rollout top-K capture remain required. Cloned choices and online draft refresh remain unimplemented; no accelerator performance measurement is included.

TPU CI currently fails ten nonuniform resident score comparisons (154 other tests pass). Checked token IDs match; static token-capacity and retry diagnostics are pending.

topics.title: Stage EAGLE draft refresh at the serving publication barrier
topics.body:
Stage all trainable draft parameters from the online trainer’s EAGLE checkpoint before pausing generation. Install them only if the target version and resident draft identity still match the staging snapshot, then clear target and draft caches. Failed staging leaves installed weights, caches, and admission unchanged. Draft-only refresh retains the target policy version.

Target publication atomically refreshes the draft embedding and output-head rows selected for the draft vocabulary while retaining learned draft parameters. FP32/BF16 tests on two CPU devices cover changed draft logits, preserved verified target generation, failed partial files, cleared caches, fresh-engine equivalence after target publication, and a target update during draft staging. The combined draft and HTTP suite passes 62 tests with two optional skips. The affected suite passes 2,399 tests with four skips and five expected failures.

Stacked on #9683, whose TPU score comparisons remain under investigation. This adds local native serving checkpoint refresh; the paired remote online-trainer draft transport remains unimplemented.

topics.title: Publish complete EAGLE drafts through the remote update protocol
topics.body:
Accept the online EAGLE trainer’s start/update/finish protocol for native resident drafts. Stage the safetensors checkpoint from the supplied immutable URI while generation continues, validate every trainable draft tensor, then install the complete candidate while generation is paused. Each update and finish request carries the native publication ID and expected target model version; stale or incomplete publications leave installed weights unchanged. Successful draft publication clears target and draft caches and retains target-owned embedding/head rows and the target model version. Setting the checkpoint object-size limit enables the feature; it is disabled by default.

Paired FP32/BF16 TCP tests ran SkyRL’s RemoteInferenceEngine at 0939f7dbe2673077c9d405b5c4e23916f70bd9be against native serving: 2 passed in 21.11 seconds. They cover failed staging and a target publication during staging. EAGLE/HTTP tests passed 64 cases with 4 skips; existing Gloo target-weight publication passed all 6 Llama, Snowball and Hero cases. The affected suite passed 2399 tests with 4 skips and 5 expected failures. A final shared-publication-barrier regression passed 14 cases with 2 skips, including the paired client and Gloo transfers. Lint and type checking pass.

Stacked on #9684; paired client [MarinSkyRL #913](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/913). Tests use local file URIs; cloud transfer, online capture/training and accelerator performance remain untested. The underlying resident scheduler’s TPU retry and model-shape numerical failures remain under investigation. No Marin fork pin changes.

topics.title: [grug] Add hero launch controls for a context-length switch
topics.body:
The scaling-ladder launcher holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, and gate/router weight decay therefore match the 4K run. The hero's context length, QK multipliers, and capacity factor live in HERO_MODEL. --qk-mult and --qk-mult-long-scale (global layers only) override the QK multipliers for trial arms and ladder rungs; trial arms set the context length on their branch alongside the history. Eval packs at the training context, as on main, so the eval_dropless/* series shift at each switch. For short trial arms, --eval-every overrides the eval cadence.

The hero's context history is checked in, like the data mix's switch point: HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES in launch_scaling_ladder.py lists each context the d6144 hero trained at before its current one with the step it ended at, and HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL holds the parent's cumulative training FLOPs at the last switch. A context-switch deploy PR edits Python only: it sets the HERO_MODEL fields, appends one entry to HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES, and sets HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL, so a second switch (4K to 16K, then 16K to 64K) is described exactly and trigger_hero.sh is unchanged. The launcher turns the history into a FlopsBaseline at the last end step and, through the prior_context_phases argument of harrier_mix_2026_08_18_data_config, into LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases, with each earlier phase's Harrier stage schedule and shuffle blocks at its own batch size, so the Harrier sources continue from their earlier reads. At d6144 the launcher rejects a history that does not start at 4K, repeats a length between adjacent phases (including the current context), or disagrees with whether the baseline is set. LmDataConfig rejects end steps that do not increase, and rejects any switch below the 1e23-FLOP simulated-epoching cutoff because the data offsets assume each source reads its whole cache. The narrow rungs take no history.

The live run is unchanged: trigger_hero.sh is identical to main and launches the 4K HERO_MODEL with no FLOPs baseline. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

Part of #9615

topics.title: Pod creation fails on a node with 65K empty Silo cgroups
topics.body:
On October 2, new pods failed to start on CoreWeave node `g5bc6da`, blocking new jobs. Kubernetes reported `no space left on device` while creating a pod’s cgroup, the kernel group used to track and limit container resources. The node still reported healthy, and its filesystem had 3.55 TB free.

The host cgroup tree had 65,535 descendant groups. Of these, 65,412 were under `/silo`; that entire subtree contained no processes. This strongly suggests exhaustion of the kernel’s roughly 64K memory-cgroup ID space, though we have not traced the failing allocator.

Silo is the nested container runtime running inside our privileged Iris job `muchanem.cap-pipeline-host-53`. Two sampled container IDs from its `containerd-shim` processes matched empty `/silo` cgroups. This points to a cleanup problem in that workload’s runtime, but we have not identified the code path responsible. We have no evidence that CoreWeave’s host containerd created these groups.

Please investigate whether completed containers leave cgroups and shim processes behind, and fix the cleanup path. Verify that repeated container creation and teardown do not keep increasing either count. Coordinate cleanup of the affected node with the pipeline owner; an empty cgroup alone does not establish that it is safe to remove while the runtime is active.

---

topics.title: Share Hero and Snowball checkpoint export mechanics
topics.body:
Share bounded HF shard-writing code between Hero and the Levanter converter used by Snowball. Hero reuses the converter's 5 GB file planner; a source tensor larger than that target remains whole. Local files are written directly, while remote files stage under `TMPDIR` before upload.

All JAX ranks replicate tensors in matching order. Only process zero copies weights to CPU and writes files. One writer process supports host-local paths and existing HF upload callbacks. An `ExitStack` owns each memory reservation during gathering; successful submission transfers cleanup to the shard-write task's completion callback. Process zero broadcasts writer failures at matching checks on all ranks.

Hero resume verifies the export request identity and shard checksums before reuse. It writes `export-manifest.json` after all shards and HF metadata to mark completion.

CPU export checks cover exact Hero/Snowball weights, concurrent uploads and two-rank failure/recovery. Full-size accelerator exports and live cloud/HF uploads remain untested.

topics.title: [iris] Quarantine nodes with persistent isolated S3 failures
topics.body:
Add bounded S3 write/read/delete probes to the Kubernetes node agent. Each probe uses the task storage endpoint and credentials and writes a small scratch object per node incarnation. The controller cordons persistent outliers only after a fresh majority of nodes successfully probes the same target after the failure began. Node UID, boot ID, report freshness, environment revision, and Kubernetes resource versions fence stale evidence and concurrent changes.

Group checks under `kubernetes_provider.node_health` with a shared cordon budget. The production `cw-rno2a`, `cw-us-east-02a`, and `cw-us-east-08a` configs probe the shared `marin-us-east-02a` bucket under one-day scratch expiry. The node agent continues probing while cordoned. A fresh success from the current node and configured target after the cordon uncordons a node quarantined by Iris and releases its budget, including after a reboot or credential rotation. Operator cordons remain. Running tasks are not evicted.

Health and cordon evidence remain in node annotations when Finelog is unavailable. Configuration, scratch-object lifecycle, and recovery are documented in the CoreWeave guide. The node-local storage failure that motivated this check is recorded in the [hero incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/599).
