topics.title: [experiment] Snowball SFT on GLM-5.3 traces from Skill2Env biology tasks
topics.body:
## TL;DR

**Experiment finished on October 9, 2026.** Closing with no demonstrated improvement on the primary Pi/BixBench evaluation. The remaining uncertainties are recorded as limitations; no further training, evaluation, or investigation is planned under this issue.

The biology-only SFT run is complete, but the primary evaluation on **Pi**, the harness used to collect the teacher traces and intended for deployment, has not demonstrated improved BixBench performance. On five questions selected using historical runtime, **Pi with thinking enabled scored parent 1/5 versus SFT 0/5**, with all attempts graded. The final response contained an unexecuted tool call in the parsed reasoning field in 1/5 parent attempts and 5/5 SFT attempts. The affected parent attempt had already written the correct answer and still received credit. Two SFT attempts executed no tools, while three executed tools before that ending. This failure therefore also exists in the parent; it was observed more often after SFT in this small sample. With thinking disabled, the parent scored 1/5; SFT had one correct and one incorrect graded attempt plus three verifier timeouts. Those missing grades prevent a complete accuracy comparison and are not counted as zero. This is a small diagnostic sample, not a full BixBench result. See the [primary Pi results and matched controls](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6069563534).

The run used the September 21 Datakit parent, biology traces only, three epochs, peak LR 1e-4, 128k sequences, effective batch 16, and a final-only checkpoint. The dataset contains 5,120 reconstructed windows and 73,894,261 assistant target tokens per epoch from 1,319 attempts across 264 tasks, without reward/completion filtering or replay data. The [published-input audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6069710545) found no supervised tool tags inside open reasoning; the cause of the observed Pi behavior remains unresolved.

Terminus-2 and the synthetic tasks are **secondary diagnostics** of format adherence and transfer to other harnesses. Terminus scored parent 1/5 versus SFT 0/5 on the same real questions; this is not the primary measure of the Pi-trained model. The [Terminus trace analysis](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6083049902) and [completed prompt ablation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6083809697) investigate format sensitivity. The latter accepted 36/36 parent versus 0/36 SFT first responses under the Terminus schema; this remains a secondary format-transfer diagnostic. A Terminus-specific workaround would not establish a fix for Pi.

## Description

Use the existing [Skill2Env Harbor release](https://hub.harborframework.com/datasets/skill2env/skill2env) to collect GLM-5.3 demonstrations for Snowball. This issue owns task selection, rollout collection, SFT, and the before/after experiment. [#9630](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9630) owns Skill2Env Atlas intake; [#9258](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258) owns biology evaluation coverage and protocols.

Start with biology tasks, prioritizing biological data analysis relevant to BixBench. If the usable pool is too small, consider a separately recorded expansion to general scientific data analysis and statistics. Keep relay methods, where a teacher takes over from student-generated actions, for a later experiment.

### Candidate data

The October 5 metadata inspection covered all 7,496 tasks in release revision 2, version `1.0.1`, with content digest `sha256:bef4f739bde8d865af04c04a2cb1c84ecad83b52dd558f4d582dd46c7933666c`. The 268 candidates are a source-skill and description-based shortlist, not an exhaustive taxonomy or a validated training pool.

| Candidate category | Tasks | Source-skill identifiers |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Genomics and single-cell analysis | 95 | 40 |
| Proteins and structure | 49 | 16 |
| Chemistry and drug discovery | 45 | 22 |
| Biomedical data and lab workflows | 79 | 28 |
| Total | 268 | 106 |

Examples include paired airway RNA-seq analysis with PyDESeq2, sparse CELLxGENE summaries, Scanpy PBMC QC and clustering, DepMap dependency analysis, and pysam BAM/VCF processing. Different skill identifiers can cover related workflows; 106 identifiers do not establish 106 independent task families. Many released tasks repair pipelines against offline fixtures. Their usefulness for BixBench remains a hypothesis.

Skill2Env's [source attribution table](https://github.com/NVlabs/Skill2Env/blob/507eab4d9952968de2be98f8729d3c66d487285a/SkillHub/skillhub_source_licenses.csv) includes K-Dense scientific skills and AlterLab academic skills. Preserve task-specific source and license records when selecting data or sharing traces. The selection rule below preserves this initial shortlist independently of temporary local files.

### Pilot sequence

1. Review candidate instructions, environments, and graders. Six initial tasks passed reference/no-op controls. The user authorized direct collection on the other 262 metadata-selected candidates; those tasks have not passed additional controls. Review grader validity when interpreting scores; it is not a selection gate for the unfiltered baseline. Record any grader defects; the existing Atlas assessment found a grader defect in a separate three-task sample.
2. Freeze the task manifest and evaluation split. Group related tasks and shared-data variants when defining development and held-out sets. BixBench-overlap checking is not a prerequisite for this collection, as decided on October 5; preserve task provenance.
3. Pin the Snowball starting checkpoint, tokenizer, training recipe, agent harness, and evaluation settings. Run a small end-to-end collection and formatting check before expanding collection. Record compute budgets before launching sandbox or training work.
4. Generate GLM-5.3 trajectories. The initial collection finished five attempts per task on the six control-checked tasks, for 30 attempted rollouts. The expanded collection targets five attempts for each of the other 262 tasks, for 1,310 new attempts. Preserve every attempt, raw conversations, tool outputs, exact model settings, task revisions, and the full native reward vector; keep incomplete and ungraded outcomes separate. Inspect component-score distributions, solution diversity, and token volume. The first SFT baseline uses all available solver traces without reward or completion filtering. Preserve interrupted prefixes and record conversion or recovery gaps without manufacturing missing content. Rewards are graded; do not reduce them to binary success or require all components to equal 1 by default. Native executable rewards do not reproduce the paper's additional rubric-scoring layer.
5. Prepare all available solver traces for the first SFT baseline; the earlier 200–500 selected-trace target is superseded. Report attempted, complete, graded, and selected traces; component-score distributions; unique tasks and task families; total tokens; and supervised assistant tokens. Size the first SFT run from those observations; the target is a planning budget, not a proven minimum. Prioritize coverage of distinct tasks when expanding collection. Additional attempts on one task do not increase task diversity.
6. Train with loss on assistant turns, preserving user and tool messages as context. Evaluate the final checkpoint against the unchanged Snowball parent on the fixed BixBench protocol using the same Pi harness and budgets. Decide on broader evaluations after reviewing BixBench. Keep infrastructure failures separate from incorrect answers.

Recent Snowball work motivates a bounded test: a [5,000-conversation GLM continuation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9719) regressed on several benchmarks, while [other agent SFT mixtures](https://gist.github.com/lukedhlee/8669f5b6f97e4e3bae72344a8fd51f4b) improved agent benchmarks. Neither establishes a BixBench benefit from this dataset.

### Agreed SFT settings

| Setting | Selected value |
| --- | --- |
| Parent | `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.09.21`; revision `b8c07f7df1df65525abbfdbcd1572318ba11c42f` and native tokenizer/template pinned |
| Data | All available GLM/Pi biology solver traces; no reward or completion filter; no general SFT or pretraining replay |
| Run count and peak LR | One run at `1e-4` |
| Duration | Three epochs |
| Training sequence length | 131,072 tokens; verify actual lengths with the parent tokenizer |
| Effective global batch | 16 sequences per optimizer update; accumulation as needed |
| Parameter updates | Full-parameter SFT; imported router biases frozen, router weights and other model weights trained |
| Optimizer | Fresh AdamH; beta1 0.9, beta2 0.95, epsilon 1e-8, weight decay 0, gradient clipping 1.0 |
| Schedule | 3% warmup, then cosine decay from 1e-4 to 1e-5 over the run |
| Checkpoints | Final model save/export only; no intermediate or per-epoch checkpoints |
| Initial evaluation | Parent and final model on BixBench with identical Pi harness and budgets; broader evaluations deferred until that result |

The nominal batch is 2,097,152 token positions per update, matching 64 × 32,768 in [the teacher-only reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9582). Masking, padding, and sequence construction determine actual supervised tokens. Three epochs and peak LR 1e-4 follow that precedent; its reported evaluations use final checkpoints, and its intermediate checkpoint cadence is undocumented. The final-only saving decision avoids repeated serialization and storage of this model.

Use reconstructed conversations with each actual assistant output supervised once, carried context masked, and interrupted outputs left without invented termination markers. The finalized dataset has 5,120 windows at length 131,072, 320 steps per epoch, and 960 steps total. Target four CoreWeave nodes with eight H100s each. BixBench comparison uses `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` (205 tasks), Pi, one attempt per task, 32,768 context / 8,192 output, and matched grading. The CPU training coordinator is submitted; GPU training remains gated on cache verification.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Unfiltered GLM-5.3 demonstrations of biological analysis improve Snowball's held-out BixBench accuracy under the same harness and execution budget. Measure paired BixBench changes and uncertainty, task coverage, tool-format failures, and response lengths. Broader evaluation is deferred until the BixBench result. Review trace completeness, native grades, and sequence handling before training; preserve negative results.

## Status

The expanded collection completed all 1,310 original task/repetition slots. The final audit proves exactly five attempts per task, with no missing or duplicate pairs. Native reward vectors exist for 1,285 attempts; 25 are ungraded. There are 946 final assistant `stop` markers, 248 output-limit endings, 49 final tool-use stops, eight final error stops, and 59 without an exported final assistant stop reason. Agent timeouts are an overlapping exception class: 86 attempts record one. No verifier-error diagnostic was recorded. Native Pi sessions and ATIF trajectories are present for 1,251 attempts.

Native score patterns across the graded attempts are 574 vectors with every component equal to 1, 381 with mixed or partial component credit, and 330 with every component equal to 0. These remain graded vectors, not binary success labels. The 946 final `stop` markers cover 238 tasks; nine also record runner exceptions, so this marker alone does not establish a clean run. A historical structural screen requiring native session and trajectory, no exception or recorded verifier error, and matched tool calls/replies retains 933 normal candidates. Of those, 558 have every component equal to 1 and cover 161 tasks. Their provider-counted output usage totals 24,112,468 tokens; this includes reasoning and possible auxiliary compaction output and is not a unique Snowball-supervised token count. Four normal traces have unresolved tool-call diagnostics. These screening counts are diagnostic subsets and do not define the unfiltered training pool.

The original batch retained 875 attempts: 829 verified per-attempt archives and 46 [verified fallback recoveries](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6016912375). The continuation executed only the remaining 435 slots and verified all 435 checkpoints, with no further checkpoint failures. It completed at 14:46:11 UTC; cleanup at 14:46:14 reported zero owned sandboxes. The small final Iris archive and completion audit were copied to private durable storage and retrieved for SHA-256 verification. Final archive SHA-256: `4b06bdb9e491145acaddddb0cd44928191386b22b80b3061a3b1a18c5511e68a` (2,240,445 bytes). Original native grades, checkpoint-failure labels, and interrupted-stream diagnostics are preserved.

Both cohorts used native Pi 0.87.0 with 131,072 total context, 32,768 solver output, thinking enabled, native compaction, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, repetition seeds 0–4, and up to 64 concurrent workers. The continuation repaired capture closure and retried a startup that was preempted before teacher generation; it did not rerun attempted slots. Original expanded protocol SHA-256: `24ebb14feb54c3ec97f4c79732a7d42efb2c8cc7c792c2bc6e714dbeb6833997`; continuation: `36e7a611fb25f8e6625934b123ad00f6b33cdace57945b32d7ac5a7ef9852a58`; 262-task manifest: `87f0276f2fe2a3675eb875079363d20d321a80ca216e265539c39a6524f7cd75`. Source archives, notices, launch snapshots, native results, and raw captures are retained.

The six-task control batch is complete: all reference reward components were 1.0 and all no-op components were 0.0, with verifier diagnostics reviewed. The other candidates remain a metadata shortlist. The [seven-attempt Terminus-2 batch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6004311716) is retained separately as diagnostic evidence; its continuation is superseded.

Pi collection completed all 30 planned attempts and retained 29 native reward vectors. Endings: 17 normal, eight output-limited, four agent timeouts, and one ungraded `DaytonaBadGatewayError`. No verifier errors were recorded. The 17 normal traces have matched tool calls and replies, with full or partial native component credit. They cover DepMap, pysam, CELLxGENE, PyDESeq2, and Scanpy; all five scikit-bio attempts ended at an output limit. They contain 869,472 provider-counted output tokens before reward selection and target-tokenizer accounting. No filtering has been applied; the first baseline retains all available solver traces.

Native Pi sessions and ATIF trajectories were retained for 26/30 attempts. Three timeouts lost native log export because `pi.txt` changed during archiving; the infrastructure failure also lacks native agent logs. Raw API captures are retained for all 30 attempts, including three interrupted response streams. The four timeout traces contain repeated identical tool exchanges. The complete archive, source notices, per-file hashes, configuration, launcher, and audit are privately preserved. Archive SHA-256: `61671f943850c0601a9febb3058bf3e1e2df3689b7ef06594280aa89ce087c9f`. No Daytona sandboxes remain.

The teacher uses native Pi 0.87.0, matching the runtime pin in [evaluation policy #9409](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9409), with the [Skill2Env paper, section 3.4](https://github.com/NVlabs/Skill2Env/blob/main/paper/Skill2Env_arXiv.pdf) teacher budget: 131,072 total context tokens, a 32,768-token solver output cap, high thinking, and native compaction. Pi's high setting maps to GLM chat-template thinking enabled; no provider `reasoning_effort` tier is sent. BixBench policy instead uses 32,768 total context and 8,192 output tokens; collection and evaluation budgets remain separate. Live requests obeyed the configured cap, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, and repetition seeds 0–4. The largest observed prompt was 98,346 tokens; compaction used a 16,384-token output cap. This is not a full context-boundary stress test.

Execution uses upstream Harbor `bf991e490394ef9c3250a6db2bc5cbda903cb4c3` with a configuration-only adapter around Pi. Native tools, prompt, loop, task resources, and component grades are retained. Setup allows the recorded package mirrors; agent execution allows the scoped model endpoint, and verification retains the task's no-network policy. The initial six-task collection used at most three concurrent trials, native 30-minute agent timeouts, a six-hour batch limit, and no whole-trial retries. The expanded batch retains native timeouts and task resources, with the concurrency and batch limit recorded above. Frozen protocol SHA-256: `33a9e03a0a426b9d1ed8c328f2743ec4efa9b0fdf4425907d4f93dce156aa338`. BixBench-overlap checking is not a prerequisite.

Before SFT, recover available recorded content, validate native-format conversion and loss masks, and count supervised tokens. Keep output limits, repeated tool loops, missing exports, and grader diagnostics as annotations. Pin the selected parent weights and tokenizer, validate the chosen training recipe and long-conversation handling, and freeze the BixBench evaluation protocol. No training or BixBench comparison has run.

## Links

- [Completed Pi collection and audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6006473943).
- Logbook: dated updates in this issue; keep this body current as decisions change.
- W&B report: pending the first training run.
- Dataset assessment and known grader issue: [#9630](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9630).
- Biology evaluation protocols and baselines: [#9258](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258).
- Source project: [Skill2Env](https://github.com/NVlabs/Skill2Env).

## Decision Log

- 2026-10-05: Start with released Skill2Env biology tasks and complete GLM-only demonstrations. Use native component rewards to select traces and assistant-only SFT. Defer relay methods.
- 2026-10-05: Treat general scientific data analysis as a possible expansion if the validated biology pool is insufficient.
- 2026-10-05: Track this experiment here and link its evaluation results from #9258. Preserve Atlas intake under #9630.
- 2026-10-05: Completed reference/no-op controls on six pinned tasks. Collection: five attempts per task, 30 total. Treat rewards as graded vectors and choose the SFT selection policy after inspecting pilot distributions; this supersedes earlier binary verified-success wording.

- 2026-10-05: Authorized the 30-rollout collection and removed BixBench-overlap checking as a prerequisite. Preserve source provenance and full component rewards.
- 2026-10-05: Superseded Terminus-2 with Pi to match the intended Snowball harness. Selected the paper's 128k context / 32k output teacher budget if supported. Retain the seven prior attempts separately; do not resume their queue.

- 2026-10-06: Completed the 30-attempt Pi batch with 29 native reward vectors and 17 normal trace candidates. Preserve all native scores and raw captures; keep output-limit endings, timeouts, and the ungraded infrastructure failure separate. SFT selection and training remain pending.

- 2026-10-06: Authorized five attempts for every remaining shortlisted biology task (262 tasks; 1,310 new attempts) while unattended. Selected 64 concurrent rollouts after checking bulk inference guidance and sandbox quota. Preserve every native reward vector and verified private artifacts; defer SFT selection and training.

- 2026-10-06: Recovered the first expanded job's 46 fallback attempts without changing native grades. Continue only the 435 unattempted slots; replace the short capture-close window with a bounded 35-minute wait outside the upload lock. Preserve all prior attempts, including incomplete and ungraded outcomes.

- 2026-10-06: Completed all 1,310 expanded slots without duplicates; all evidence is retained and continuation sandbox cleanup is complete. Keep the issue open for the planned SFT and evaluation stages.

- 2026-10-06: Selected an unfiltered first SFT baseline using all available GLM/Pi solver traces, including truncated and interrupted prefixes; supersedes earlier reward and completeness selection proposals. Preserve scores as annotations and avoid artificial termination targets. GitHub and Discord precedents support a bounded continuation but leave parent, mixture, and hyperparameters open.

- 2026-10-06: Selected September 21 Datakit SFT, biology traces only with no replay, one run at peak LR 1e-4, three epochs, 131,072-token training sequences, and effective global batch 16. Save/export and evaluate the final model only; per-epoch checkpointing was dropped because of model-size overhead.

- 2026-10-06: Confirmed full-parameter SFT with fresh AdamH (betas 0.9/0.95, epsilon 1e-8, weight decay 0, clip 1.0), 3% warmup, cosine decay from 1e-4 to 1e-5, and frozen imported router biases. Start evaluation with BixBench alone; decide on other evaluations after its result.

- 2026-10-06: Selected reconstructed conversations and CoreWeave H100 compute (32 GPUs). Finalized 5,120 windows with 73,894,261 supervised tokens per epoch; batch 16 and three epochs give 960 steps. All 58 preparation artifacts passed full SHA-256 readback. Preserve every available solver output, crop only masked context where necessary, and finish trainer validation before launch.

## Conclusion

Collection and the agreed three-epoch, biology-only SFT run are complete. Pi is the primary evaluation harness because it matches teacher collection and intended deployment. The current Pi/BixBench diagnostic does not establish an SFT improvement: thinking-enabled accuracy was parent 1/5 versus SFT 0/5, and thinking-disabled SFT has only two graded attempts out of five. An unexecuted tool call in the final parsed reasoning field was observed in one of five thinking-enabled parent traces and all five SFT traces. It is a pre-existing failure pattern that appeared more frequently after SFT in this sample; it is not unique to the SFT checkpoint. The small sample and incomplete grading limit any broader accuracy claim.

This experiment is finished at the owner's request. The unresolved cause of the Pi formatting behavior and the three missing thinking-disabled SFT grades are accepted limitations of the final result, not outstanding work under this issue. No further runs or debugging are planned here. Any future experiment would have a separate scope and should use Pi as its primary evaluation harness.

Terminus-2 and synthetic tasks remain secondary diagnostics. The [completed prompt ablation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9775#issuecomment-6083809697) accepted 36/36 parent versus 0/36 SFT first responses under the Terminus schema. These findings do not establish a remedy for the primary Pi failures. Results and analysis are preserved, and the final diagnostic inference servers have stopped.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the GLM execution foundation
topics.body:
Add `lib/taskforge`, the GLM-5.3 execution layer for Taskforge, which reimplements the
`experiments/post_training/capability_env_gen` task-generation pipeline as a library. `GlmClient`
streams chat completions, retries 408, 429 and 5xx responses and broken streams, waits without
spending attempts while the router reports no workers for its pool, detects stalls by time since
the last token, and continues a reply cut at `max_tokens`. A context-overflow 400 lowers
`max_tokens` to the remaining context measured by a one-token probe; a prompt that fills the
window, or a lowered budget the server still rejects, raises `GlmContextExhausted`. On top of the
client: structured output through one forced strict tool call with one repair, an on-disk call
cache keyed by request and sample index, an agent loop with Parallel web tools and RolloutEngine's
shell tool (`rolloutengine.shell_tool`) that returns the turns so far when the context fills, a
RolloutEngine model adapter, and a ledger of timed spans written to per-item JSONL and, on Iris,
Finelog. The agent loop was chosen over pi, omp and LangChain after all four ran the same tasks
live.

Every GLM call made through `run_agent` or `GlmRolloutModel` is recorded by one function,
`llm.recording.recorded_complete`, as an `LLM_CALL` span with the call's attempt record: the
attempt count, a count per failed outcome, the non-200 statuses in order, and wall time including
backoff and holds. A call that runs out of attempts keeps the same fields beside its `cause`.
Before this, rollout calls recorded nothing, so a validation round's 429s and retries did not
reach the ledger. `GlmRolloutModel` takes the `CallLedger` its spans go under.

`llm.client.complete_prefilled` sends a prefix as the start of the assistant turn, through the
same `continue_final_message` request the client uses to continue cut-off reasoning, and returns
content that starts with the prefix. Measured live on GLM-5.3: a prefilled turn does not think,
because the chat template renders an empty think block before the prefilled text, and vLLM's
reasoning parser then files the whole continuation under `reasoning`. Sending
`enable_thinking: false` renders the same prompt tokens and returns the continuation as `content`
with zero reasoning tokens, so the function sends it. The template strips the prefilled text, so a
prefix with surrounding whitespace is rejected. The Parallel key for live tests is read only from
the file `TASKFORGE_PARALLEL_KEY_FILE` names.

Taskforge is a standalone uv project with its own `uv.lock`, the same pattern as `lib/rolloutengine`:
RolloutEngine and Shellbox are not root workspace members, so Taskforge cannot be one. It locks
TaskCompendium (TaskSpec schema 0.25), RolloutEngine, Shellbox and verifyit from the sibling
checkouts. Its lockfile needs `prerelease = "allow"`, a `marin-rigging` override to the sibling checkout, a pinned
`marin-finelog-server` dev build (newer releases ship no arm64 macOS wheel), and `httpx<1` (the
prerelease setting otherwise resolves an httpx 1.0 dev release without `AsyncClient`). A
`taskforge-unit` CI job runs its unit tests and pyrefly from that lockfile on Linux. Since #9980,
RolloutEngine defers its import of shellbox's local backend, whose `bubblewrap-bin` dependency is
Linux-only, so the unit tests and pyrefly also run natively on macOS.

The ledger's Finelog table `taskforge.ledger` names its duration column `wall_time`, like
`LedgerEntry.wall_time`, at `TableSpec` version 1. Finelog accepts only the next consecutive version
and a later version may only add nullable columns; no reachable deployment has the namespace
registered, so version 1 was never committed with the earlier `wall` name. The JSONL ledger stays
authoritative. Live tests write evidence under `$TASKFORGE_EVIDENCE_DIR`, or a directory in the
system temp directory, never inside the checkout.

The RolloutEngine adapter cannot always keep the exact token prefix. It checks each served prompt
against the rollout's token prefix and raises `RolloutContractError` at the first divergent index.
Chat completions re-render and re-tokenize the replayed conversation, so a sampled token sequence
that is not the tokenizer's canonical encoding of its text comes back changed: a sampled `),` `(`
(ids 701, 7) returns as `),(` (23482). This failed 2 of 7 live reruns of one build draft. Empty
reasoning, content beside tool calls, and multi-line tool arguments re-rendered token for token in
all 29 recorded turns. A fix needs a tokens-in generation path, which the GLM router (SMG in front
of vLLM 0.28) does not offer: it rejects integer prompts on `/v1/completions` and serves no
`/generate` or `/tokenize`.

vLLM's GLM tool parser reports a tool call cut at `max_tokens` as `tool_calls`, so the client
reports a tool-call reply that spent its whole budget as `length`. Text continuation on length is
lossy at the splice (dropped spaces and punctuation), and a cut in reasoning can change the
answer. `web_fetch` can return a cached page: Parallel served a five-day-old copy of the shellsim
PyPI page during testing, so its description points the agent to `curl` from the sandbox for
fast-moving sources. Live runs exercised a 131,072-token completion, a 250k-token context overflow,
continuation, structured repair, and 20 concurrent agents on the interactive endpoint. The Finelog
ledger was tested against finelog's embedded server, not the cluster.

Stacks on #9838.

topics.title: [taskforge] Triage proposals with structural checks and a GLM rubric
topics.body:
`taskforge.triage` runs deterministic checks first; a fatal failure or a null proposal rejects with
no model call. `GlmRubric` then scores seven integer axes in independent samples, and code decides:
ACCEPT or REJECT needs a strict majority of the per-sample rule, anything else is REPAIR.
`GlmRubric.repair` rewrites a proposal in one call and returns it for the caller to re-evaluate.
The axes are top-level tool fields because GLM sent a nested `scores` object as a JSON string.

Live on the GLM-5.3 interactive endpoint, 103 capability proposals were scored with 3 samples at
temperature 0.7: 311 calls, 0 rubric output errors, 31 ACCEPT and 72 REPAIR. Majority decisions
agreed with an earlier run on 57 of 63 shared proposals. Two of three repairs reached ACCEPT. The
live test that produced these numbers needs the capability source and lands with it in
taskforge/07-capability.

The rubric has never recommended REJECT live, so that branch is unit-tested only. The advisory
`resources_in_build_plan` check has known false positives.

Stacks on #9785.

topics.title: [grug] Keep AdamH updates finite on zero-norm matrices
topics.body:
scale_by_adamh projects onto the parameter's Frobenius sphere by dividing by
the updated matrix norm. A zero matrix stays zero through a zero learning-rate
or zero-gradient step, so the division is 0/0 and the update is NaN. Floor
that norm at 1e-10, the same floor the direction step already uses.

Fixes #9054

topics.title: [grafana] Prepare GPU history by requested priority
topics.body:
Prepare seven-day H100 and Blackwell (GB200) allocation-history panels grouped by each child job's requested priority. An Interactive request dispatched as Batch stays in the Interactive group. There is no applied-priority lookup or toggle. Iris and Finelog server code, persisted schemas, retention and writes are unchanged.

The projection sums requested GPU sizes over recorded attempt execution intervals at common sampling instants, with cadence chosen from the selected range: one minute through six hours, five minutes through two days, and fifteen minutes through seven days. Exact historical pod binding/cleanup intervals and allocatable capacity remain unavailable. The requested-GPU series therefore recovers only part of allocation; every point is marked incomplete and idle stays blank. Missing regional inputs leave blank spans. Coverage compares Finelog per-root Running task counts with retained attempt intervals, including CPU tasks; differences flag incomplete or inconsistent task history. It also reports setup tasks and unresolved GPU models. Without assignment creation times, the reader cannot establish when setup began, so setup GPU quantities stay blank.

The production metadata reader remains to be implemented and wired; without one the bridge returns HTTP 503. An approved temporary pilot used Grafana's actual CW service identity plus five-minute Iris dashboard-role cookies over the public Kubernetes controller proxy in all three regions. Existing job/resource/full-retry reads succeeded, GetCurrentUser reported dashboard, and SELECT1 was denied by Iris with HTTP 403. All temporary Role/RoleBinding objects were deleted and absence verified; Grafana's original proxy403 returned afterward. No production grants, credentials or deployment remain from the pilot. The minimal tested transport scope is services/proxy on iris/iris-controller-svc:10000; this reader's POST RPCs need the Kubernetes create verb, plus separate read-only Iris authentication.

A straightforward job/task-API reader would require at least 44,398 inventory calls over the captured sampled cohort, before additional pages and full-retry calls. This is a request-count estimate, not measured production latency. Existing controller backups offer a possible bulk alternative without controller changes: recent backups exist in all three regions. One GB200 backup was 25.4 MB compressed and 421.6 MB decompressed; it downloaded in 1.17s, decompressed in 0.22s, and returned 5,712 retained attempts in a 0.032s immutable local SQL query on devbox. Regional coverage, Cloud Run memory/refresh cost, and scoped object-read credentials still need validation before choosing and wiring that reader. Existing backups already contain requested band and current task band; older attempts do not have their own applied-band field.

All 421 Grafana tests and pre-commit checks passed. The requested-only preview uses captured task-state and regional metadata, with 672 common fifteen-minute instants per model. Every point is incomplete; 226 instants show a difference between per-root Running counts and retained intervals. Earlier applied-view replay timings are retained as prior measurements; production requested-reader loading and refresh costs remain unmeasured.

![Requested-priority captured-data preview](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yonromai/marin/23b45cce17be7ce8d7d3fb533c8c8ce5416e80a0/docs/images/grafana-gpu-allocation.png)

- **Relaxing XLA's gate is not enough.** XLA lowers `ragged_dot` to hipBLASLt's grouped GEMM only where `CanBeHandledByGpublasltGroupGemm` in `xla/hlo/transforms/expanders/ragged_dot_rewriter.cc` allows it: fp16 and bf16 on gfx942, fp16 only on gfx950 (openxla/xla#38088, unchanged on XLA `main`). The gate follows hipBLASLt's kernel coverage. The gfx950 kernel libraries in hipBLASLt from ROCm 7.1 and 7.2 (the cluster's system installs) and ROCm 10.0 (pip) have grouped-GEMM kernels for fp16 only, and `ROCm/rocm-libraries` `develop` has no bf16 grouped-GEMM tuning logic for gfx950. A plugin rebuilt with the gate relaxed would have no bf16 kernel to call.
- **The gfx950 fp16 grouped GEMM has one kernel.** Each gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM logic file in [`rocm-libraries`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/tree/develop/projects/hipblaslt/library/src/amd_detail/rocblaslt/src/Tensile/Logic/asm_full/gfx950/gfx950/GridBased) (about 9 KB) lists a single solution with a 16x16x32 tile. The gfx942 bf16 grouped-GEMM files list 4-7 MB of tuned solutions per layout. In the profiles, that `MT16x16x32` kernel accounts for the whole fp16 call. bf16 and fp16 matrix-core throughput is the same on gfx950, so a bf16 build of the same kernel would not be faster. XLA's setup kernel (`SetUserArgsKernelRaggedIn*Dim`) takes about 6 µs per GEMM.
- **XLA's default bf16 path does 32x the useful work.** It runs one hipBLASLt matmul of every row against every expert's weights at 1.20-1.42 PFLOP/s, then masks the result. The matmul is 68-91% of the call, and transposes and the mask take the rest. fp16 with `--xla_gpu_experimental_use_ragged_dot_grouped_gemm=false` takes the same path at 25-34 TFLOP/s.
- **The possible gain is small.** On MI300X, where hipBLASLt has tuned bf16 grouped kernels, XLA's grouped GEMM took 11-28% less time per call than tuned Triton (#9904, microbenchmarks only). Triton `ragged_dot` was 21% of the MI350X batch-64 step in [this profile](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6026123445), taken before the kernel rewrite and flash attention. If the MI300X edge carried over to gfx950, it would save about 2-6% of step time (21% × 11-28%), and less now that the rewritten Triton kernels are faster.
- **If someone picks this up:** test fp16 first, because it needs no plugin rebuild. Generate large-tile gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM solutions from the `rocm-libraries` tag that matches ROCm 10.0.0, and set `HIPBLASLT_TENSILE_LIBPATH` to a copy of the stock gfx950 library directory with the new files added. Add bf16 solutions and rebuild the plugin with the gate relaxed only if fp16 beats Triton. The other route is to ask AMD to ship tuned gfx950 grouped-GEMM kernels in hipBLASLt. Until then, MI350X keeps Triton `ragged_dot`.

</details>

topics.title: [eval] Run each evaluation as a StepSpec
topics.body:
Run each selected evaluation as its own StepSpec. StepRunner owns locking, retries, and success caching at each result path. An Iris restart skips successful steps before starting their model servers. Each step starts its candidate and optional judge server; `--max-concurrent` bounds simultaneous evaluations (default 8). A server startup failure writes a failed record only for the affected evaluation.

The eval launcher binds StepSpecs when it submits a prepared batch, after caller changes to priority or executor. Each submission gets fresh run IDs, including AIME repeats. Step identities include the resolved model and evaluator configuration, runtime revisions, judge configuration, and policy version. Verified policy versions retain their pinned benchmark sources and Harbor/Evalchemy commits.

EvalDash reads the StepSpec status file in each run's record directory. It withholds scores from running or failed steps while showing those states in run views. Shared measurement extraction reads record contents without depending on dashboard enrichment. Historical records without a step status retain their existing display.

A crash after writing a record but before StepRunner marks the step successful can rerun that evaluation. The [October 6, 2026 incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/627) showed a successful record replaced after a duplicate eval was cancelled.

The safe affected repository suite (`uv run --no-project infra/ci/run_tests.py`) passed 2,390 tests, with 3 skipped and 5 expected failures. Another 95 EvalDash tests passed. The four Docker-backed EvalDash kernel tests were not run here; their local PostgreSQL fixture timed out in an earlier attempt.

topics.title: [iris] Give tasks a token that acts as the job's owner
topics.body:
Stacks on #9817.

A controller with auth enabled now mints a control-plane token for each
dispatched task, with the job's owner as subject and the new role "task". It
rides on RunTaskRequest.task_token, and the Docker worker and the Kubernetes
pod builder put it in IRIS_TASK_TOKEN for every profile except
CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX. The in-task client (iris_ctx, IrisClient.in_cluster,
ClusterResolver) presents it on every controller RPC.

Today a task reaches the controller only through auth.trusted_cidrs, which
makes it the anonymous admin. On every production cluster tasks share their
node's address, so those ranges cannot be narrowed while tasks have no other
credential. With the token, child-job submission, endpoint registration and
resolution, and ExecInContainer work under the owner's identity.

The task role has no admin authority. A task may give a child job an elevated
container profile or the PRODUCTION or SYSTEM band only when the child's
parent already holds it, so existing privileged and production job trees keep
launching children. Raw SQL queries and budget changes fail for a task that
presents its token, and a root job a task submits is owned by the job's owner.
Each dispatch mints a fresh token, valid for 30 days and not revocable. Under
null auth no token is minted. On Kubernetes the token is a plain env value in
the pod spec, readable by anyone who can read pods in the Iris namespace.

This change does not narrow auth.trusted_cidrs, so a task that drops its token
is still the anonymous admin. The proposed per-cluster values are in the issue,
not in this change; they need this change deployed first, and on GCP and
CoreWeave the node ranges they keep still include every non-sandbox task.

Part of #9816

topics.title: [levanter] Replace the Pallas short convolution with a Triton kernel
topics.body:
Short convolutions on GPU run in a new streaming Triton kernel that reads each tensor once, instead of once per tap. The Pallas kernel is deleted, and the package moves from `levanter.kernels.pallas.short_conv` to `levanter.kernels.triton.short_conv`. In a single-GPU hero block, short-convolution time per step falls from 4.45 to 1.76 ms.

| Shape | Direction | Previous Pallas | Triton |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | forward | 423.9 us | 226.4 us |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | backward | 1024.3 us | 380.7 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | forward | 103.2 us | 59.3 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | backward | 262.9 us | 105.3 us |

Median kernel time per call on one GB200, 9 documents per sequence. The forward runs at the HBM floor of a read-one-write-one stream on the same tensor, and the backward at 1.14 times its floor. A port of the same algorithm to Pallas reached 230.0 and 403.7 us at C=6144, and needed code-generation workarounds (an inline-asm FMA, program ids clamped to the grid) that steer XLA's Triton pipeline.

The kernel takes kernel size 4, a channel count that is a multiple of 64, and bfloat16 or float32. The wrapper right-pads each local sequence to a multiple of 128 rows with the out-of-range segment id and drops the padded outputs, so any sequence length runs on the kernel. Other calls fall back to `short_conv_reference` with a warning. Every caller gets the kernel, so `GrugModelConfig.sconv_implementation` is removed; checkpoints are unchanged.

The forward and dx are bit-identical to `short_conv_reference` in bfloat16 and float32; dw changes only in fp32 summation order. On SM90 and newer the bf16 multiplies and adds are packed PTX (`mul.rn.bf16x2`, `add.rn.bf16x2`). Older GPUs take an fp32 op and a bf16 cast, which rounds the same way, and Triton's fp fusion is off so that LLVM cannot contract that fallback into a bf16 FMA that rounds once. The fallback has run on GB200 with the capability check forced, but not on an SM80 GPU.

Each program walks a sequence chunk of one channel block. It carries the previous three rows of x (in the backward also the next three rows of dy) and their segment ids in registers, and loads every row of a step before storing any; the backward writes one fp32 dw partial per chunk. A step whose rows lie in one document skips the segment masks, which cuts a backward step from 467 to 275 SASS instructions.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that was 7-15% slower per call shortened the step by 0.55%.

topics.title: [grug] Select the hero router's top-k experts with a Triton kernel
topics.body:
The hero router's top-(K+1) expert selection runs in a Triton kernel instead of a full XLA sort of every row: 0.096 ms per call instead of 0.856 ms at [65536, 384], k = 9 on one GB200, once in the forward and again in the recompute. The indices and their order match `jax.lax.top_k` bitwise for every input, including ties, signed zeros, infinities and NaNs.

XLA:GPU uses its own top-k kernel only for rows of at least 1,024 elements, so 384-expert rows fall back to a sort. The new kernel takes float32 rows narrower than 1,024 on a GPU device; everything else keeps `jax.lax.top_k`. Its gate asks the default device whether it is a GPU, because a hero test stubs `jax.default_backend` to trace a GPU-only path on CPU devices. The Triton gather-sum's gate makes the same check.

One warp holds one row in registers, as one power-of-two tile or, when that pads less, three equal ones (a 384-wide row is three 128-wide tiles), and takes k successive maxima over XLA's float32 total-order key, breaking ties by the lower column. A row in one warp keeps both reductions inside the warp; Triton reduces across warps through shared memory. A taken or absent entry gets the smallest key and the column n, which the lowest-column reduction never returns, so a negative NaN with payload 0xFFFFFFFF, whose key is also the smallest, is not mistaken for one. The kernel reads an int32 view of the input, so autodiff never asks it for a JVP rule. For k above 16 the steps run in a loop, which compiles in 0.2 s where unrolled steps take 36 s at k = 384.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that took 0.125 ms per call shortened the step by 0.53%.

topics.title: [grug] Correct hero remat and collective scheduling; build PGLE profiles
topics.body:
Carry-offloaded hero runs stop recomputing ~10 GiB of backward values per step that already fit in HBM, which shortens the step by 1.04% (13.874 to 13.732 s against #9830 on one 64-GPU hero rack, restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps). Ragged runs without the carry offload run their collectives one at a time, and `pgle_profile` builds an XLA PGLE profile from one trace of the train step. No model code changes.

With the layer carry offloaded to pinned host memory, XLA's `HloRematerialization` charged the 36 GiB carry stack against the device memory limit and recomputed values that fit (143 remat clones, 0.63 s/step of compute). The launcher now defaults `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading=true` whenever the carry is offloaded, so remat counts host buffers as host memory. Only the remat pass reads the flag, after scheduling and copy insertion, so it cannot reorder the carry reload against its consumer. The flag also lets remat offload values to host itself when its estimate of the step exceeds its budget, and that path aborts compilation in XLA's `OffloadInstruction` (hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118) when it picks the operand of a collective still in flight. At memory fraction 0.75 and slop factor 85 the budget is 87.7 GiB and remat estimates the step at 96.8 GiB, so the hero crashed at compile. The carry offload therefore also defaults to 0.78 and 105, a 114 GiB budget, and remat then leaves the step alone ("Rematerialized 0 instructions").

A ragged run without the carry offload keeps the latency-hiding scheduler off, and the collective overlap limit binds only that scheduler, so XLA's default scheduler can start two ragged transports at once. Compiled for a mocked EP64 topology, the program does so in the forward and in the backward, and on GB200 several collectives in flight have hung the ragged transport or given run-to-run different gradients. The launcher now forces `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES` for that configuration.

XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so with one collective in flight it treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under one GEMM. A profile built by `pgle_profile` from the program's own trace shortened the hero step with all of #9708 from 12.611 to 12.515 s (+0.77%). A profile applies only to the program it was traced from, so nothing uses one by default; the README describes the trace, build and rerun loop, and #9879 tracks using one in production.

topics.title: [grug] Leave ragged MoE transport rows unwritten when nothing reads them
topics.body:
The ragged all-to-all MoE stops zero-filling and overwriting transport rows that no consumer reads, and on GPU builds its dispatch buffer with one scatter. Outputs, drops and gradients are bitwise unchanged. One MoE layer's forward and backward is 4.4-4.8% faster and its compiler temp 1.37 GB smaller, and the hero step shortens by 1.41% (13.732 to 13.541 s against #9831, over 26 scored steps).

The expert chunks write disjoint rows of the dispatch and return buffers, but the custom VJP around `ragged_all_to_all` differentiated each write as an overwrite, so every layer's backward spent a [TK, H] select, add and zero fill on rows the next chunk would ignore. Each written row holds nothing before its one write, and for such a row an overwrite has the derivative of an add, so the transpose passes the output cotangent through unchanged. With every consumer reading only rows a collective wrote, the buffers need no fill: on GPU they come from a Triton kernel that writes nothing, elsewhere they are zero-filled. Each buffer is tied to a loop-carried value, because XLA would otherwise hoist an input-free buffer out of the layer loop and copy it into every layer's output slot. Dropped and padded slots get combine weight 0, and the combine and dispatch-gradient sums skip them. A GPU test fills every buffer with NaN instead of zero and requires identical outputs, drop counts and gradients under 22 routings, among them an expert no token selects, a receiver chunk and a whole receiver with no rows, a sender with only padding, and near-total drops, with two chunks of three experts per GPU as on the hero.

On GPU, a Triton kernel builds the expert-sorted dispatch buffer by reading each token's row once and writing it to the token's accepted slots, where a gather read every row topk times: 0.535 ms (6.6 TB/s) at the hero's per-GPU routed shape (TK = 524288 rows of the 3072-wide latent). Its weighted form serves #9833's backward. The gather-sum's forward loops over 1024-wide hidden tiles, which keeps more programs resident: 0.508 ms against 0.574 ms.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0), each head compiled fresh.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.
topics.head: bb67a1250359e1418632884abe71cf56ac2c44b9

topics.title: [grug] Compute the MoE routing-weight gradient on the expert side
topics.body:
With QuACK's expert MLP, the ragged all-to-all MoE takes its routing-weight gradient from the expert MLP's own backward, so the backward needs neither the expert outputs nor their return transport, and the hero saves the routed output instead of recomputing the expert down projection, the return all-to-all and the combine. The step shortens by 4.12% (13.541 to 13.005 s against #9832, over 26 scored steps). Peak HBM rises to 125.4 GiB of the 143.75 GiB pool.

The backend chooses the gradient together with its expert MLP kernel; `moe_mlp` takes no option for it. QuACK's expert MLP (SM100, SiLU, QuACK installed) takes the expert-side gradient for bfloat16 and float32 tokens, which is the hero's configuration. The portable `ragged_dot` expert MLP takes the exact gradient, <dout, y> over the kept expert outputs: it keeps y anyway, so the expert-side gradient would save it only the returned [TK, H] buffer and the return transport. QuACK with float16 tokens takes the exact gradient too. The expert-side gradient is zero at a zero weight, and zero or inexact wherever |w * dout| falls below the cotangent dtype's smallest normal number: 2^-126 in bfloat16 and float32, which only output cotangents near underflow reach, and 2^-14 in float16, which ordinary magnitudes reach. The hero's routing weights are positive renormalized sigmoids and its cotangents bfloat16. Forward, dx, dW13 and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; the routing-weight gradient differs at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp) at nonzero weights.

The gradient with respect to the combine weight w[t,k] is dS[t,k] = <dout[t], y[t,k]>, the only backward consumer of the expert down projection's output y. Since dy = w * dout and dh = dy W2^T, the same value is rowsum(dh * h) / w, built from tensors the expert MLP backward already holds. One custom VJP from dispatch to combine returns s = <h, dh> per expert row, sends it back with one [C, 1] f32 all-to-all per chunk, and forms dS = s / w in f32; dropped and padded slots get 0 by selection. The backward's transports reuse the forward transfers' offsets, swapped, and on GPU its weighted output cotangents come from #9832's scatter kernel.

The saved routed output fits the 114 GiB remat budget that #9831 gives the carry offload; the backward needs ~105 GiB. With the backward's transports no longer ordered after the recompute's, several collectives in flight gave run-to-run different gradients or hung on GB200, so every ragged run forces a collective overlap limit of 1.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0), each head compiled fresh.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.
topics.head: 596db268e9b682ca2660a983d9e57bd2a758a899

topics.title: [grug] Fuse the expert dSwiGLU and skip recomputed pre-activation stores
topics.body:
Two changes to the routed experts' QuACK kernels, each bitwise or within bf16 rounding:

| Change | Kernel | Hero step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SwiGLU backward and the routing-weight row dot in the dh GEMM's epilogue | 3.54 ms against 5.10 ms per expert chunk | 13.059 to 12.943 s (+0.89%) |
| No gate/up pre-activation store in a forward whose residuals are recomputed | 6.14 ms against 6.48 ms per median chunk, 96 chunks per step | 12.652 to 12.611 s (+0.33%) |

The expert MLP backward wrote dh = dy @ W2^T to HBM and read it back with the gate/up pre-activations in an elementwise pass for the SwiGLU backward and the row dot <h, dh>. A QuACK epilogue on the grouped dh GEMM now unpacks the interleaved (gate, up) tile, applies the SwiGLU backward to the fp32 accumulator, writes the packed (d_gate, d_up) and reduces the row dot, so dh is never materialized. Outputs, drops and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; dx, dW13 and dS change at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp), because the SwiGLU backward runs on the unrounded accumulator.

Under the hero's layer remat, the forward's gated GEMM wrote the [C, 2I] pre-activations of every chunk, which the backward recomputes. `_routed_experts` declares `optimize_remat`, so such a forward runs a primal that calls the expert MLP's new `apply`, which returns the output alone, and the gated GEMM gains a launcher that never writes the pre-activations. Each chunk's dispatch still waits on the previous chunk's gate/up output. The forward is bitwise unchanged, and removing the change from all of #9708 slowed the step by 0.47%.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.
topics.head: 8be8d83267cb613874b1cc14fc7c915b3383db84

topics.title: [grug] Hide the hero's bare MoE transports behind shared and chunk GEMMs
topics.body:
Under the hero's carry offload, every MoE transport except one ~1 ms routing-weight return now runs beside a GEMM, which shortens the step by 0.73% (12.730 to 12.638 s) and cuts exposed collective time from 1.19 to 0.85 s/step. Before, with one collective in flight, the first forward dispatch and both recomputed dispatches of the backward ran bare (0.63 s/step), and small collectives inside the routed-MoE section held the slot through expert GEMMs. Three changes that only work together fix the schedule:

- The MLP section's FSDP weight all-gathers, the QB router statistics and the drop count complete before the first dispatch. The statistics are saved for the backward, so its recompute does not rerun their all-reduces.
- The routed MoE runs caller work beside its first dispatch (`DispatchOverlap`), and the block hands it the first shared expert's gate/up projections. Barriers order the remaining transports so that each has an expert or chunk GEMM beside it, in the forward and in the backward's recompute.
- Each layer's carry offload copy starts after the layer's weight slices. XLA puts the 4.3 ms carry copy and the slices on the same memcpy streams in program order, and without this ordering the weight prefetch lands a slice behind the copy and stalls the layer (98-152 ms/step on the production wheel). On #9708's head, disabling only this ordering slowed the step by 0.79%.

Configurations without the carry offload keep the plain path. Neither path is safe under XLA's default scheduler, which can start two transports together, so the launcher refuses a ragged carry-offload run whose XLA flags switch the latency-hiding scheduler off. `forward_barrier` is an `optimization_barrier` whose backward passes cotangents straight through, so a weight gradient's all-reduce and FSDP slice still fuse into a reduce-scatter.

In a four-GPU gate, loss and drop counts are bitwise unchanged and gradients change at rounding level, within the difference between two runs of the same code. In the hero the carry ordering also moves fusion boundaries, so its forward changes at rounding level.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.
topics.head: 2de381d757b3f720e1352f449b81ea2511b3e419

topics.title: [grug] Run the shared experts' SwiGLU in QuACK GEMM epilogues
topics.body:
The hero's shared experts run their gate/up and down projections as QuACK GEMMs with SwiGLU and its backward in the epilogues: forward and backward of one shared expert take 13.93 ms instead of 14.51 ms at the hero's per-GPU shape (65536 tokens, width 6144, intermediate width 3072). Removing the change from all of #9708 slows the step by 0.35% and 0.22% in two pairs of runs.

With every PR of this stack and #9829, one 64-GPU hero rack ran 12.590 s/step (31.18% MFU), against 13.899 s (28.24% MFU) for main at #9708's base, with loss within 4.9e-4 of a run of #9708.

Each shared expert runs as two per-shard ops: a gate/up GEMM against interleaved weights with SwiGLU in its epilogue, returning the pre-activations and h, and a down op whose backward runs the SwiGLU backward in the dh GEMM's epilogue. dx and the gate/up weight gradient are single GEMMs on the interleaved layout. The split keeps the gate/up projection movable, so #9835 can run the first shared expert's gate/up beside the first dispatch. The weights stay separate FSDP leaves, gathered inside the shard map, so their gradients still reduce-scatter. Without QuACK, for another activation, or for operands other than bfloat16, the same ops run as XLA einsums.

Since only the down op reads h, the gate/up op stops h's gradient; otherwise the dispatch overlap would hand back dense zeros for h and the backward would run a SwiGLU backward over [T, 2I] per layer that adds nothing. SwiGLU now runs on the fp32 accumulator. Against an fp32 reference in a 4-GPU model gate, the loss error moves from 5.1e-5 to 4.5e-5 and the shared-expert gradient error from 1.22e-2 to 1.15e-2.

Directly on #9835 the change measured -0.11% (12.638 to 12.652 s): there the shared GEMMs cover the transports, and the shorter GEMMs left 0.24 s/step more transport exposed. Measured without #9835 it gained 0.72%, with peak HBM 123.4 to 121.9 GiB.

The QuACK availability check moves to `levanter.grug._moe.availability` and asks the default device for its platform. The shared experts' kernel selection calls it outside the ragged backend, where a test that stubs `jax.default_backend` on CPU devices would make the old check's `jax.devices("gpu")` raise.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

topics.head: 29d1e2fe9fcab4dcc1ce439ae540da16f95256c4

topics.title: [shellbox] Stop retrying an Iris exec after the machine closes
topics.body:
`IrisMachine` retries an exec that the controller refused for a full exec pool (#9828), under Iris's 30-minute RPC retry budget (#9780). When a command's timeout expires during that loop, `run()` closes the machine and reports `TIMED_OUT`, but `asyncio.wait_for` cannot stop the worker thread, so it could keep resending the command and have it admitted after the caller returned. Each attempt now checks whether the machine has closed and raises instead of sending. `close()` sets that flag before it terminates the job, so no attempt starts after a timed-out `run` returns.

Reported by the Codex review on #9780 after it merged.

Admit the identity through both IAP backends and allow GPU submission to cw-rno2a, cw-us-east-02a, and cw-us-east-08a through the hubs. Preserve existing TPU access and other accounts' policies. topics.title: [grug] Add a Triton flash attention for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
Add `gpu_triton_flash`, an opt-in fused causal attention for Grug on AMD GPUs, where Grug had no fused kernel. Existing backends are unchanged. The forward, dQ and dK/dV kernels are Triton kernels launched through `jax_triton`, like the top-k and Sonic MoE kernels. Earlier revisions of this PR used the Pallas Triton backend. JAX 0.11 deprecates it and tells Triton users to switch to the official Triton bindings and `jax_triton`; its other route, Pallas on Mosaic GPU, does not target AMD GPUs.

The kernels reduce each mask to one inclusive key lower bound per query, `max(segment start, q - W + 1)` for window `W`. Key blocks outside `[lower bound, q]` are skipped, and blocks fully inside it skip the mask computation. GQA indexes the shared KV head instead of repeating K/V. The dK/dV kernel computes `K Qᵀ`, so P and dS come out of their matmuls already transposed for the dV and dK matmuls. Under a mesh, batch and heads may be sharded; sequence and head_dim may not.

One layer's forward plus backward at the June model's per-GPU shape (8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16), median of three interleaved rounds in one process (jobs 457836, 457837):

| Mask | GPU | reference | Pallas Triton (earlier revision) | `gpu_triton_flash` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | MI350X | 20.19 ms | 6.77 ms | 5.11 ms |
| causal | MI350X | 22.26 ms | 10.04 ms | 8.38 ms |
| window 2048 | MI300X | 31.17 ms | 12.04 ms | 10.17 ms |
| causal | MI300X | 32.32 ms | 17.28 ms | 15.25 ms |

Pallas hands its Triton IR to XLA's bundled Triton, while `jax_triton` compiles with pip triton 3.6. With the Pallas revision's tiles, the port ran 11-13% slower than Pallas, so the tiles were swept again on both GPUs. MI350X (gfx950) runs the forward with two pipeline stages and MI300X with one; the other tiles are shared.

Value and gradient parity tests against `reference_attention` pass on MI300X and MI350X. CI has neither a GPU nor jax-triton, so it skips them. All dots run at IEEE precision: by default Triton runs float32 dots as xf32 on MI300X, which failed the float32 tests. Float32 inputs get smaller tiles, because the bf16 tiles overflow MI300X's 64 KiB of shared memory.

On ROCm the kernels need jaxlib 0.11.1 or newer with jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6; jaxlib 0.11.0 never loads `jax_rocm10_plugin`'s Triton launcher. The measurements above used jax 0.11.1, jax_rocm10_plugin 0.11.1+rocm10.1.0, jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6.0. #9989 moves the HPC Fund venv recipe to these versions.

Each run of equal segment IDs is one document, so a segment ID that reappears after a different ID starts a new document; `reference_attention` lets the two runs attend to each other. Masks that carry FA4 precomputed bounds are rejected, which excludes the moe_hero_ep, moe_hero_fsdp and fast_track variants.

jax-triton kernels fail today when one process drives several AMD GPUs: on a kernel's first launch, jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so all but one GPU fail and the step stalls at the next collective (repro in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9853#issuecomment-6090140907). #10014 lands the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels in the meantime; this PR replaces it once AMD's jax fork fixes the race.

topics.title: [grafana] Bound bridge memory during queries and pod scans
topics.body:
Release query inputs when a cached failure is recorded, and allow at most two dashboard computations, with each slot held from source loading through projection. Cached errors preserve their message and HTTP classification without retaining traceback locals or response bodies. Arrow cache accounting includes full referenced buffers.

Stream Kubernetes pod scans one page at a time and query watched deployments directly for the control-plane crashloop alert. Malformed Kubernetes JSON responses produce HTTP upstream failures rather than partial results. Keep Grafana's Cloud Run memory limit at 4 GiB in Pulumi.

The incident exhausted both the previous 2 GiB limit and a 4 GiB replacement. Local reproductions retained 192 MiB through failed queries in a cache capped at 128 MiB; the change releases those tables. A 2,500-pod synthetic scan fell from 108 MiB to 32 MiB peak Python allocations with identical results. These reproductions establish memory defects; they do not identify every contributor to the production OOMs.

[Incident and reproduction details](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/655).

topics.title: [haliax] Add tile-map Triton ragged_dot kernels for AMD Instinct GPUs
topics.body:
Do not merge yet: on ROCm, jaxlib 0.11.1 races when the GPUs of one process first launch the same jax-triton kernel, and an 8-GPU training step with these kernels hangs at its first collective. The cause and evidence are below; merging waits for a jaxlib fix. Until then, #10009 lands the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels, and this PR replaces it.

On AMD Instinct GPUs, `ragged_dot(..., implementation="triton")` now runs a second family of grouped-GEMM kernels, called tile-map kernels, written in Triton and launched through `jax_triton.triton_call` as Grug's routing top-k (#9942) is. JAX 0.11 deprecates the Pallas-Triton backend, and Mosaic GPU, the replacement JAX suggests, does not support ROCm. AMD Instinct GPUs use the tile-map kernels when jax-triton imports, which on ROCm needs jaxlib 0.11.1, and fall back to the group-grid kernels otherwise. NVIDIA GPUs, TPU and megablox behave exactly as before. NVIDIA keeps the existing Pallas-Triton group-grid kernels and block sizes, including the Blackwell `block_n` of 256. `_TILE_MAP_GPU_FAMILIES` lists the GPU families that use the tile-map kernels. Adding NVIDIA to it is a one-line change, for a follow-up once H100 and B200 have been measured.

The existing kernels give every group a full grid over all row tiles and exit early on most of them. In the tile-map kernels, the forward and input-gradient (dlhs) kernels launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a tile map built on device from `group_sizes`, as in megablox's `make_group_metadata`. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. The weight gradient (drhs) uses one flat grid over all groups and reads its lhs tile transposed. Rows past `sum(group_sizes)` are zero-filled. The old kernels leave them unwritten. Block sizes come from a per-GPU-family table swept on MI350X. Two launch-order options are new: chiplet-aware program numbering (`num_xcds`) and grouped tile rows (`group_m`).

Per-call times on one MI350X, bf16, balanced groups. Each cell is TFLOP/s for the old kernels, then the new ones (job 457866). The June expert shapes are G=32, with w13 at K=N=2560 and w2 at K=1280, N=2560.

| Shape | M | fwd | dlhs | drhs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13 | 16384 | 95 → 621 | 88 → 632 | 382 → 506 |
| June w13 | 131072 | 598 → 784 | 570 → 806 | 433 → 689 |
| June w13 | 196608 | 542 → 800 | 526 → 826 | 435 → 707 |
| June w2 | 131072 | 569 → 725 | 555 → 764 | 415 → 639 |
| Mixtral-like w1, G=8, 4096x14336 | 16384 | 423 → 815 | 383 → 864 | 443 → 756 |
| Mixtral-like w1 | 65536 | 633 → 857 | 601 → 907 | 457 → 777 |

A dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs runs at about 730-960 TFLOP/s on this GPU.

An earlier revision of this PR wrote the tile-map kernels in Pallas-Triton. At every shape above, the jax-triton kernels return outputs bitwise identical to that version on MI350X and MI300X (jobs 457866, 457867). XLA compiles Pallas-Triton kernels with its bundled Triton, while jax-triton uses pip triton 3.6, and with the same block config the jax-triton drhs kernel ran 29-33% slower on MI350X. Reading the lhs tile transposed and a new drhs sweep (job 457862) fixed that: 256x256x64 blocks with 8 warps and 2 stages reach at least 94% of the best of 272 configurations at each of five shapes. Against the Pallas-Triton version, drhs now runs 4-30% faster on MI350X and 31-76% faster on MI300X, fwd 2-8% faster and dlhs up to 2% slower on MI350X, and fwd and dlhs within 3% on MI300X. The fwd and dlhs entries are the ones swept with the Pallas-Triton version.

On ROCm, jax-triton hands jaxlib the path of a temporary hsaco file. On a kernel's first launch, `GetModuleImage` in `jaxlib/gpu/triton_kernels.cc` misses its cache, then reads the file and deletes it without holding its lock. When the 8 device threads of one process launch a new kernel together, all but one fail with `/tmp/tmp...; No such file or directory` and skip the rest of the step, and the others wait at the next collective until XLA aborts. In the June model on 8x MI350X with EP8, recompute_all and batch 64, any one of the three layouts on jax-triton triggers it (job 457945). A gdb breakpoint on `XlaCustomCallStatusSetFailure` caught the error (job 457957), and strace showed the 8 threads unlinking the same file within 0.3 ms (job 457961). Other jax-triton kernels in multi-GPU ROCm runs hit the same race, including #9942's top-k. The fix belongs in jaxlib: compile under the lock, or stop deleting the file. With the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels, the same step took 2.420 s against 2.627 s with the group-grid kernels (job 457874, reference attention).

The edge-case tests (empty groups, unaligned boundaries, rows past the last group, partial tiles, every VJP layout) run for both families on a GPU. All 88 pass on MI350X (job 457875). On MI300X, 58 pass and the 30 f32 cases skip, because Triton runs f32 dots in TF32 on gfx942 as it does on NVIDIA (job 457876). The tile-map kernels no longer run on CPU, so a CPU test checks that the tile map assigns every row to exactly one tile of its group. The per-call numbers and block sweeps come from `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py`, which is in #9894, stacked on this PR.

Background and earlier measurements: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027367267

topics.title: [grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds for GPUs
topics.body:
Add a `ring_gather_combine` MoE implementation: the ring expert-parallel backend with its dispatch and combine done as gathers in both directions. `implementation=None` resolves to it on GPUs, CUDA and ROCm alike. On other backends, TPU included, `None` still resolves to `ring`, which keeps the scatter-add combine, and `moe_implementation="ring"` selects `ring` on any backend. Like the other expert-parallel implementations, it runs only on an expert mesh axis of size two or more. Without one, `moe_mlp` falls back to the local `scatter` path, so a single-device call never reaches the gather code.

On AMD GPUs the combine `zeros_like(x_global).at[token_local].add(...)` and the transpose of the dispatch `jnp.take` compile to scatter-adds that run at about 0.8-1.2 TB/s. With `--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true`, which RL training on H100 enables, XLA lowers GPU scatter-adds to sorts. `ring_gather_combine` builds an inverse map from each (token, k) assignment to the dispatch slot that holds it. The dispatch take and the combine get custom VJPs, so activation rows move only by gather in both directions: each token sums its at most K slot rows (K = 4 in the June model). The inverse map itself is an int32 scatter-set (`ep_common._assignment_sources`, 0.04 ms at June shapes), and the routing-weight gradient still scatter-adds one scalar per slot, as in `ring`. `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local` takes the dispatch and combine pair as an argument, and `moe_mlp` binds it when it picks the backend, so the ring code has no platform check. The default is picked by `resolve_moe_implementation` from `jax.default_backend()`, which initializes JAX. The experiment configs' `__post_init__` checks can run before `jax.distributed.initialize`, so they now call `validate_moe_implementation`, which only checks the name. The combine's profile scope is renamed from `scatter` to `combine`, the name the other EP backends use.

In bf16 the two backends round differently. `ring_gather_combine` sums each token's rows in f32 and rounds to bf16 once, in the combine and in the dispatch gradient. `ring`'s bf16 scatter-add rounds after every add, on CPU and on MI300X, so the two can differ in the last bits of a token's sum. A bf16 test checks the gather sums bit for bit against an f32 sum rounded once, on inputs whose products and f32 sums are exact. On CPU the test fails if the sums run in bf16. On MI300X it cannot catch that, because XLA on ROCm keeps the fused bf16 sum in f32. At June shapes on one MI350X (job 453908), the combine matched an f32 scatter-add rounded to bf16 bit for bit. The order of a scatter-add's f32 adds is unspecified, so other inputs can differ in the last bit.

With `implementation="ring"`, the traced program is the same as on the merge base. Exporting its forward and backward for CUDA (8-way expert parallelism, bf16) gives an identical jaxpr and debug-stripped StableHLO with the XLA `ragged_dot`, and an identical jaxpr with the Triton `ragged_dot` that H100 uses by default. Pallas Triton cannot be lowered without a GPU, so that path was compared at the jaxpr level only. The profile scope name is the only difference.

Step time with `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py` and `--moe-impl` set to each backend: full June width and sequence length (hidden 2560, 256 experts, top-4, seq 4096), cut to 4 layers to fit 8x 80 GB, with 32,768 tokens per device and `recompute_all`. Each figure is the median over steps 5-24 of two fresh-compile runs per backend, alternating on one node (Iris jobs `/dev/ring-gather-9860-h100x8-b` and `/dev/ring-gather-9860-v5p8-b`):

| Hardware | XLA flags | `ring` | `ring_gather_combine` | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8x H100, EP8, `xla_flash` attention | default | 0.636 s | 0.623 s | 1.9% faster |
| 8x H100, EP8, `xla_flash` attention | `--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true` | 3.232 s | 0.756 s | 4.3x faster |
| TPU v5p-8, EP4, `tpu_splash` attention | default | 1.064 s | 1.162 s | 9.2% slower |

Repeat runs agree within 0.4%. Losses agree within 2e-5 on H100 and are identical on TPU.

The MI350X measurements below ran on an earlier revision that chose the gather path with a ROCm check inside `ep_ring.py`. The gather code is unchanged, except that the inverse map now comes from `_assignment_sources`, which runs the same scatter-set.

Single-MI350X microbenchmark at June per-GPU shapes (`bench_grug_ring_combine_top_k.py` from #9891, job 453908):

| | scatter-add | gather |
|---|---|---|
| combine forward | 2.420 ms | 0.969 ms |
| dispatch + combine, forward and backward | 5.436 ms | 1.790 ms |

Full June model, batch 64, flash attention, 8x MI350X, fresh compiles, step time with the gather path and the routing top-k from #9889 together:

| remat policy | before | after | jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.823 s (12.40% MFU) | 1.735 s (13.03% MFU) | 453972 / 453979 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.848 s | 1.788 s | 453841 / 453957 |

Losses agree within 4e-4. These runs used the flash attention from #9853 and the tuned Triton `ragged_dot` from #9859. This PR does not depend on either.

With the GPU default, `test_grugformer_moe.py` passes on CPU (job 461508) and on one MI350X, where the multi-device tests skip (job 461652). On 8x H100, `None` resolves to `ring_gather_combine` and every ring test passes, including the one that hangs on MI300X. 6 `ragged_all_to_all` tests fail there, the same way on `main` (Iris jobs `/dev/ring-gather-9860-h100x8-tests` and `/dev/ring-gather-9860-h100x8-ragged-ab2`). The experiment-config tests pass on CPU (job 461652). The ring tests in `test_grugformer_moe.py`, including `ring_gather_combine` against `ring` with capacity drops, pass on 8x MI300X (12 tests) and on CPU (9 tests; 3 in-process multi-device tests skip) in job 456128. The bf16 test and the other `ring_gather_combine` tests pass on 8x MI300X and on CPU in job 458228. With #9928 and #9880 stacked on top, the 17 ring tests pass on 8x MI300X in job 456022. Some MI300X runs hang in `test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available[all_valid-ring]`, with one GPU busy and the other seven idle. The same test hangs on `main` (job 456135: 2 of 4 runs on this branch, 1 of 4 on `main`). On 8x MI350X (job 454059) the earlier revision passed the whole file except 5 ragged all-to-all tests, which also fail on `main` (job 454060) because `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` cannot parse `gfx950` as a compute capability.

#9928 and then #9880 (`ring_dedup`) are stacked on this branch. `ring_dedup` reuses `_dispatch_rows` and `_combine_rows`.

topics.title: [levanter] Preserve staged mixture indices beyond 2^31
topics.body:
Staged mixtures now preserve child indices when a stage begins after 2^31 samples. Cumulative counts previously used 32-bit storage, and multiplying a stage's block count by samples per block also overflowed before accumulation. Reads in the next stage could therefore use negative child indices.
