topics.title: [grug] Run the production hero with a PGLE latency profile
topics.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

topics.title: [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE backend
topics.body:
Add `ring_dedup`, an opt-in expert-parallel MoE backend selected with `moe_implementation="ring_dedup"`. `ring` all-gathers every token to every expert shard and reduce-scatters a full-size output. With top-4 of 256 experts over 8 shards, a token reaches 3.3 shards on average, so most of those bytes go to shards that do no work on them.

`ring_dedup` sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its top-4 experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`. A small metadata `all_to_all` carries the combine weights and local expert ids, and a trailer row holds the sender's valid count. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule, local assignment selection (`_select_local_assignments`, #9928) and `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32, and returns one row per token. Every hidden-width movement is a gather through ring's `_dispatch_rows` and `_combine_rows` (#9860), so neither pass uses a scatter-add.

The sender capacity per destination is `pooled_transport_capacity_factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing, scaled by the sender's valid tokens, and `moe_mlp` raises if it is unset. It reuses the `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` parameter so one benchmark flag sets the sender capacity for both backends. The capacity has no worst-case guarantee: correlated routing can drop a token's assignments to a destination that still has expert capacity. A factor of 1.1 gave no sender drops on the June benchmark (`--pooled-transport-capacity-factor`, #9852) and on uniform routing; other workloads may need another value. At batch 64 each collective moves 537 MB per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring.

On CPU in f32, the 8-shard tests match a dense reference to 1e-5 in outputs and all four gradients with sender drops, receiver drops, both together under uneven padding with an empty sender shard, and an all-padding batch, and match ring wherever no sender drops. In bf16, `ring_dedup` also keeps the routing-weight gradient in f32. Against f32 ring on one full-shape layer on 8x H100, its outputs and gradients are within 0.47-0.52%. bf16 ring is within 0.50-0.57% except the routing-weight gradient, at 5.75%, because ring casts the routing weights to bf16. On MI350X and TPU v6e the two backends' routing-weight gradients agree to 0.17%. The full-model drop rate on MI350X is 1.00-1.12%, against 0.93-0.99% for ring.

June Snowball 67B-A2B, 8x MI350X, EP8, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile caches:

| Remat | ring | ring_dedup | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.730 s (13.07% MFU) | 1.580 s (14.31% MFU) | 454012 / 454021 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.798 s | 1.688 s | 454022 / 454026 |

The MI350X ring column ran ring with the gather combine, now `moe_implementation="ring_gather_combine"`, with the ROCm routing top-k from #9889 in place. One `ring_dedup` run (job 454010) ran out of memory on GPU 7 at step 5 and hung; its retry passed. That was allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer, which also hits ring at batch 96, and #9901 fixes it with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` in the HPC Fund wrapper.

On NVIDIA `ring_dedup` is faster than the GPU default `ring_gather_combine`. On TPU it is slower than `ring`, so TPU should keep `ring`. One MoE layer at the June batch-64 shapes (262,144 tokens, uniform routing, capacity factor 1.0), forward and backward, median of 20 calls, transport 1.1:

| One layer | 8x H100 | TPU v5p-16 (8 chips) | TPU v6e-8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| ring | 36.0 ms | 109.9 ms | 106.0 ms |
| ring_gather_combine | 33.4 ms | | 225 ms |
| ring_dedup | 25.6-26.1 ms | 131.6 ms | 182.7 ms |

topics.title: [grug] Add a one-GPU Grug attention layer benchmark
topics.body:
Add `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention.py`, which times one Grug attention layer on one GPU. For each mask (2048-token sliding window, global causal) and each implementation passed to `--impl`, it reports forward and forward-plus-backward time and the max absolute output difference against the first implementation. With `--sweep --sweep-part fwd|dq|dkv` it times a grid of tile sizes, warps and stages for one of the three Pallas-Triton flash kernels (forward, dQ, dK/dV) and keeps the defaults for the other two. TFLOP/s counts only the FLOPs the mask needs over the allowed (query, key) pairs. Each time is the median of ten 0.2 s windows after a 1 s warmup. Results are printed as `RESULT {json}` lines.

Defaults are the June per-GPU shape at global batch 64 on 8 GPUs: 8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16.

```bash
python lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention.py --impl reference xla_flash gpu_pallas_triton_flash
python lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention.py --impl gpu_pallas_triton_flash --sweep --sweep-part dkv
```

Forward plus backward time on one MI350X with jax 0.11.1 and the ROCm 10.1 plugin (job 460980):

| Mask | reference | xla_flash | gpu_pallas_triton_flash |
|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | 18.84 ms (96 TF/s) | 22.66 ms (80 TF/s) | 6.74 ms (268 TF/s) |
| causal | 20.89 ms (115 TF/s) | 22.89 ms (105 TF/s) | 10.02 ms (240 TF/s) |

In the same job, the dK/dV sweep with the window mask ran all 36 configs. The default tile, 128 queries x 64 keys with 4 warps and 1 stage, was the fastest at 6.80 ms.

The script imports `TritonFlashBlockSizes` and `pallas_triton_flash_attention` from #10014 and is stacked on that branch. Merge after #10014. If #9853's jax_triton kernels replace the Pallas-Triton module, the script's imports and default `--impl` must change with them.

topics.title: [levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch
topics.body:
Harrier's shuffle blocks change from a fixed 256 sequences to a fixed 2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K the two are identical, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer context, the token-sized blocks keep the outer block permutation the same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle window changes. With the old 256-sequence blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T.

The new LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases describes the earlier context lengths of a resumed run, one ContextPhaseConfig per length. With prior_context_phases set, each source skips the unread rest of the shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a change in the active sources is rejected. So is a phase at the same sequence length as the one before it, since there a source could continue in place and the skip would only discard data. The seed, the source order, and restoring at the last switch step cannot be checked from the config, so the field docstring states them. The offsets come from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at 16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

topics.title: [grug] Keep hero eval and FLOPs metrics continuous across a relaunch
topics.body:
GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len fixes the held-out eval context independently of the training context, so a run that changes context can keep scoring at 4K and its eval_dropless/* series stays comparable. The dropless eval reports evaluation start and end progress events, as the other evals do.

Per-example FLOPs rise with context length, so the cumulative throughput/total_gflops would jump at a context switch. A FlopsBaseline (completed steps and cumulative FLOPs at the handoff) adds the parent's history to the new shape's count; current MFU uses the new attention cost.

topics.title: [levanter] Add a benchmark for the Triton ragged_dot kernels
topics.body:
Add `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py`, which times the Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM behind `haliax.nn.ragged_dot` on one or more GPUs. For each layout (fwd, dlhs, drhs) it times both Triton kernel families (`tile_map` and `group_grid`), XLA's `ragged_dot_general` and a dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs. Each timing is the median of repeated windows after a warmup. Rows are written as JSON lines.

With `--sweep`, the script times the tile-map kernel for every block config in a bounded grid over block sizes, warps, stages, `num_xcds` and `group_m`. `--shard i/n` runs every n-th config, so the GPUs of one node can split the grid. The AMD block-size table and the per-call numbers in #10009 came from this script on MI350X.

With `--devices N`, each implementation runs on the first N local GPUs at once, as one `shard_map` program in which every GPU computes its own copy of the case, as a training step runs the expert GEMMs from one process. Times stay per GPU, and rows record N in `device_count`. On 8x MI350X (job 461032, the w13 cases at M=16384 and 131072), every Triton and XLA row with 8 GPUs busy was within 1.2% of its one-GPU time. The same mode on #9859's jax-triton kernels (job 460977, another node) hit the jaxlib hsaco race in 3 of 6 tile-map rows and ran 0-7% slower per GPU with 8 GPUs, dense matmul included; we have not found the cause of that slowdown.

The script calls the tile-map kernels and block-config lookup that #10009 adds, so this PR is stacked on #10009. Merge #10009 first. #9859 ports the same kernels to Triton launched through jax-triton, with `_tile_map_triton_call` as the tile-map entry point. Branch `levanter/bench-ragged-dot-triton-jax-triton` keeps a version of this script for that port.

On one MI350X (job 460986), the timing mode and a five-config `--sweep --shard 1/3` ran with no errors. At the June w13 shape (G=32, K=N=2560, M=16384), the tile-map kernels ran fwd, dlhs and drhs at 594, 639 and 486 TFLOP/s, against 594, 635 and 483 in #10009.

topics.title: [zephyr] Abort ThreadedBatchWriter output when the producer fails
topics.body:
When the body of a ThreadedBatchWriter `with` block raised, `__exit__` sent
the normal end-of-stream sentinel. The write function then completed, and
`write_parquet_file` committed the partial file through `atomic_rename`.
Stages that treat an existing output file as "shard done" then skipped the
shard on a re-run and kept the partial output. The normalize main/dups writer
and the datakit quality writer use this pattern.

`__exit__` now sets an abort event before it wakes the thread. The next read
of the write function's stream raises `WriterAbortedError`, so `atomic_rename`
removes its temporary file and nothing is committed. A normal close is
unchanged.

The datakit quality stage in #9694 removes partial outputs after the fact
(`_discard_outputs`); with this change, that code is not necessary.

topics.title: [levanter] Stop background iterators after completion
topics.body:
Buffered background iterators now remain stopped after the producer finishes or raises. Previously, consuming the single end marker or error left later `next()` calls waiting forever on an empty queue. Levanter uses this iterator to prefetch data loader batches and evaluation requests.

Regression tests reproduce the hang after normal exhaustion and producer failure in bounded and unbounded queues. The affected safe suite passed 1,063 tests with 13 skips.

topics.title: [haliax] Prefer XLA ragged_dot on AMD MI300X and MI325X
topics.body:
On AMD MI300X and MI325X (gfx942), `ragged_dot(implementation="auto")` now tries XLA before the Pallas Triton kernels. MI350X (gfx950), NVIDIA, TPU and CPU keep their current order. `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL` still overrides the choice.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X found that XLA's bf16 grouped GEMM takes 11-28% less time than the best Triton config for each fwd, dlhs and drhs triple. For example, the June w13 projection at M=131072 took 10.91 ms with XLA and 12.25 ms with tuned Triton. These numbers come from microbenchmarks only. We have not run a full-model A/B on MI300X. MI350X must keep Triton because XLA rejects bf16 `ragged_dot` on gfx950.

XLA's hipBLASLt grouped GEMM crashes with `ROCM_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` when HIP command buffers are on, so ROCm runs must pass `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`. The MI300X timings above used that flag. The Grug training entry points already set it by default, and so does the HPC Fund Slurm wrapper, `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` on `main`.

`_GpuFamily` gains an `AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` member, detected from the compute capability that ROCm reports (`"gfx942"`). gfx942 keeps the tile-map kernels and the block configs swept on MI350X, so the Triton fallback is unchanged. #9905 is stacked on this PR and reuses `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` for its MI300X block configs, so merge #10009, then this PR, then #9905.

At #9905's head, which contains this PR, the file gives 46 passed and 30 skipped f32 kernel cases on MI300X (job 458222) and 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223).

Stacked on #10009. Merge #10009 first, then retarget this PR to `main`.

topics.title: [haliax] Tune tile-map ragged_dot dlhs and drhs blocks for MI300X
topics.body:
Give MI300X and MI325X (gfx942) their own dlhs and drhs tile-map blocks for the Triton `ragged_dot` kernels: 128x256x32, 4 warps, 8 XCDs, group_m=2, with 2 pipeline stages for dlhs and 1 for drhs. Until now gfx942 reused the MI350X (gfx950) blocks. gfx942 has 64 KiB of LDS per CU, against 160 KiB on gfx950, and the MI350X dlhs and drhs blocks run 20-35% slower on MI300X than the swept tile. The forward pass keeps the MI350X block (256x256x64). 128x256x32 is 16% faster for fwd at the June shape with M=16384, but no faster at M=131072 and 15-22% slower at a Mixtral-like shape.

The table is keyed on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` from #9904. That PR makes `implementation="auto"` prefer XLA on gfx942, so these blocks apply when Triton is selected explicitly. Merge order: #10009, then #9904, then this PR.

The f32 skip in `test_triton_kernel_families_match_ragged_dot_general`, which #10009 adds for gfx942, now keys on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942`. Triton uses xf32 for f32 dots on gfx942, and the group-grid f32 tiles exceed the 64 KiB LDS.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X (partition `mi3001x`; jobs 454650, 454673, 454679 and 454683; sweeps 454658, 454659, 454667 and 454668) show that the tuned dlhs and drhs blocks cut a fwd+dlhs+drhs triple by 9-24%. For example, the June w13 shape at M=131072 drops from 14.67 ms to 12.25 ms.

At this branch's head, `lib/haliax/tests/test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py` gives 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223) and, on MI300X, 46 passed and 30 skipped (job 458222).

Eval records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals//record.json` (every record id is in the final comment's ledger). GPU-hour method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298. ## Not in scope Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval). ## Decision log - 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher. - 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro (B 44.1) and GPQA-D (B 41.9) measured as fallbacks and not used. - 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain. - 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm. - 2026-10-08: E frozen at step 272 for every arm; E+ built as a separate reference only. Arms changed from the plan: one sample per prompt for both SFT arms (not up to 4), no LR sweep, 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD. The arms ran in parallel on Iris. - 2026-10-09: RS-SFT and OPD final checkpoints not selected (drops on one direction with paired CI excluding 0); epoch-3 checkpoints selected on two-pass means. Final results posted in one comment; the running-log comments were removed and are archived with the ledger.

🤖 Final results: SFT vs rejection-sampled SFT vs on-policy distillation for transferring the CruxEval expert back into B

TL;DR. All three arms recover most or all of the expert's CruxEval gain. Every arm trains on prompts drawn from the same 1,600 the evaluator scores (800 input-prediction and 800 output-prediction problems; plain SFT and OPD use all 1,600, RS-SFT the 1,503 with an execution-correct E sample), so this is transfer on seen prompts. Two-pass means on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0 (400 updates), RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9 (283 updates), OPD 79.6 / 75.2 (75 updates); the expert E scores 79.4 / 71.4 and B scores 55.4 / 57.8 (CruxEval input / output, pass@1 on 800 problems each). RS-SFT's two-pass means are 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD's; two passes on one run per arm do not resolve that ordering. Both are above plain SFT by 5.7–6.9 pp on input and 3.2–5.9 pp on output. Training cost: OPD 287 H100-h from allocation to the selected checkpoint (376 for the full 4-epoch run); plain SFT 62 and RS-SFT 57 for their full 4-epoch runs (the RS candidate is update 283 of 376 and was not timed separately). RS-SFT also used ground-truth execution results to pick its demos, which the other arms did not have. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K (B 90.4) or MATH500 (B 89.8); OPD 75 scores 90.4 on MATH500, 1.8 below E, inside MATH500's binomial 95% half-width of about 2.6 pp at n=500. These numbers do not measure generalization to unseen prompts.

Setup (the design doc is linked from the issue body).

- Student B: [`open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab).
- Expert E: B after full SFT on 1,454 [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) CruxEval traces, LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, step 272 (35.9 H100-h); export [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`). E+ (E + 2 epochs at 1e-6, 80.2 / 75.1) is a reference only.
- Evaluator: Evalchemy [ae362881](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8) (corrected 2026-10-13: the revision that actually ran is `ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`, recorded in every record's `eval_runtime` field; `c131e5ab` was the code constant in `eval_policy.py`, which the launcher did not use. The scorer and sampling settings are the ones at ae362881 throughout, so no number changes.), vLLM H100x8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap, thinking enabled, unseeded sampling at vLLM's default temperature 1.0 (the lm-eval chat client sends no sampling parameters). One pass has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp at n=800 (p≈0.55) and 3.0 pp at p≈0.75. Paired deltas use a problem-resampling bootstrap conditional on the sampled completions. Gist of all evaluator configs: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71.
- Matched AdamW hyperparameters across arms, in different implementations (Levanter for the SFT arms, Megatron for OPD): LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen (E froze it too; all exports verified to carry B's 26 router-bias tensors).
- Plain SFT: B + 4 epochs on E's first sample per prompt (1,600 rows, unfiltered), batch 16, 32 H100. 1,452,363 supervised tokens per epoch.
- RS-SFT: all 12,800 E samples (k=8) execution-graded in an isolated container; first correct sample per prompt kept. 1,503 of 1,600 prompts covered (774 input / 729 output); the 97 uncovered prompts stay in the eval denominator. 4 epochs, 376 updates. 1,056,479 supervised tokens per epoch.
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, B samples 4 rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E scores them (sampled reverse KL on the chosen tokens, coefficient 1.0, reward replaced by the distillation signal, no verifier). 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch, 4 epochs. 4 learner nodes (PP2 × EP8) + 1 rollout node + 1 teacher node, all H100x8.
- Selection procedure used (the rule 'prefer the final checkpoint when similar or better on both directions' was agreed before the final checkpoints were scored; the operational reading of similar as 'paired 95% CI includes 0' was fixed while applying it): if the final checkpoint is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions on the first pass, select it; otherwise run a second pass on both checkpoints and choose on the two-pass means. GSM8K and MATH500 run on the selected checkpoint and on any terminal checkpoint that lost the selection.

Results. CruxEval pass@1 (%), input / output. "Gap closed" is the gain over B divided by E's two-pass gain over B (24.06 pp input, 13.63 pp output). GSM8K (flexible-extract, 0-shot) and MATH500 are single pass for every model.

| Model | Input | Output | Gap closed | GSM8K | MATH500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 |
| E (CruxEval 2-pass mean) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT, 400 updates (2-pass mean) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 |
| RS-SFT, 283 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 |
| OPD, 75 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 |

Learning curves (single pass per checkpoint; the training trajectory, not the selection basis):

| Arm | Epoch 1 | Epoch 2 | Epoch 3 | Epoch 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain SFT (101/201/301/400 updates) | 69.6 / 67.5 | 73.5 / 69.9 | 69.4 / 71.8 | 74.8 / 71.3 |
| RS-SFT (95/189/283/376 updates) | 75.5 / 72.0 | 82.0 / 75.8 | 81.4 / 77.1 | 77.0 / 76.5 |
| OPD (25/50/75/100 updates) | 74.9 / 68.9 | 81.8 / 75.8 | 79.0 / 76.8 | 80.9 / 72.3 |

Selection. Plain SFT's final checkpoint was similar or better than its epoch-3 checkpoint on both directions (+5.4 / −0.5 pp), so it was selected and repeated (second pass 73.1 / 72.8). RS-SFT's final checkpoint was 4.4 pp below epoch 3 on input, and OPD's final checkpoint was 4.5 pp below epoch 3 on output, each with a paired CI excluding 0. Both arms got a second pass on their last two checkpoints. RS-SFT: 376 updates 76.1 / 76.2 against 283 updates 80.8 / 77.9 (two-pass means); the final is lower on both directions, so 283 was selected. OPD: 100 updates 79.875 / 72.0 against 75 updates 79.625 / 75.19; input differs by 0.25 pp and the final is 3.19 pp lower on output, so 75 was selected. The terminal checkpoints are reported in the curve table, not as the method result. The second passes reuse the same runs, so the four pass pairings per arm are one comparison, not four. Same-checkpoint pass pairs moved by up to 3.1 pp (OPD 75 output: 76.75 on pass 1, 73.6 on pass 2, paired CI [−6.0, −0.25]), so the conditional problem-bootstrap intervals do not capture all generation variability; two repeats are too few to estimate it. The final-checkpoint drops are therefore suggestive, not established.

Paired comparisons at the selected checkpoints (pass 1 vs pass 1; 95% bootstrap CI): RS-SFT 283 vs OPD 75: +2.4 [−1.0, +5.8] input / +0.4 [−2.5, +3.3] output on pass 1, and 0.0 [−3.4, +3.3] / +5.0 [+2.0, +8.0] on pass 2. RS-SFT 283 vs plain 400: +6.6 [+3.1, +10.1] / +5.9 [+2.8, +9.3] (pass 2: +7.1 / +5.9). OPD 75 vs plain 400: +4.3 [+0.9, +7.9] / +5.5 [+2.3, +8.8] (pass 2: +7.1 / +0.9 [−2.3, +4.0]). Against E (pass 1): RS-SFT 283 +2.0 [−1.5, +5.5] / +6.9 [+3.8, +10.1]; OPD 75 −0.4 [−3.8, +3.0] / +6.5 [+3.5, +9.5]; plain 400 −4.6 [−8.4, −1.0] / +1.0 [−2.4, +4.5]. Pass-1 and pass-2 pairings share the training runs; they are two draws of the evaluator, not two experiments.

Response shape: B leaves no final answer after the thinking block in 1,110 of 1,600 CruxEval responses; E in about 90. The same count was not made for the three arms, so part of each arm's gain may be this shape change. The 97 prompts with no execution-correct E sample among 8 (26 input, 71 output) score low for every model. Correct/n on pass 1 and pass 2: B 1/26, 1/71; E 2/26, 1/71 and 1/26, 4/71; plain 400 0/26, 3/71 and 0/26, 4/71; RS-SFT 283 4/26, 8/71 and 4/26, 9/71; OPD 75 3/26, 6/71 and 2/26, 2/71. The slice was selected by E failing all 8 samples on these prompts, so E's low score is selection-induced. RS-SFT saw no demos for these prompts. Comparing different methods on 97 selected prompts does not identify the effect of omitting them, so these are counts only.

Cost (H100-hours, Iris task-runtime accounting). Training figures are full-run costs for 4 epochs and include in-gang startup, native saves and exports; they exclude CPU preprocessing, demo generation and evals. The selected RS-SFT checkpoint is update 283 of 376 and the selected OPD checkpoint is update 75 of 100; costs are not pro-rated to the candidate. OPD's allocation-to-checkpoint figure comes from the run's log timestamps and ends at the checkpoint request, so it excludes the native save; plain SFT's 61.6 runs through its final HF export and job teardown. The two selected-cost endpoints are therefore not identical.

| Arm | Training (full 4-epoch run) | Demo generation | Exports | Allocation to selected checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E (expert) | 35.9 for 3 epochs (+15.3 in aborted attempts) | GLM traces via relay, no GPU-h on our side | in-gang | — |
| Plain SFT | 61.6 | shares the one k=8 E collection (14.6 measured once for all 12,800 demos, plus a 0.7 pilot; plain used 1 of the 8 samples, and no standalone 1-sample generation run was timed) | in-gang | 61.6 (final checkpoint selected) |
| RS-SFT | 57.4 | the same k=8 E collection (14.6, counted once for both SFT arms) + CPU execution grading | in-gang | full run 57.4; update 283 was not timed separately |
| OPD | 376.4 (6 nodes × 7h50m) | none (on-policy) | 58.8 (4 export-only jobs, 14–15 each) | 286.9 from allocation start to the update-75 checkpoint request (before the native save completes), plus its 14.2 export job |

OPD also spent 73.5 H100-h on smoke tests, debugging and the export path and 4.6 on a startup failure (missing W&B key) before the full run. These training-only figures are not the experiment total; the ledger adds evaluation (about 3.3 per CruxEval pass), failed-eval overhead, E and E+ training, and the reference runs. OPD per-update wall time was 4–5 min (256 sampled responses, 30,720-token cap) against about 17 s per SFT update; one prompt epoch is 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD and 1 demo for SFT, so epochs are matched on prompts, not on tokens or compute. One CruxEval pass costs about 3.3 H100-h; the ledger lists every eval run. Failed eval groups (serve preemption with a stale endpoint in the eval runner, and one preflight disconnect; see below) cost about 11 H100-h.

Confidence. The gains over B are large relative to noise (the lower 95% bound of every arm's paired gain over B is at least 9.8 pp). Between arms, the measured two-pass means put RS-SFT 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD and both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; each arm is one training run with no LR sweep, same-checkpoint pass pairs moved 0.5–3.1 pp on the six repeated checkpoints, and two repeats do not estimate run-to-run variance, so the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering is unresolved and the gap to plain SFT is the better-supported difference. The last-checkpoint drops in RS-SFT (input) and OPD (output) are each supported by two passes but one training run; see the selection paragraph for the statistical limits.

Deviations from the plan in the issue body.

- Plain SFT used one sample per prompt (E's sample 0, 1,600 rows), and RS-SFT used the first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows), instead of up to 4 samples per prompt. Uncovered prompts stayed in the eval denominator.
- No LR or epoch sweep was run for any arm; every arm used LR 1e-6 and 4 epochs, with per-epoch checkpoints as the only sweep.
- OPD used 4 rollouts per prompt, so its prompt epochs are not token- or compute-matched to the SFT arms.
- GSM8K and MATH500 are both reported as collapse checks (the plan named GSM8K only).

Material failures and fixes.

- Levanter could not HF-export from an S3 reference checkpoint; fixed by plumbing `hf_save_reference_code=False`.
- MarinSkyRL accepted teachers only as HF repo ids; added staging of the teacher from S3. The export-only job's config inherited the run's distillation objective, which requires a teacher the export job does not start, so the export failed at config validation; the fix drops the distillation block from the export config. Learner nodes ran out of host memory at checkpoint save with 512 GB; the full run reserved 1024 GB.
- MarinSkyRL does not convert checkpoints to HF format during training; it writes a small export request per checkpoint, and the conversion is a separate 4-node export-only job (about 14–15 H100-h each).
- The Marin eval runner keeps the serve address it first resolved. When the serve job is preempted and re-registers on another host, the eval loops on connection errors until its timeout. Two RS eval groups were lost this way and relaunched as fresh groups; no partial outputs were reused. Not fixed yet.
- Evalchemy sends no temperature or seed, so every run samples at vLLM's default. One GSM8K run failed Evalchemy's preflight request 9 s after the serve registered (server disconnected); relaunched alone, it passed.
- GPQA-D (41.9%, needs an HF token and a 28,672-token generation cap) and MMLU-Pro (44.1%) were measured on B while choosing the benchmark, as fallbacks in case CruxEval failed the teacher gate; they were not used further.

Next. Weight merging is out of scope here (it needs RL-trained experts that share B's initialization). topics.title: [grug] Move ring's local assignment selection into a helper
topics.body:
The next PR in this stack, #9880, adds a `ring_dedup` expert-parallel backend that selects each GPU's local expert assignments exactly the way `ring` does. This PR moves that selection into a shared helper first, so `ring_dedup` can call it instead of copying it.

`_select_local_assignments` in `ep_ring.py` covers the per-expert counts, the prefix capacity cap, the top-k selection ordered by (local expert id, flat position) and the padding of the `ragged_dot` group sizes. The computation moves without edits, so ring's behavior is unchanged. The existing ring tests in `test_grugformer_moe.py` pass on 8x MI350X (9 tests) and on CPU (6 tests; the 3 multi-device tests skip), in job 455432.

Stack, in merge order (each PR is based on the one before):
1. #9860 [grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds for ROCm (base `main`). It also edits `ep_ring.py`, so this PR sits on top of it.
2. #9928 this PR (base `grug/rocm-ring-combine-top-k`, #9860's branch)
3. #9880 [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE backend (base `grug/ring-select-local-assignments`, this PR's branch)

topics.title: [rl] Select PivotRL pivots from frozen-policy pass rates
topics.body:
This PR implements a few of the key components from the NVIDIA's [PivotRL paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.21383).

**PivotRL in a nutshell:**
1. make a bunch of `(trajectory, turn): (context up to turn) -> teacher action` tuples (I usually call this `long` or `melted` format).
2. generate `k` roll-outs from a frozen student at each of those points
3. grade them using "functional" verifiers
4. identify "pivot" turns -- ones that have non-zero reward variance and are meaningfully difficult
5. (... single-turn RL...)
6. ???
7. profit

**This PR is split into 4 commits, I recommend reviewing in that manner.**
1. add original nemotron graders
2. add datasets, initial data pre-processing and prediction code
3. prediction post-processing/filtering
4. add openhands dataset & grader for a novel experiment (I added this separately, to give a flavor for what it's like adding a new pivotRL task--tbd if any of this helps).

### Agent Generated

Build PivotRL's training data in Marin as artifact steps: candidates, pass rates under a frozen policy, then the pivots that Eq. 5 of the PivotRL paper selects (0 < passed < K and pass rate below λ), written as `train.parquet` in the candidate schema. Each λ and selection criterion is a small artifact over the same pass rates.

Candidates come from three releases. `marin.rl.nemotron_pivot` turns NVIDIA's SWE and Terminal pivot releases into one candidate per expert turn of each trajectory's longest row, keeping earlier turns' reasoning as `reasoning_content` and dropping NVIDIA's pass-rate fields; `experiments/datasets/nemotron_pivot.py` publishes them as `processed/nemotron-pivot-{swe,terminal}-long`. Validation holds out whole SWE instances (100) and Terminal tasks (30) by hash bucket and keeps four evenly spaced turns per held-out trajectory, about 500 rows each, since a trajectory's rows share almost their whole prompt. OpenHands candidates are prepared from `nebius/SWE-rebench-openhands-trajectories@3545538`: one row per expert tool call in a resolved trajectory, with the working directory replayed from earlier bash observations.

`marin.rl.pass_rates.measure_pass_rates` serves the policy with vLLM, sends one `n=K` chat request per row so each prompt is prefilled once, and grades every reply with a `PassRateTask` returning a verifyit `Reward`. Every grading component is its own column (`c_<name>` per sample, `passed_<name>` per row), so selection can switch criterion without resampling. Context overflows, persistent request failures, and grader errors exclude a row rather than scoring it 0. Rows commit in atomic chunks, so a rerun samples only missing chunks, and `config.json` refuses to resume under a different config. Every run sets `enable_thinking` explicitly: SWE and Terminal think, matching prompts that carry the teacher's reasoning; OpenHands does not, since its teacher never thinks. Grug runs keep special tokens so graders can strip its `<|start_think|>` block.

The graders live in verifyit. `nemotron_pivot.grade_tool_call` scores SWE replies with NeMo Gym's word-overlap argument match (the reward), the PivotRL paper's tool-name-only match, and an exact-argument match. `grade_terminus` ports the string-only Terminus-2 verifier, parsing the reply after any reasoning. `openhands_next_action` grades by what a call does and to which paths, so `cat core.py` from the package directory matches viewing `widgets/core.py`; pairs the rules cannot settle go to an LLM judge only when one is configured. MarinSkyRL computes training rewards with the same algorithms but pins the standalone verifyit repository, so sharing these graders there needs that pin moved to `lib/verifyit`.

This replaces profiling inside MarinSkyRL's generate entrypoint, which reached 63-79 samples/min on 16 H100s while vLLM ran 2-10 of 16 sequences, because each request group waited on single-writer trajectory retention.

Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05 smoke runs on one 8xH100 node each, the first 64 candidates per dataset and K=8 (seed 1), graded all 1,536 replies with no exclusions:

| dataset | thinking | replies that think | passes / 512 | pivots |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SWE | on | 462 | 113 (tool name only: 264) | 24 |
| Terminal | on | 181 | 20 | 9 |
| OpenHands | off | 0 | 280 | 40 |

On SWE, the prompt length vLLM reports is within 10 tokens of a local render that includes earlier reasoning and about 490 tokens above one without it, so the reasoning reaches the model; Terminal and OpenHands match exactly. Grug's thinking never leaks into tool-call arguments.

topics.title: [grug] Route QBRoutedMoE through the jax_triton top-k kernel
topics.body:
QBRoutedMoE now selects experts with `levanter.grug._moe.topk.top_k_indices`, called per token shard inside `shard_map`, in place of `jax.lax.top_k`. That is the jax_triton kernel from #9830, which the hero model already uses. `jax.lax.top_k` still handles rows of 1,024 or more (XLA:GPU runs its own top-k kernel on those), non-float32 inputs, non-GPU backends and environments without jax-triton.

On AMD, jax-triton 0.3.1 with triton 3.6.0, Levanter's GPU pins, compiles the kernel for ROCm with jaxlib 0.11.1 or newer. jaxlib 0.11.0 never loads `jax_rocm10_plugin`'s Triton launcher, so there the kernel falls back to `jax.lax.top_k`.

Time per call in ms, from 16 calls on distinct inputs in one executable, median of 5 runs. The shapes are the router logits per call of the hero model and of the June Snowball model:

| shape, k | GPU | `lax.top_k` | jax_triton (this PR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | GB200 | 0.837 | 0.0754 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | H100 | 1.107 | 0.0954 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI300X | 0.847 | 0.0665 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI350X | 1.000 | 0.0570 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | GB200 | 0.229 | 0.0207 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | H100 | 0.308 | 0.0238 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI300X | 0.351 | 0.0246 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI350X | 0.402 | 0.0167 |

The AMD rows ran on jax 0.11.1, jax_rocm10_plugin 0.11.1+rocm10.1.0, jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6.0, with the AMD HPC Fund cluster's ROCm 7.2 libraries on the library path, as `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` leaves them. The `lax.top_k` baseline depends on that: with only the wheel's own ROCm libraries loaded, `lax.top_k` on MI350X takes 2.4 ms (hero) and 1.7 ms (June), while the kernel times do not change. The kernel code is unchanged since #9830; the NVIDIA rows are earlier measurements of it with the same harness.

On NVIDIA, the models that use QBRoutedMoE (`experiments/grug/moe`, `experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp` and `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe`) now run the kernel, because Levanter's GPU extra installs jax-triton. In the optimized HLO of the June training step on H100 and GB200, the 4 `sort` ops of main's routing become 2 `triton_kernel_call`s, and the all-gathers, all-reduces and reduce-scatters are unchanged. Step time does not change measurably. June model at full width with 4 layers and sequence length 4096, ring expert parallelism over the node, `xla_flash` attention and XLA `ragged_dot`; median of steps 2-19 per run, runs alternating between main and this PR:

| GPU | Tokens per GPU | Runs per side | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4x GB200 | 8,192 | 4 | 0.5742 s (0.5723-0.5759) | 0.5740 s (0.5719-0.5760) |
| 8x H100 | 16,384 | 5 | 1.457 s (1.403-1.508) | 1.513 s (1.336-1.539) |

On H100, step time varied between runs of the same code: main's five runs spanned 1.403-1.508 s (7%) and this PR's 1.336-1.539 s (15%). Five runs per side cannot separate the two. Scaled to these shapes, the per-call times above put the saving below 0.1% of a step. At 16,384 tokens per GPU on GB200, runs of both variants intermittently hung in a training step or ran out of memory, so those runs are left out. TPU step time was not measured; there `top_k_indices` falls back to `lax.top_k` inside the same `shard_map`.

On MI300X and MI350X the kernel's indices equal those of `lax.top_k` computed on the CPU, for widths 37 to 1,023 and k up to 37, on random, tied, constant, ±0, ±inf and NaN rows. ROCm's own `lax.top_k` ties -0 with +0 and orders NaN payloads differently, while the kernel follows XLA:CPU and CUDA. The GPU tests therefore check the kernel's output against `lax.top_k` run on the CPU backend.

The AMD venv recipe in `experiments/amd/hpcfund/README.md` still installs jaxlib 0.11.0 without jax-triton, so runs from it silently keep `lax.top_k` until that recipe moves to 0.11.1.

Supersedes #9889, which added a separate ROCm-only Pallas kernel for power-of-two widths.

topics.title: [grug] Let the hero launch use the carry-offload memory budget
topics.body:
`trigger_hero.sh` passed `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.75` and `--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor=85` to the hero coordinator. Without the two overrides the launch resolves to 0.78 / 105 with host-memory offloading, the configuration measured in the #9831–#9834 rack benchmarks. The live hero is unaffected: Iris retries reuse the bundle it was launched with.

topics.title: [eval] Iris retries overwrite completed run records
topics.body:
An Iris retry can reuse an evaluation's serialized `EvaluationIdentity.run_id` and `output_dir`. The replayed Evalchemy process then appends samples and overwrites `record.json` under an already sealed result URI. A tracker link can therefore change its score after it has been sealed.

Reproduce:
1. Submit an evaluation batch through `experiments/evaluation/launch.py` and let an Evalchemy process finish and seal its FineStore archive.
2. Cause Iris to classify the parent task or Evalchemy child task as retryable after that write, such as a post-completion `PodDeleted` or worker preemption.
3. Observe that the replay has a new Iris attempt or child-job ID but writes to the original FineStore path and run-level `record.json`.
4. Compare the first completed attempt, replayed attempt, and current record at that URI.

Expected: an Iris retry must preserve completed results as immutable artifacts. It should either skip a successfully sealed evaluation or allocate attempt-specific run IDs and output paths. A later failed attempt must not downgrade or replace an earlier succeeded record.

Confirmed examples:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261003-210313-Aleph-Alpha-Kolibri-1-mbppplus-b75b/results` first completed at 262/378 (`0.6931216931`). A parent-task retry ran a second MBPP+ child against a new serving endpoint and wrote 274/378 (`0.7248677249`) to the same path. The current `record.json` and FineStore view report the second score.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261002-002728-laion-snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203-gpqa-diamond-5b7b/results` changed from `0.636` to `0.5993265993` after a parent `WORKER_FAILED` retry replayed GPQA-Diamond against a new serving child.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-nupa-9a91/results` held a sealed 5,000-item attempt with 2,414 correct answers (`0.4828`). Iris classified the completed Evalchemy child attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted`, retried the same task and path, and the final canonical record became `0.4788`.
- The Kolibri retry also changed MATH500 from `0.984` to `0.992` and HumanEval+ from `0.774` to `0.7682926829` under unchanged result URIs. When the retried parent was later killed, several earlier succeeded Kolibri `record.json` files were rewritten as `infra_failed`.

`_run_id()` is evaluated while constructing the batch in `experiments/evaluation/launch.py`; Iris retries replay the serialized batch. `write_record()` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py` then writes unconditionally to `{prefix}/{run_id}/record.json`.

topics.title: [Post-training][Model merging] Initial Experiments in Model Merging with Snowball 67B A2B
topics.body:
We implemented eleven model-merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 Snowball 67B A2B checkpoint variants with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores. Sequential merging via selective expert transfer retained almost all of the NUPA source's performance and matched the BFCL source's score, but the three best merges retained essentially none of the Base model's routed experts. We have not yet run the complete cohort of policy evals needed to judge non-targeted performance.

[Earlier RLVR experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735) showed that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can strongly and unpredictably affect non-targeted benchmarks. It can introduce or repair behavioral defects that change scores while leaving the model's underlying “knowledge” essentially untouched. For example, a model might return every numeric answer, such as “31.7,” as “final_answer.31.7” instead of the requested “Final Answer: 31.7,” collapsing a benchmark score. We conservatively treat these as model defects to remedy under normal use conditions rather than grader defects to smooth. Each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats, so we investigated efficient ways to combine checkpoints.

Model merging is popular among hobbyists and is rumored to be used extensively at frontier labs, though the scientific literature is thin. Most merging methods use very few FLOPs and often require no GPUs. This makes merging relevant to our goal of reaching the frontier quickly and FLOP-efficiently.

The target Snowball checkpoint had largely improved but acquired two severe behavioral defects that sharply reduced NUPA and BFCL performance. We used two other Snowball models as merge sources. Each was an expert on one target benchmark, but both were generally inferior to the target, or Base, model. The objective was to raise performance on both disparate target benchmarks without degrading non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all standard merging approaches we tried failed to raise both target scores strongly. They restored capability weakly on both benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. Extensive experimentation led us to try sequential merging via selective expert transfer. It retained performance on both targets, but required discarding essentially all Base parameters from the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

These three merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched the source BFCL score. None appears to meet the objective of avoiding degradation on non-targeted benchmarks; we will reserve judgment until the complete policy eval cohort has run.

Sequential merging via selective expert transfer appears promising for complex MoE merges. Our best strategy combined weights from the NUPA, BFCL, and Base models:

1. Start with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template.
2. Replace selected NUPA routed experts with BFCL experts. In each layer, select 32 expert positions using BFCL activation measurements and copy BFCL weights into them. This discards all Base routed experts.
3. Change NUPA's shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We made three versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

The percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version had the highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model:

- Starting with BFCL, copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts yielded only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA, copying 32 BFCL-selected experts yielded 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor, the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We found no better joint result with those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights, and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce. This was likely an unusually difficult merge target because tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently:

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA's tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base's tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers. This affects benchmarks even with unchanged weights: the same input text can produce different token IDs, and the same output token ID can decode to different text. The numerical vocabulary did not change. Both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

The chat templates also formatted tool use differently:

- NUPA's template presents tool definitions as one JSON array; Base's presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA's template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided; Base's omits those IDs.
- The templates differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Using the other template changes the model input and therefore the benchmarks. In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input:

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA's own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

The agent's experimental design was flawed and needs a follow-up study. It drifted almost immediately from adding specialist capabilities to Base toward combining the two specialists. We will enforce that specialist changes target only a small, measured fraction of Base weights in the follow-up study, and may also control for the tokenizer confound.

---

## Campaign 4: Policy-compliant sparse routed-expert transfer

### TL;DR

This follow-up tested whether a narrow, audited edit to Antidoom Step12 could recover capabilities from Reference-KL Step20. All 20 candidates passed the weight and file policy, and all 100 evaluation cells completed. The best candidate, `serial-06`, raised the four-target sum from Base's 174.90 to 186.63 while changing 2.40% of Base scalars; its MATH500 canary was 94.00 versus Base's 95.00.

The observed gain was concentrated in BFCL-Parity: `serial-06` moved from 5.70 to 15.45, alongside smaller gains on HumanEval+ (72.60 to 75.00) and MBPP+ (66.90 to 68.52), while OlympiadBench fell from 29.70 to 27.67. Expanding the eligible support to 15.25% and 19.90% did not beat the 9.50%-support winner. The strongest extension, `dare-linear-10`, reached 184.13 while changing 2.26%.

These are single-run, in-distribution search results. The campaign establishes a useful policy-compliant sparse edit, but it does not show broad retention or a statistically resolved ordering between nearby variants.

### Public result

- **Best checkpoint:** [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Serial-06-2026.10.13](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Serial-06-2026.10.13/tree/704f2fcbcced784acf41ef1993ec29c2ca068786), immutable revision `704f2fcbcced784acf41ef1993ec29c2ca068786`.
- **Exact recipe and frozen support:** [serial-06.json](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Serial-06-2026.10.13/blob/704f2fcbcced784acf41ef1993ec29c2ca068786/provenance/campaign4/serial-06.json).
- **Readback audit:** [audit.json](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Serial-06-2026.10.13/blob/704f2fcbcced784acf41ef1993ec29c2ca068786/provenance/campaign4/audit.json).
- **Protocol and sealed-result provenance:** [Campaign 4 public artifacts](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Serial-06-2026.10.13/tree/704f2fcbcced784acf41ef1993ec29c2ca068786/provenance/campaign4).
- **Merge implementation:** #9974.

### Experiment design

**Parents and objective.** Base was [Antidoom RLVR1 Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02/tree/50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e), pinned at `50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e`. The extraction target was [Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04/tree/fd07ef0f2b78a83099a0042e59c00de986e7b647), pinned at `fd07ef0f2b78a83099a0042e59c00de986e7b647`. Selection maximized the unweighted sum of HumanEval+, MBPP+, OlympiadBench and BFCL-Parity percentages. MATH500 was a regression canary and did not enter selection.

**Weight policy.** A candidate could change at most 20.00% of Base's indexed scalar parameters. Only rows of routed-expert gate, up and down projections were eligible. All other weights and every non-weight checkpoint file had to remain byte-for-byte identical to Base. Serial stages were always measured against original Base, so an intermediate checkpoint did not reset the budget.

**Support.** The fixed support ordering reused Campaign 2's seed-0, benchmark-independent R25 ordering. R25 is the deterministic routed-expert support whose whole expert blocks fit under Campaign 2's 25% scalar budget; [this frozen Campaign 2 recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/dare-linear-02.json) contains the inherited ordering. Campaign 4 took the first 16, 24, 40 or 52 of the model's 256 expert rows per projection and layer. Those prefixes covered approximately 6.10%, 9.14%, 15.24% and 19.81% of Base scalars, below declared caps of 6.25%, 9.50%, 15.25% and 19.90%. The audit counted final stored values that actually differed from Base; the largest observed changed fraction was 6.32%.

**Methods.** Ten DARE-linear candidates varied DARE density and delta scale. Ten serial candidates first applied DARE-TIES with density 0.20, TIES density 0.20, scale 0.25, coefficient 1.00 and seed 0, then applied offline [ISO-Merger](https://iso-rlvr.github.io/) on the same support. ISO-Merger composes donor displacement directions in singular-vector coordinates while reconstructing with Base's singular values. Variants 01–08 crossed the two smaller supports with four DARE settings or four retained singular-mode fractions; variants 09–10 extended both families to the larger supports. `serial-06` used the 24-row support and retained 0.50 of available singular modes after the fixed DARE-TIES stage.

**Construction gate.** Each output was read back and checked for aligned parent tensors, routed-expert-only support, declared support compliance, no more than 20.00% changed scalars, byte-identical non-weight files, unchanged tensor names/shapes/dtypes and shard layout, and a complete object inventory. All 20 candidates passed. Tracker merge time includes construction and this readback audit.

**Evaluation.** Each candidate received its own eight-H100 vLLM server, shared by that candidate's five evaluations; up to eight candidate groups ran concurrently. Serving used tensor parallelism 1, data parallelism 8, enabled expert parallelism, a 73,728-token maximum context, Base's tokenizer and chat template, and the Hermes tool parser. Code was pinned to Marin `aaf1878ce65a1a05b386aef257b952fa7205283a`, Evalchemy `958cdb8019b7a4c8432fe85eb9572538ceb75950`, and Harbor `2203bacd03d82e9d4f2a9422f0b3f7e9bb7952cc`. The suites used all 164 HumanEval+ tasks, 378 MBPP+ tasks, 30 OlympiadBench tasks, 123 BFCL-Parity trials, and 500 MATH500 tasks. The public checkpoint includes redacted copies of `serial-06`'s five records with effective configs, source digests, coverage, metrics, and original record hashes.

### Complete tracker

Scores are percentages. Target sum is HumanEval+ + MBPP+ + OlympiadBench + BFCL-Parity using unrounded values. Merge time includes construction and readback audit.

topics.title: [Post-training] Explore capability-preserving model merging
topics.body:
TL;DR: Model merging is a promising direction for Marin: different Grug/Snowball checkpoints have complementary strengths, but we do not yet have a reliable way to combine them while preserving the base model's other capabilities. Cheap weight-space operations could make this orders of magnitude less expensive than on-policy distillation (OPD). We would benefit from expert input on how to make that tradeoff work for our mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.

The policy evaluation tracker illustrates the problem (percentages; higher is better):

| Checkpoint | MATH500 | GPQA-Diamond | HumanEval+ | NUPA | BFCL-Parity/Pi |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [Grug Antidoom Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02) | 95.00 | 67.30 | 72.60 | 0.10 | 5.70 |
| [Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92) | 89.60 | 42.90 | 68.90 | 40.60 | 16.30 |
| [Grug Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04) | 92.60 | 63.00 | 86.60 | 0.30 | 43.90 |

Source: [policy-tracker snapshot](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/inputs/TRACKER.md). These are policy NUPA scores; the merge study instead optimized NUPA200, a 200-task subset of the policy’s 5,000-task panel. BFCL-Parity/Pi is the policy's tool-use evaluation with the Pi agent. No checkpoint in this comparison achieves the best score in every column.

Our [initial study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975) shows both the appeal and the unresolved problem. Static merge construction typically required roughly 1e11–1e12 estimated arithmetic FLOPs per checkpoint, often without GPUs. This supports the prospect of a large compute advantage over OPD, which requires rollout generation and training; we have not run a matched OPD cost comparison. Evaluation and any calibration or expert-selection work add costs beyond static construction.

The best merge scored 36.50% on NUPA200 and 48.78% on BFCL-Parity, versus historical specialist references of 38.00% and 43.90%, respectively. But its recipe copied only 0.76% of all parameter values unchanged from the intended Base (Step12). On non-target benchmarks, it scored 89.80% MATH500 and 52.19% GPQA-Diamond, versus Base’s historical policy scores of 95.00% and 67.30%; these were not matched reruns. That study did not establish capability-preserving transfer into Base.

We would welcome advice from people with model-merging experience, especially on transferring specialist behavior into an existing MoE checkpoint with limited weight changes, handling expert/router compatibility and the tokenizer differences observed in #9975, and choosing retention evaluations that expose damage outside the target benchmarks.

Done when: expert feedback informs a concrete follow-up design with a fixed Base, explicit limits on weight changes, and pre-agreed target and non-target evaluation criteria.

comments.body:
Hi, I can comment a bit on this (also tagging @marcociccone who has been doing a lot of work along these lines).

Anecdotally it seems that merging may work better* than OPD in the MOPD setup when merging RL-trained checkpoints:
- [This paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12566) which seems to have invented MOPD without credit (?) includes merging as a baseline, where it compares favorably.
- The ["MOPD paper"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30406) includes task arithmetic (a weak merging baseline) where it performs roughly on par with OPD
- The [Open-MOPD paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19098) also has some merging results and it works reasonably well.
- [This very recent paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04272) also has some promising results with merging in the MOPD setting.
- The fact that merging can work well in the RL setting is explored in [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22039).

The trouble is that there is some conflicting evidence, which I think stems from the following:
- We generally do not have a precise characterization of how well merging will work in a particular setting.
- Most work that evaluates merging takes the simplest possible method off the shelf (generally task arithmetic). This can work ok (anecdotally especially for larger models, see [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03617)) but there has been a ton of work on more sophisticated merging methods that have been pretty conclusively demonstrated to work better. The additional trouble, though, is that there are details that people often get wrong, for example how to merge the embedding/unembedding matrices, or other nuisance details (see e.g. the discussion of incorrect implementations of RegMean in [our recent work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01329)).
- Underlying merging is the choice of mixing coefficients for the constituent models, which is rarely explored but turns out to be important in practice.
- To get to the asterisk above, there often is only a cursory notion of what "better" means; often it is found e.g. that merging works better than MT/OPD on some tasks and worse on others, but this seems to largely be a consequence of the implicit mixing weights used by a merging method where no mixing weight tuning is done.

As mentioned above @marcociccone is finishing up a project investigating this much more thoroughly; the end product is a method for tuning merging coefficients and strong results using strong merging methods. It's a bit hard to claim "pareto-optimality" in terms of the merged model dominating the MT/OPD model for *every* task, but merging at the very least seems to be on par and also has the huge advantage of being much cheaper to use (and in particular much cheaper to try out new mixing coefficients to balance capabilities to your preferred profile).

HTH.

Thank you very much @craffel for the detailed comment here! As a Grug-brained newbie in the space of model merging, I would certainly be happy to experiment with the method of @marcociccone if he would like to check something into our monorepo!

Naively, it seems that model merging can produce models that look OK (even strong) under our eval policy but then acquire weird tics / behavioral quirks that would make them pretty unappealing as an official release. So we're looking into how to harden our eval policy against these kinds of failures (and also hopefully get better at merging models)

topics.title: [analysis] Independent pre-registered forecast of the hero's final loss, with 80/95% intervals
topics.body: Hi @ClassicLarry @dlwh, To add uncertainty to the Aug 19 pre-registration in #8435, I made an independent forecast of the hero's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` (4K eval packing). It is frozen at 58% of training and uses only public data. **Result:** median **2.035**, 80% interval [2.023, 2.047], 95% [2.016, 2.054]. The Aug 19 pre-registration (2.039) sits at our 68th percentile, so the run looks on track for it. A finish near 2.10 looks very unlikely. **Method in brief** - The ladder is used only for the remaining drop from now to the end. The level comes from the hero's own post-swap evals, which makes the forecast nearly independent of the floor E. - Backtests set the drift persistence, the method error and an allowance for distance-dependent bias. They use held-out ladder rungs and the 67B-A2B run (#6044). In nested leave-one-out, the 80% intervals cover 14–15 of 16 held-out cases. - PTB gets its own term because of its noise and the exposures in #9874. A PTB-free companion target is forecast too: 2.047 [2.036, 2.059]. **One finding:** most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap comes from counting lm_head FLOPs in compute. On the H100 d768–d1536 runs, excluding them moves the fitted floor from 1.913 to 1.573 and the forecast from 2.116 to 2.037 (see the comment below for the refit's exact setting). **Pre-registration, code and scoring rules:** https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/prereg-v2-2026-10-09/preregistration_v2.md - The scoring rules were fixed in advance, including what happens if the context or the schedule changes. - This is v2. I revised v1 (median 2.045) the same day after re-auditing its backtests, on the same data. Both versions are tagged, and every change is listed. - I'll post a check-in at 70% and the scored comparison after the run ends.

comments.body:
**Scored at the 16K switch.** The hero moved to 16K context at step 257,553 (#10101). Under condition 2 of the pre-registration, v2 is scored at the last 4K eval before the switch: step 254,999 (W&B `_step`; step 255,000 in #8506), 65.3% of training. Later evals pack at 16K, so nothing after it is scored (condition 6).

| At step 254,999 | Paloma macro (16 subsets) | Quantile score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Realized | 2.1114 | |
| v2 (scored) | median 2.1245, 80% [2.1184, 2.1305], 95% [2.1153, 2.1336] | 0.0076 |
| v1 | median 2.1256, 80% [2.1197, 2.1314], 95% [2.1165, 2.1346] | 0.0088 |
| Aug 19 trajectory | 2.1231 | 0.0117 |

- **Coverage: a miss.** The realized value is 0.0039 below v2's 95% interval (PIT about 0.003), and v1 misses too. The PTB-free companion, 2.1169, is also below v2's companion 95% interval [2.1257, 2.1396].
- **Quantile score:** 2 × the mean pinball loss over the five frozen quantiles, which equals the absolute error for a point forecast. v2's is the lowest of the three thanks to its lower quantiles; its median missed by 0.0130, more than the Aug 19 point's 0.0117. v2 also had the hero's evals through step 227,999, which the Aug 19 trajectory predates.
- **Since the freeze** (this also serves as the 70% check-in, because no 4K evals follow): all 9 new 4K evals came in below v2's median. 4 fell inside the 80% band and 5 below the 95% band. The 5 misses are the 5 evals where PTB and WikiText together were lowest; the macro of the other 14 subsets fell gradually, from 2.1929 to 2.1773. Refitted with the 9 new evals, the residual slope b (how fast the hero's 15-subset loss moves relative to the ladder curve, per unit of training fraction) goes from +0.0050 to −0.0137; without the two evals with WikiText drops (239,999 and 254,999), it would be −0.0050.
- **At step 254,999** WikiText fell 0.168 to 1.271, its lowest so far (earlier drops: #9874). That is 0.0105 of the eval's 0.0120 drop.

No PTB exposure window covers step 254,999, and condition 5 covers PTB only, so this drop stays in the score. In hindsight WikiText deserved a similar rule: in #9874 Larry suggested scanning it on Oct 7, two days before the freeze, and my audit found its drops about eight hours after the freeze. But no WikiText read has been mapped, and adding a rule now would be scoring after the fact. As condition 2 says, I'll still report the end-of-run value, unscored.

The two methods trade off by domain and are not matched controls for each other (RS-SFT had verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and a different token budget; MOPD cost 6× more H100-hours). Plain SFT recovers less; merging is a cheap partial substitute at half strength only. ## Caveats - One evaluation pass per checkpoint except the stated repeats; plain SFT's 803-vs-603 selection used two passes each. Intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons or checkpoint selection. - Both primary targets are test-exposed (training-is-test); the held-out MMLU-Pro questions are an additional probe, never a selection input. - The RS-SFT demo selector used an older answer-extraction rule than the evaluator: 14 of its 1,400 MMLU-Pro demos are wrong under the evaluator's rule, 15 prompts would have been gained and 1 lost, 45 would have used a different sample. Reported as trained; no corrected run. - Two records (B and MOPD-100 on MMLU-Pro) had a retried evaluation attempt; all numbers come from each record's pinned FineStore manifest (an earlier reading gave B 43.9 and MOPD 65.3 on the subset). - Evaluation infrastructure cost 1,752.6 H100-h of serve time, 894.5 of it in 31 groups that produced no record (serves left running on stale endpoints, #10030). ## Links | | | |---|---| | Full report with record manifest | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9984#issuecomment-6144923850 | | Single-expert experiment | #9920, https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 | | Record manifest (machine-readable) | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/records-manifest-20261013.json` | | Canonical MMLU-Pro labels and subset | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/` | | GLM traces and captured prompts | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/glm-bench-traces/` | | Demo pools | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/teacher-traces/mopd2/` | | MOPD config | https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/76fc4be980aff1b14a42bfa549b5fe7479744701/cloud/iris/configs/snowball_mopd2_cruxeval_mmlupro.yaml | | Merge tools | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974 | | GPU-hour method | https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298 | | Trace browser | https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/ | Weights are being uploaded to Hugging Face under open-athena; the S3 paths above will be replaced by HF links as each lands.

🤖 **Final report: two experts into one student (MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merging)**

## Summary

E_2 reached 66.4% on the MMLU-Pro subset used for its fine-tuning (B 44.5%) and 64.0% on the remaining docs (B 44.1%). Its CruxEval output score was 4.9 percentage points below B in one pass. Its IFEval instruction-strict point estimate was also below B (80.2% versus 81.1%), with an interval spanning zero; the other reported probe point estimates were above B. At the selected finals, mixed SFT-RS step-727 exceeds MOPD step-100 on the MMLU-Pro subset by 4.0 pp [1.6, 6.3]; the held-out difference is unresolved (+0.4 [−0.5, 1.4]). MOPD exceeds RS on CruxEval input by 4.9 pp [1.6, 8.1]; the output difference is unresolved. RS-727 and MOPD-100 are the selected finals of their arms (RS-727 similar to 546, MOPD-100 similar to 50 on every target). They use unequal compute, token budgets and verifier access. Plain-SFT step-803 was selected on two-pass means. The RS arm's demo selector used a different answer-extraction rule from the evaluator (quantified under Caveats). Weight merging at half strength scores above B in both domains with no training (CruxEval input 76.5, output 67.6; MMLU-Pro subset 63.2), below the trained arms on CruxEval output; the full-strength task-arithmetic merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs. Training-gang allocations: RS-SFT 93.6 H100-h, MOPD 557.9 (2 epochs, 7 nodes; plus 28.3 of export-only jobs). Evaluation serve allocation across the 82 eval groups: 1,752.6 H100-h, of which 894.5 in 31 groups with no successful eval child (details under Costs).

## Setup (unchanged from #9920 except where stated)

B = [`open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab). E = #9920's CruxEval expert (step-272; [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`)). E_2 ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254 @ acb97183](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254/tree/acb97183af633533df4f4f63d83adc1e0a7a9748) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task157-e2/checkpoints/karan/e2-mmlupro-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.09.1/hf/step-254`)) = B + full SFT on [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) MMLU-Pro traces with E's exact recipe (AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3% warmup then cosine, 3 epochs, fresh optimizer, frozen router bias, 32 H100), 1,359 usable traces over a seeded category-proportional draw of whole question-text groups (1,589 questions = 1,606 docs); the other 10,426 docs are held out from this fine-tuning and used as an additional probe (prior exposure of either split during B's own training is not ruled out; both primary targets are test-exposed). Labels: the GLM collection had keyed the dataset by question text, so 190 docs carried a wrong gold; every doc was re-joined to TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro test @ `b189ec76` by exact question + ordered options (artifacts and SHA-256 at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/`, independently verified against the pinned source and captured prompts; verification artifact `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/task162-candidate-verification-v4/`). Transfer arms start from B with matched AdamW hyperparameters (LR 1e-6, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, gradient clip 1.0) and frozen router bias, implemented in Levanter for SFT and Megatron for MOPD. The shared evaluation universe has 3,206 prompts (1,600 CruxEval + 1,606 MMLU-Pro). Plain SFT trains four epochs on 3,206 sample-zero demonstrations; RS-SFT trains four epochs on 2,903 covered prompts. MOPD runs two epochs with four rollouts per sampled prompt and domain-routed teachers (100 optimizer updates of 64 prompts; 50 per epoch). These budgets are not token- or compute-matched. MOPD = MarinSkyRL on-policy distillation with two pinned teachers, CruxEval prompts scored by E and MMLU-Pro prompts by E_2 (sampled reverse KL, 4 rollouts per prompt, 1:1 route mix). Mixed SFT = one demo per prompt (E's and E_2's sample 0 from k=8 pools). Mixed SFT-RS = the first sample per prompt in index order that is execution-correct (CruxEval) or accepted by the implemented answer selector (MMLU-Pro) from the same k=8 pools (1,503 + 1,400 covered prompts; uncovered prompts stay in every denominator). Merges = #9974 tools, B anchor, E and E_2 donors: task arithmetic at a = b = 0.5 and a = b = 1.0, and TIES (density 0.5, a = b = 1.0); CPU only.

## Frozen evaluator

Evalchemy [`ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8) (recorded in every record's `eval_runtime`; the `c131e5ab` label in earlier text was an unused code constant and has been corrected in #9920), vLLM H100x8 DP8+EP8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap (28,672 for GPQA-D), thinking on, unseeded sampling at temperature 1.0. MMLU-Pro runs score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record's active FineStore snapshot against the canonical gold; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro (subset 1,589, held-out 10,212) and problems within each CruxEval direction (800), conditional on the observed sampled completions; they do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability. At ae362881, MMLU-Pro extraction uses final content when available, falls back to reasoning for REASONING_ONLY responses, and returns no answer for truncated reasoning-only responses; it applies `final_response_text`, then the three answer-letter regexes, and uppercases the result. Exact replay reproduced native predictions on all 12,032 rows of each of B-220c, E_2-254, RS-727 and MOPD-100. The broader matrix has uniform runtime-revision metadata; it was not replayed in full. The stored normalized output is not always the scorer input (the scorer saw the parser-split final content), so re-grading must start from the native completions. All comparisons are paired on the same docs.

## Paired deltas (pp, 95% bootstrap)

All plain-803-versus-other-model intervals below use its pass 1; both passes are shown in the tables, and selection uses their mean. The following CruxEval-versus-E deltas use E's first CruxEval pass (635/800 input, 562/800 output), not the two-pass E mean displayed in the table; plain-803 deltas here use its first pass, and both plain passes are reported together for selection.
