## Reading the result

(1) At RS-727 and MOPD-100, both domains improve over B. Relative to the specialists, MOPD's MMLU-Pro subset difference from E_2 is −2.24 pp [−4.47, +0.06], while RS's is +1.74 pp with an interval spanning zero. Intervals spanning zero do not establish preservation or equivalence. Both checkpoints have higher CruxEval output scores than E's first pass; their input differences from E are unresolved. Paired changes versus B on each split: MOPD-100 +19.7 pp on the subset and +20.3 on the held-out docs; RS-727 +23.7 and +20.7. (2) RS-SFT and MOPD differ by domain: RS higher on the MMLU-Pro subset, MOPD higher on CruxEval input, output unresolved. RS-SFT had ground-truth verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and an unequal token budget; MOPD had on-policy samples scored by the teachers. Neither is a matched control for the other. (3) Plain mixed SFT recovers less than either (MMLU-Pro −5.8 pp vs RS; CruxEval below E on input). (4) Merging recovers CruxEval input (76.5 at a = b = 0.5) and most of MMLU-Pro (63.2) with no training, but its CruxEval output (67.6) is 2.6 pp below E's first pass (70.25), 3.8 below E's two-pass mean (71.4), 8.8 below MOPD-100 (76.4), 9.65 below RS-727 (77.25) and 3.9 below plain-803's first pass (71.5); TIES output (68.1) sits 0.5 pp above TA-0.5 on each of those comparisons; at full strength (a = b = 1.0) the merge shows a large regression on valid GSM8K (50.0) and GPQA-D (30.0) evaluations with unusually long outputs (median 85–95k characters), so it was withheld from the rest of the matrix. (5) Probes on the two finals (single pass each; 0 infrastructure-error rows; MATH500 median output 2,496 and 1,525 characters): RS-727 MATH500 92.4, GPQA-D 57.6, IFEval instruction-strict 78.3 (below B with the interval excluding 0: −2.76 [−5.21, −0.24]; loose −0.36 [−2.66, +2.03]); MOPD-100 MATH500 90.0, GPQA-D 47.5, IFEval 80.0 (−1.08 [−3.59, +1.21] vs B). RS-727's GPQA-D score is above every other model in this matrix (B 41.9, E 44.8, E_2 47.6, MOPD-100 47.5, merges 47.1–47.3); it is one evaluation with three generations for each of 198 questions and is reported with its paired interval, not interpreted.

## Caveats

One pass per checkpoint except the explicitly reported repeats; plain 603/803 selection uses per-item two-pass means. Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons and checkpoint selection; additional-probe findings are exploratory. Targets are 800 problems per CruxEval direction and 1,606 docs; intervals resample question-text groups for MMLU-Pro and problems within each CruxEval direction, conditional on the observed sampled completions, and do not estimate generation or training run-to-run variability (E's two CruxEval passes differed by 0.1 / 2.25 pp in #9920). The MMLU-Pro subset was the fine-tuning set for E_2 and the training prompt set for every arm; the 10,426 held-out docs are an additional probe, reported and never used for selection. RS demo selector mismatch: the k=8 demo grader implemented the older first-match-anywhere extractor on the whole text, while the evaluator grades the final answer after the think block; under the evaluator's rule 14 of the 1,400 selected RS MMLU-Pro demos (1.0%) are wrong, 15 more prompts would have been covered and 1 lost, and 45 prompts would have used a different sample. The RS arm is reported as trained; no corrected run was made. Record provenance: two records (B MMLU-Pro and MOPD-100 MMLU-Pro) had a retried eval attempt that left a second full sample stream; all numbers here come from each record's pinned active FineStore manifest (HEAD), with the native writer taken from the active source-blob provenance (normalized sample rows can carry null correctness); superseded attempts are kept as overhead and evidence, not as independent repeats (an earlier reading of the first stream gave B 43.90 and MOPD-100 65.32 on the subset and has been superseded). Three merge MATH500 records from 2026-10-10 are invalid (Evalchemy `AgentTimeoutError` in 500/500, 455/500 and 300/500 rows) and were rerun for TA-0.5 and TIES; TA-1.0 was not rerun.

**Costs (H100-hours = GPUs × Iris task or attempt duration; method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298; every figure labelled by what it includes).** Training-gang allocations (image pull, load, steps, in-gang checkpoint/HF export and teardown; queue time excluded): E_2 60.6 (3 epochs, 32 H100). Mixed SFT-RS 93.57 (728 updates, 32 H100). Mixed SFT 107.83, plus 14.21 for a first attempt evicted by Kueue after 16 updates and relaunched from B. MOPD 557.9 for the 2-epoch run (100 optimizer updates, 7 × H100x8; the launch plan said ≈102, the sampler yielded 50 full windows per epoch; the W&B run `skyrl/snowball-mopd2-cruxeval-mmlupro-2ep` logged 99 steps and is marked `crashed`; coordinator logs record 100 updates and the terminal export at global_step 100 succeeded), plus 28.3 in two separate export-only jobs (step-50 13.8, step-100 14.5), which the SFT figures include in-gang; allocation to the step-50 checkpoint ≈ 317 and to step-100 ≈ 531 from timestamps (full run, not pro-rated). E_2 k=8 demo pool 8.91 (counted once, shared by both SFT arms; #9920's CruxEval pool is reused and its cost stays in #9920). Merges: CPU only (33, 28 and 68 min). Excluded from every total: GLM trace generation, E's construction (#9920), CPU preparation and audit jobs, the MOPD smoke run (≈60.6, reported in the design ledger). Evaluation serve allocation (serve attempt `started_at`→`finished_at` × 8 H100; queue time and CPU eval tasks excluded; two sweeps, 2026-10-13 05:20 and 11:40 UTC, 82 groups): 1,752.6 H100-h. Of this, 858.2 belongs to 51 groups with at least one successful eval child, including groups with invalid or superseded records; 894.5 belongs to 31 groups with no successful eval child. Per evaluated model (record / no-record): B 121.7 / 0; E 46.2 / 0; E_2 167.5 / 284.9; mixed plain 111.7 / 0; mixed RS 73.3 / 13.6; MOPD 112.0 / 0 (the step-50 retry alone 72.4: its MMLU-Pro eval ran 8 h 41 min without errors); merge TA-0.5 94.4 / 231.6; merge TA-1.0 79.9 / 241.6; merge TIES 51.6 / 122.7. Eight serves ran 13.8–14.6 h (110–117 H100-h each): six in the no-record bucket (`20261010-043736` E_2-85 MMLU-Pro, `20261010-030122` and `…030230` TA-1.0, `20261010-042000` and `…042104` TA-0.5, `20261010-042136` TIES; 689.4 together) and two in the record bucket (B's MMLU-Pro group `20261007-172014-…-9225`, 116.9, whose MMLU-Pro eval ran two attempts while its GPQA-D eval failed; E_2-85's `20261010-003548`, 110.3). Several of these groups have documented stale-endpoint failures after a serve preemption (#10030; its fix #10033 was not applied to this frozen evaluator), and B's group is documented as an eval retry after `PodDeleted`; the totals include all serve allocation regardless of cause, and the per-group attribution is only as complete as the overhead ledger's entries. These are infrastructure allocation costs, not inference-compute estimates. For scale, the #9984 training-gang allocations listed above sum to 834.1 H100-h (E_2 60.6 + RS 93.57 + plain 122.04 + MOPD 557.9), plus 28.3 of MOPD export-only jobs and 8.91 for the demo pool.

## Hugging Face weights

All evaluated checkpoints are public under open-athena (model cards carry recipe, scores and S3 source):

topics.title: [ci] Instrument the levanter-tpu setup to locate the pre-uv stall
topics.body:
Some levanter-tpu jobs print nothing for 2 to 19 minutes between "Using Docker image" and uv's first line. Job 112705467654 was silent from 08:39:02 to 08:56:51 on 2026-10-07 and was later cancelled at the job time limit.

The stall only happens on TPU VMs in their first hours. Across 756 levanter-tpu jobs from 2026-09-28 to 2026-10-09, it hit 11 of 83 jobs that started within an hour of the VM's first job, 1 of 76 between one and three hours, and 0 of 510 after that. It affected 9 of the 51 VMs seen. Before #9899, package installs showed the same pattern: the 90th-percentile install took 1,123 s in a VM's first hour and 96 s after three hours. Both point at a slow boot disk on new VMs. Two causes fit. The startup script writes the Docker image, a 4.7 GB uv cache and a copied venv just before the runner registers. A disk created from an image may also read slowly until it is fully copied. Stalls 20 to 66 minutes after a VM's first job favour the second. On two VMs older than 15 hours, a 256 MB O_DIRECT probe wrote at 133 to 135 MB/s and read at 102 to 110 MB/s.

This branch instruments the step. Every run records dirty and writeback memory, per-disk I/O counters and the probe; on a VM older than two hours it then exits. On a younger VM it repeats the container setup three times. Each attempt prints a marker after container start, venv removal and the workspace copy, and runs uv with -v. A host sampler prints processes with their kernel wait channel every 30 s while pytest is not running. The TPU job runs only test_jax_utils.py. GitHub timestamps every log line, so the markers carry no dates.

Not for merge. No run has landed on a VM under two hours old yet. A candidate fix is to have the startup script in infra/tpu-ci/vm_manager.py flush writes and read the whole boot disk before it registers the runner.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the Taskforge pipeline skeleton
topics.body:
This draft is kept as the reference implementation of Taskforge and as the surface for its line-by-line review. A minimal PR cut from main supersedes it for merge: it adds the real GLM client through Ortet and an experiment that prompts GLM with a catalog.json entry to write a program, runs the program in Shellbox and saves the TaskSpec the program emits. The follow-ups are cut from this draft, roughly one per stage: proposal, triage, builder author and builder runtime, validate, review, the stage coordinator, the ledger if it is still needed, and Zephyr. The inline review comments on this draft are their to-do list, and each comment names the PR that fixes it. The branch is not rewritten, so the comments stay anchored to 8dbf74d5.

The draft adds lib/taskforge, the task-generation library, and experiments/post_training/capability_driven_envs, which runs it over the capability catalog with scripted models and in-process ShellSim.

A build program is a DAG of pure steps with one sink. Steps declare their inputs, and a step's cache key is its own source plus the digests of its inputs, so editing one step reruns only it and the steps downstream of it. The proposal is a declarable input; steps that do not read it keep their cache across proposal changes. One runner sequences the steps and records them. The library ships no concrete steps.

Taskforge is a state machine over stages: triage, author, build, validate, review and done, with the edges as a transition table and an item's state as a pure fold over its JSONL event log. The caller passes the stage functions as a typed bundle, so the type checker validates the composition; the loop coordinates them, records one event per stage and resumes an interrupted item from its log. Run inputs are pinned to the run root: the policy, including the session limits validation imposes on every trial, is written once, and a relaunch with a different policy or a changed idea record is refused. The modify edge from review back to the author is in the table and never taken here.

Proposals and build call models through one surface, ModelClient, and every call is recorded with its item, round and step. Validation runs the solver through RolloutEngine: a ModelFactory builds one rollout model per trial from the policy's sampling. Triage accepts every proposal, validation lowers the task onto ShellSim and runs k solver trials, and review decides from the band rules. A grading infrastructure error retries the trial; it does not reject the task.

Taskforge is a root-lock workspace member with a dedicated CI suite, as RolloutEngine is. The draft has no GLM client (only the ModelClient protocol and NoModel), no reference step SDK, no triage repair, no controls or adversary trials, and no queue or Docker machines.

topics.title: [zephyr] Add opt-in intra-shard map execution
topics.body:
Add `ZephyrContext(intra_shard_execution=IntraShardExecution.AUTO)` to execute row maps, filters, selections, and flat maps within an existing shard across workers. Callbacks must not depend on per-shard mutable state. The default is `OFF`. The planner adds `Split → Map → Concat` when Parquet source fragments can feed idle workers or a later reshard leaves fewer shards than workers. It reads footer row counts and aims for four source tasks per worker, capped at one task per row. There is no byte minimum because row callbacks can be expensive inference calls. Existing source shards that fill the worker pool keep fused row execution. Maps following `group_by` stay on whole output shards. Ordered concatenation restores original shard IDs, row order, and output filenames before shard-level operations and writes.

Maps immediately preceding an explicit-schema Parquet sink produce Parquet fragments for an Arrow-batch final writer. Other map intermediates use pickle chunks. Concatenation avoids a key shuffle, but final assembly still decodes and re-encodes Parquet. Batch-mode sources retain their batch boundaries, and `map_shard` callbacks remain indivisible.

Fixed local samples from TaskTrove dataset revision `02923004846e4e73862c20962f823a6d05100e7a`, each with one row group, used [conversion code at ee20e03517](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ee20e03517/experiments/post_training/task_curation) through Zephyr's `SubprocessRunner`. All columns use `AUTO`; one worker retains fused execution. Single-run wall times on a shared Ryzen 7 3800X include startup, intermediate I/O, final write, and shutdown:

| Sample | Rows | 1 worker | 2 workers | 4 workers |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Structured outputs | 10,000 | 79.81s | 58.77s | 34.93s |
| SWE-smith | 2,000 | 33.93s | 31.09s | 21.83s |
| SWE-rebench | 2,000 | 19.90s | 23.33s | 20.37s |
| TACO | 2,000 | 68.80s | 36.74s | 24.44s |

All runs matched the one-worker baseline's complete record content, rejection outcomes, source order, and single output file layout. Four-worker final Parquet read/write took 3.47–9.75s; SWE-rebench showed no end-to-end improvement. Peak summed process-tree RSS ranged from 2.25 to 3.00 GiB at four workers. Workers still read overlapping row groups in full, so row offsets increase read work and memory. Host load varied during these runs; they are not stable throughput estimates. These runs used the earlier source task sizing; the four-task target has not been benchmarked. The sizing design and edge cases are recorded in the [design artifact](https://loom.oa.dev/s/68n20qo1/artifacts/design).

comments.body:
> Parallelism sizing - I would worry most about splitting input files too finely. Maybe we can set a minimum size when cutting them into fragments?

We can - I also don't think we need to make this setting the default. I observed the current behavior slowing down some of the curation pipelines. There you often have a single parquet file with 1 million records, and the current `map` behavior won't parallelize across it.

> If we're worker-bound (e.g., as many shards as workers) then we add a bunch of i/o overhead without benefit. from what I can tell.

Yes, I think this is the right heuristic: we should split to feed the workers, not more than that.

> so in combination with setting the the parallelism factor to worker_limit with AUTO, could this result in many small files? E.g., 10 files and 1000 workers.

> row_groups_in_span,                            # never cut inside a row group
>         max(1, span_bytes // MIN_FRAGMENT_BYTES))      # e.g. 64 MiB minimum per fragment

This is actually for cases where you have a small amount of data but the processing is expensive (in this case we're running GLM inference over every row). Many of the files only have a single row-group, and they might only be 100MB total, so we actually want to split aggressively.

The concatenation phase should resolve the number of files issue in general.

@weaverbot can you review the comments and make some of the requested changes. My proposal is that we have the controller analyze the parquets and:

* when splitting is active, try to split to workers * N shards, with N being something like 4 to allow load balancing
* don't split beyond the capacity of the input, so no zero row inputs etc

give me an artifact with your design and analysis as well as updating the PR

The advisory review's stale descriptions were corrected in a follow-up commit. All 36 CI checks passed or were skipped on the updated branch; GitHub shows the PR approved.

topics.title: [iris] Cached job env reaches child jobs after the job scrubs its secrets
topics.body:
Iris caches a job's environment before the job's own code runs, so a job that scrubs secrets from `os.environ` and `IRIS_JOB_ENV` at startup still hands the unscrubbed environment to any non-sandbox child job it launches.

Observed on `cw-us-east-02a` during a Zephyr feasibility spike for Taskforge: the Taskforge queue job removes `GLM_API_TOKEN`, `WANDB_API_KEY` and the other host secrets from its environment at start (`scrub_child_environment`), and afterwards both `os.environ` and `IRIS_JOB_ENV` are clean. The job environment Iris had already cached still held `GLM_API_TOKEN` and `WANDB_API_KEY`, so a non-sandbox child job would inherit them. Sandbox children (ShellSim, bwrap, gVisor) received no env in this run; gVisor sandboxes did see the `IRIS_*` variables and the Kubernetes service addresses, including the controller's.

Asks: (1) a documented way for a job to launch children with an explicit environment that does not include the parent's cached env (an allowlist on the child job spec, or a per-submission `inherit_env=False`); (2) sandbox pods should not receive `IRIS_*` variables or the controller's service address unless the submitter asks for them, since model-controlled code runs there.

Related earlier notes on the Taskforge side: CoreWeave `task_env` injecting object-store keys into pods (not reproduced on `cw-rno2a` in this spike) and child jobs inheriting a parent's explicit `-e` secrets.

evalchemy209.title: Make Evalchemy results and resume state FineStore native
evalchemy209.body:
Write evaluation aggregates, normalized samples, and request checkpoints directly to FineStore. The evaluator restores committed requests by default and skips a completed result before model setup. Results and samples enter the archive in one transaction, so a retry leaves a completed result unchanged.

`--output_path` and `--finestore_output_path` now select the same FineStore archive. Existing scripts keep `--output_path` and use distinct archive paths for distinct evaluations. Remove native JSON/JSONL result serialization, SQLite resume state, and temporary output staging. The serve-and-eval runner and regression gate read the same archive. Concurrent writers to one archive have not been exercised locally.

Part of marin-community/marin#9972. The Marin retry work is tracked in marin-community/marin#9813.
